questions.a: He says he is 'inclined to reserve all judgments,' yet in Ch. 1 alone he judges Tom as brutal and arrogant and Daisy and Jordan as careless; he judges constantly, so the reader must be cautious.

days.guide: Reread the end of Ch. 1. Model the first row of the symbol tracker for the green light, then have the student map East Egg, West Egg, and New York on a sketch and add them to the tracker.

questions.q: What is the green light and what does it suggest?
questions.a: The light at the end of Daisy's dock across the bay; Gatsby stretches his arms toward it, suggesting his longing for Daisy and, more broadly, a dream that is always just out of reach.

days.guide: Read Ch. 2. Have the student describe the Valley of Ashes in their own words and explain why Fitzgerald places it between the Eggs and New York. Today's task from the plan: Read the Valley of Ashes chapter; explain the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What do the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg suggest?
questions.a: They are on a faded billboard above the Valley of Ashes, staring over a gray, morally empty world; they suggest an absent God or a watching conscience that no one heeds.

questions.q: What happens at the end of Ch. 2 in the apartment?
questions.a: Tom breaks Myrtle's nose with his open hand when she keeps shouting Daisy's name, showing his violence and control.

days.guide: Read Ch. 3, Gatsby's party. The student lists every rumor about Gatsby and notes how Nick first meets him. Today's task from the plan: Read Gatsby's party; collect rumors about Gatsby and evaluate Nick's reliability. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: List two rumors guests tell about Gatsby.
questions.a: That he once killed a man and that he was a German spy during the war (others say he went to Oxford).

days.guide: Give a 10-question reading quiz, then the student writes a paragraph on how setting (the Eggs, the Valley of Ashes) comments on class. Today's task from the plan: Reading quiz Ch. 1–3 and a paragraph on setting as social commentary. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How is Nick related to Daisy?
questions.a: She is his second cousin once removed (his cousin).

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz key: 1) Nick Carraway, from the Midwest, sells bonds. 2) He rents in West Egg. 3) Daisy is his cousin. 4) Tom Buchanan is a wealthy former Yale football player. 5) Jordan Baker is a professional golfer. 6) Myrtle Wilson is Tom's mistress; George Wilson runs a garage in the Valley of Ashes. 7) Eckleburg's eyes are on a billboard. 8) Tom breaks Myrtle's nose. 9) Gatsby throws lavish parties. 10) Nick meets Gatsby without recognizing him. Setting paragraph rubric (4-point): claim about class; two quotations (e.g., the Valley of Ashes as 'a fantastic farm where ashes grow'); explanation of how place reflects class division; conventions.

weeks.prep: Finish The Great Gatsby (Ch. 4–9). Find the party or ending scene from the 1974 (Robert Redford) and 2013 (Baz Luhrmann) films. Print an argument rubric.
misconceptions: Saying Gatsby killed Myrtle. Daisy was driving Gatsby's car; Gatsby lets others believe he was, which leads Wilson to him.
Treating Gatsby as purely heroic or purely fraudulent. Nick says he is 'worth the whole damn bunch put together' while also showing his ties to the criminal Wolfsheim; a strong essay holds both.

days.guide: Read Ch. 4–5. The student compares Gatsby's story of himself (Ch. 4) with what Ch. 6 later reveals, and tracks the weather during the reunion at Nick's house.

questions.q: How does the weather mirror the reunion in Ch. 5?
questions.a: It is pouring rain while the meeting is awkward and tense; as Gatsby and Daisy reconcile the rain stops and the sun comes out, matching Gatsby's joy.

days.guide: Read Ch. 6–7. Trace the Plaza Hotel confrontation and how Tom attacks Gatsby as new money. Today's task from the plan: Read; trace the confrontation at the Plaza and how money divides 'old' and 'new' wealth. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Gatsby mean when he says Daisy's voice is 'full of money'?
questions.a: Her charm is inseparable from her wealth and class; what he loves in her is tied to the status he wants.

questions.q: Who is driving when Myrtle is killed?
questions.a: Daisy, driving Gatsby's yellow car; Gatsby plans to take the blame.

days.guide: Read Ch. 8–9. Have the student annotate the last page and the 'careless people' paragraph. Today's task from the plan: Finish the novel; annotate the final page's 'boats against the current' passage. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Interpret 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'
questions.a: People keep striving toward the future but are constantly pulled back by the past; Gatsby's dream of repeating the past was impossible.

questions.q: Why does Nick call Tom and Daisy 'careless people'?
questions.a: They 'smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money,' letting others (Gatsby, Myrtle, Wilson) pay for their actions.

days.guide: Watch the same scene from both films. The student charts music, color, narration, and casting and decides which version better captures Fitzgerald's critique.

questions.q: What should a strong film comparison evaluate?
questions.a: Specific choices (e.g., Luhrmann's modern hip-hop soundtrack and spectacle vs. the 1974 film's restraint) and whether each criticizes or glamorizes the excess the novel critiques.

days.guide: The student writes the 900-word literary argument (critique or celebration of the American Dream), including a counterclaim. Today's task from the plan: Write a 900-word literary argument: Is The Great Gatsby a critique or a celebration of the American Dream?. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Give a strong thesis for the critique side.
questions.a: Fitzgerald critiques the American Dream: Gatsby's self-made wealth cannot buy acceptance or Daisy, and the 'careless' rich escape all consequences while Gatsby dies alone.

weeks.assessment_key: Literary argument on Gatsby rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper takes a clear position, uses at least four quotations (e.g., the green light, 'careless people,' Daisy's voice 'full of money,' the final 'boats against the current'), and answers a counterclaim about Gatsby's 'extraordinary gift for hope.'

weeks.prep: Print Hughes ('The Negro Speaks of Rivers,' 'Harlem,' 'I, Too,' 'The Weary Blues'), McKay ('If We Must Die'), Cullen ('Incident'), and Hurston ('How It Feels to Be Colored Me'). Have a classic blues recording ready (e.g., Bessie Smith). Parent note: 'Incident' contains a racial slur; discuss before reading.
misconceptions: Thinking traditional forms can't carry protest. McKay's Shakespearean sonnet uses a formal, dignified structure to call for resistance after the violence of 1919's Red Summer.
Reading Hurston's essay as bitter or angry. Her tone is confident and playful: 'I am not tragically colored.'

days.guide: Read the four Hughes poems aloud. Play a blues song and have the student mark the AAB stanza (line repeated, then answered) in 'The Weary Blues.' Today's task from the plan: Read three Hughes poems; listen to a blues recording and identify blues structure in 'The Weary Blues'. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What do the rivers in 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers' represent?
questions.a: The Euphrates, Congo, Nile, and Mississippi trace the long history of people of African descent; 'My soul has grown deep like the rivers' claims ancient endurance and dignity.

questions.q: What is the effect of the questions in 'Harlem'?
questions.a: Each simile ('dry up / like a raisin in the sun,' 'fester like a sore') imagines a consequence of a delayed dream, building to the final warning: 'Or does it explode?'

days.guide: Read 'If We Must Die' and 'Incident.' The student identifies each form (sonnet; ballad quatrains) and explains how form carries protest. Today's task from the plan: Read 'If We Must Die' (sonnet) and 'Incident'; compare how traditional forms carry protest. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What happens in 'Incident'?
questions.a: The eight-year-old speaker, riding in Baltimore, smiles at a white boy who sticks out his tongue and calls him a slur; of his whole stay, 'That's all that I remember,' showing how one act of racism lasts.

days.guide: Read Hurston's essay. The student marks shifts in tone and explains two figures of speech. Today's task from the plan: Read 'How It Feels to Be Colored Me'; analyze tone and figurative language. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Explain 'I do not weep at the world—I am too busy sharpening my oyster knife.'
questions.a: She refuses self-pity; the world is an oyster full of opportunity, and she is preparing to seize it.

questions.q: What does 'I feel most colored when I am thrown against a sharp white background' mean?
questions.a: Her race feels significant only when others' contrast and prejudice make it so; it is not a constant burden.

days.guide: The student researches one Harlem Renaissance figure (writer, musician, painter) using two reliable sources and builds 5 slides. Today's task from the plan: Research one Harlem Renaissance artist (writer, musician, painter) and build a 5-slide presentation. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Name three Harlem Renaissance figures besides Hughes.
questions.a: Zora Neale Hurston (writer), Duke Ellington (musician), Aaron Douglas (painter); others include Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, and Jessie Fauset.

days.guide: The student presents for 5 minutes and answers two questions; then give a short quiz on the poems. Today's task from the plan: Deliver a 5-minute multimedia presentation and answer questions; quiz on the poems. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the closing claim of 'I, Too'?
questions.a: 'I, too, am America': though sent 'to eat in the kitchen,' the speaker will sit 'at the table' tomorrow and claims equal belonging.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (4-point): accurate content with two cited sources; at least one example of the artist's work explained; clear visuals; confident delivery and answers to questions. Poetry quiz key: 1) 'Harlem' asks what happens to a dream deferred. 2) 'I, Too' claims equality. 3) 'If We Must Die' is a Shakespearean sonnet answering the 1919 riots. 4) 'Incident' uses ballad stanzas. 5) Blues lyric form = AAB. 6) Hurston's tone = confident, humorous.

weeks.prep: Hemingway's 'Hills Like White Elephants' and Faulkner's 'A Rose for Emily' (library anthology). Parent note: Hemingway's story centers on an implied abortion; Faulkner's ending implies Emily slept beside a corpse. Preview both.
misconceptions: Expecting Hemingway to state the conflict. His 'iceberg' method leaves most meaning beneath the surface; the reader infers from dialogue.
Reading 'A Rose for Emily' as if events were in order. Faulkner scrambles chronology to delay the revelation and mimic town memory.

days.guide: Read 'Hills' aloud as a dialogue (you read the man, the student reads Jig). The student lists everything never stated and infers the conflict. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Hills Like White Elephants'; list what is never stated and infer the conflict from dialogue alone. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is the 'awfully simple operation' the man keeps mentioning?
questions.a: It is implied to be an abortion; the man pressures Jig while she seems to want the baby and a different life.

questions.q: Why does Jig say 'Would you please please please please please please please stop talking?'
questions.a: The repetition shows her frustration with his insistent reassurances; she sees through him.

days.guide: Read 'A Rose for Emily.' The student reconstructs the true chronology on a timeline and compares it to the story's order. Today's task from the plan: Read 'A Rose for Emily'; reconstruct the chronology on a timeline and explain the effect of the nonlinear order. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is found in Emily's house after her funeral?
questions.a: Homer Barron's decayed body in the bridal room, and a long strand of iron-gray hair on the pillow beside it, revealing she poisoned him and lay beside him for years.

days.guide: Discuss the narrator 'we.' The student finds three places where 'we' reveals the town's attitudes. Today's task from the plan: Analyze the communal narrator in 'Emily' and how it builds suspense. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does Faulkner use the communal narrator 'we'?
questions.a: It represents the town's gossiping collective voice, which both pities and spies on Emily; its partial knowledge builds suspense until the end.

days.guide: Review Hemingway's style rules. The student writes a 500-word scene using only dialogue and gesture, implying (not stating) the conflict. Today's task from the plan: Write a 500-word scene in Hemingway's minimalist style using only dialogue and gesture. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: List three features of Hemingway's minimalist style.
questions.a: Short declarative sentences, dialogue carrying the meaning, and no direct statement of characters' emotions.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test: an unseen Modernist passage plus terms. Today's task from the plan: Unit 6 test: unseen Modernist passage analysis plus terms. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is Hemingway's 'iceberg theory'?
questions.a: Like an iceberg, most of a story's meaning lies beneath the surface; the writer omits what readers can feel without being told.

weeks.assessment_key: Style imitation rubric (4-point): conflict clearly implied but never named; mostly dialogue and gesture; short, plain sentences; an ending that resonates. Unit 6 test key: Modernism traits (fragmentation, alienation, experimentation); iceberg theory; stream of consciousness; nonlinear chronology; communal narrator; unseen passage answers must cite lines and identify implied meaning.

weeks.prep: A public library card for database access (Gale, JSTOR free articles, EBSCO). Purdue OWL MLA 9 guide. A research folder or document.
misconceptions: Choosing too broad a topic ('the 1920s'). Narrow to a specific, arguable question linking one author to one context.
Trusting a source because it is first in search results or looks professional. Evaluate every source with the CRAAP test.

days.guide: Brainstorm 10 author-plus-context pairs from the year (e.g., Miller and McCarthyism, Hansberry and redlining). Model narrowing one into a question that can be argued, then let the student narrow their own.

questions.q: Narrow 'Fitzgerald and the 1920s' into a research question.
questions.a: Example: 'How did Prohibition-era bootlegging shape Fitzgerald's portrayal of new money in The Great Gatsby?'

days.guide: Show how to log in to the library databases and use keywords with AND/OR. The student finds six sources, including two scholarly articles. Today's task from the plan: Use public library databases to locate at least six sources, including two scholarly articles. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What makes a source scholarly?
questions.a: It is written by experts, usually peer-reviewed, published in an academic journal or press, and cites its own sources.

days.guide: Model the CRAAP test on one source. The student rates all six and discards weak ones. Today's task from the plan: Apply the CRAAP test to each source and discard weak ones. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does CRAAP stand for?
questions.a: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

days.guide: Model one MLA 9 entry and annotation. The student writes five. Today's task from the plan: Write MLA 9 entries with 3-sentence annotations for five sources. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What should a three-sentence annotation do?
questions.a: Summarize the source's main point, evaluate its credibility, and explain how it will be used in the paper.

days.guide: The student submits question, working thesis, and annotated bibliography; give written feedback within two days. Today's task from the plan: Submit research question, working thesis, and annotated bibliography for feedback. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is a working thesis?
questions.a: A tentative, arguable answer to the research question that will guide (and may change during) research.

weeks.assessment_key: Annotated bibliography rubric (4-point): 4 = five correct MLA 9 entries (author, title, container, publisher/date, URL or DOI), alphabetized with hanging indents, at least two scholarly sources, annotations that summarize, evaluate, and state use; 3 = minor format errors; 2 = annotations summary-only or fewer scholarly sources; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Research notes and sources; an outline template. Notecards or a digital notes document with columns for source, page, note type.
misconceptions: Patchwriting (swapping a few words while keeping the source's sentence structure). Teach read–cover–write–compare and always cite paraphrases.
'Dropping' quotations into paragraphs with no introduction. Every quotation needs a signal phrase and analysis after it.

days.guide: Model one note of each type (quotation, paraphrase, summary), each labeled with source and page. The student takes notes from three sources. Today's task from the plan: Take notes using quotation, paraphrase, and summary, labeling each with source and page. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What is the difference between a paraphrase and a summary?
questions.a: A paraphrase restates a specific passage in your own words at about the same length; a summary condenses the main ideas of a longer section. Both must be cited.

days.guide: Give three tricky passages. The student paraphrases from memory, then compares with the original to find borrowed phrasing. Today's task from the plan: Practice paraphrasing three tricky passages and compare with originals to avoid patchwriting. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Is changing a few words of a source sentence an acceptable paraphrase?
questions.a: No. That is patchwriting; a true paraphrase changes both wording and sentence structure, and it still needs a citation.

days.guide: Model one outline section (sub-claim, evidence A and B, analysis). The student completes a full outline. Today's task from the plan: Build a detailed outline with thesis, sub-claims, and assigned evidence. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What belongs in each body section of the outline?
questions.a: A sub-claim supporting the thesis, the specific evidence assigned to it (with sources), and a note on the analysis connecting evidence to claim.

days.guide: The student drafts the introduction and first two sections (about 1,000 words) with signal phrases and in-text citations. Today's task from the plan: Draft introduction and first two body sections (about 1,000 words) with signal phrases and in-text citations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Write a model signal phrase with MLA citation.
questions.a: As historian Lizabeth Cohen argues, '...' (Cohen 45). Or: Fitzgerald describes the valley as 'a fantastic farm where ashes grow' (Fitzgerald 23).

days.guide: The student drafts the remaining sections and conclusion and submits the full 1,800–2,200 word rough draft. Today's task from the plan: Draft remaining sections and conclusion; submit full rough draft (1,800–2,200 words). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should a research paper's conclusion do?
questions.a: Restate the thesis in fresh words, synthesize the main points, and explain the significance or a broader implication; no new evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Rough draft checkpoint (complete/incomplete with comments): 1,800–2,200 words; clear thesis in the introduction; every body section has a sub-claim, cited evidence, and analysis; signal phrases and MLA in-text citations; Works Cited draft. Flag any uncited paraphrase immediately.

weeks.prep: Word processor; slide software. Print the MLA sample paper from Purdue OWL for format comparison.
misconceptions: Thinking revision means fixing commas. Revision means rethinking structure and argument; editing (commas, spelling) comes last.
Overloading slides with paragraphs. Slides support the speaker; one idea and a visual per slide.

days.guide: Model a reverse outline: one sentence summarizing what each paragraph DOES. The student checks each against the thesis and moves, cuts, or rewrites. Today's task from the plan: Reverse-outline the draft; revise so each paragraph advances the thesis. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is a reverse outline used for?
questions.a: To see the draft's actual structure, spot paragraphs that don't advance the thesis, and reorder for logic.

days.guide: Line-edit two paragraphs together for wordiness and passive voice. Teach compound-modifier hyphens. Today's task from the plan: Edit for concision, active voice, and varied syntax; check hyphenation of compound modifiers. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Correct the hyphenation: 'a well known author' and 'the author is well-known.'
questions.a: 'A well-known author' (hyphenated before the noun); 'the author is well known' (no hyphen after the noun).

days.guide: Format to MLA 9 (header, title, double spacing, Works Cited). The student checks every quotation against its source. Today's task from the plan: Format to MLA 9 with Works Cited; run a self-check for plagiarism and citation accuracy. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Format an MLA in-text citation for page 180 of Gatsby.
questions.a: (Fitzgerald 180) — author's last name and page, no comma, inside the sentence's period.

days.guide: The student builds a 6-minute presentation (6–8 slides) and practices twice with a timer. Today's task from the plan: Create a 6-minute presentation of findings with visuals and practice delivery. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What makes slides effective?
questions.a: Few words, one idea per slide, readable fonts, and relevant images or data with sources.

days.guide: Collect the paper; the student presents and takes questions. Today's task from the plan: Submit final research paper and deliver the presentation with Q&A. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How should a presenter handle a question they can't answer?
questions.a: Acknowledge it honestly, offer what they do know, and explain how they would find the answer.

weeks.assessment_key: Final paper rubric (4-point per row): Thesis (arguable, specific); Evidence (credible, cited, integrated); Analysis (explains significance, connects to literary text); Organization (logical, transitions); MLA format and conventions. Proficient = clear thesis supported by at least five credible sources with accurate citations. Presentation rubric: content accuracy, visuals, delivery (eye contact, pace), and Q&A.

weeks.prep: Lorraine Hansberry's A Raisin in the Sun (library). Hughes' 'Harlem' (the play's title source). A short article on redlining and restrictive covenants in Chicago. Parent note: Ruth considers an abortion in Act I.
misconceptions: Seeing Walter only as selfish. His dream grows from frustration with limited opportunity as a chauffeur; the play asks us to understand him.
Missing Lindner's euphemisms. His polite language ('our community,' 'common background') hides the demand for segregation.

days.guide: Reread 'Harlem' and read the redlining article. The student predicts which dreams the play will explore. Today's task from the plan: Reread 'Harlem'; read a short article on redlining and restrictive covenants in Chicago. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What was redlining?
questions.a: A practice in which lenders and federal maps marked Black and immigrant neighborhoods as 'hazardous,' denying mortgages and reinforcing segregation.

days.guide: Read Act I aloud in roles. The student charts each Younger's dream and conflicts. Today's task from the plan: Read Act I; chart each Younger family member's dream and conflicts. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does each family member want from the $10,000 insurance check?
questions.a: Walter: to invest in a liquor store; Beneatha: money for medical school; Mama: a house with a yard; Ruth: a better home and relief from strain.

days.guide: Model one sentence of symbol analysis. The student writes a paragraph on Mama's plant with two quotations. Today's task from the plan: Analyze Mama's plant as a symbol in a paragraph with two quotations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Mama's plant symbolize?
questions.a: Her dreams and her care for the family: it barely survives with little sunlight, just as the family's hopes survive in a cramped apartment.

days.guide: Read Act II. The student lists Lindner's euphemisms and translates each. Today's task from the plan: Read Act II; analyze Karl Lindner's visit and his euphemistic language. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Karl Lindner offer, and what does he really mean?
questions.a: The Clybourne Park Improvement Association offers to buy the house back at a profit; he means the white neighborhood doesn't want a Black family.

days.guide: Give a reading quiz; the student builds a foil chart (Walter vs. Beneatha). Today's task from the plan: Reading quiz and a character foil chart (Walter vs. Beneatha). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How are Walter and Beneatha foils?
questions.a: Walter seeks money and business success; Beneatha seeks education, identity, and her African heritage; their clashes highlight different versions of the dream.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz key: 1) South Side of Chicago. 2) $10,000 insurance check from Big Walter's death. 3) Walter wants a liquor store. 4) Beneatha wants to be a doctor. 5) Mama buys a house in Clybourne Park. 6) Joseph Asagai, Beneatha's Nigerian suitor. 7) George Murchison, wealthy suitor. 8) Karl Lindner. 9) Willy Harris runs off with the money. 10) Ruth is pregnant. Foil chart rubric: three contrasts with quotations; explanation of what the contrast shows.

weeks.prep: A Raisin in the Sun Act III; the final scene of the 1961 film (Sidney Poitier).
misconceptions: Thinking Walter's final choice is about money. He refuses Lindner's offer, choosing his family's dignity over profit.
Ignoring stage directions. Hansberry's directions (e.g., Mama returning for her plant) carry meaning.

days.guide: Read Act III. The student traces Walter's change from planning to accept Lindner's money to refusing it. Today's task from the plan: Read Act III; trace Walter's transformation and what 'come into his manhood' means. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Mama mean by 'He finally come into his manhood today'?
questions.a: Walter chooses pride and his father's legacy over money, standing up for the family's dignity and right to move.

days.guide: Watch the 1961 final scene. Compare to the script's stage directions. Today's task from the plan: Watch the 1961 film's final scene and compare it to the script's stage directions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Mama take at the very end, and why does it matter?
questions.a: She returns for her plant, showing her dream, still alive, comes with them to the new house.

days.guide: Assign roles for a 3-minute scene. Rehearse twice for subtext. Today's task from the plan: Rehearse and perform a 3-minute scene with family members, focusing on subtext. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is subtext?
questions.a: The meaning beneath the words — what a character thinks or feels but doesn't say directly.

days.guide: The student writes a 600-word theme essay connecting the play to Hughes. Today's task from the plan: Write a 600-word essay on how Hansberry answers Hughes' question 'What happens to a dream deferred?'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does the play answer 'What happens to a dream deferred?'
questions.a: Some dreams 'dry up' or 'explode' (Walter's lost investment), but the family's long-deferred dream of a home moves forward when they choose dignity.

days.guide: Collect the essay; give a short play test. Today's task from the plan: Submit essay; short test on the play. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Who steals the money?
questions.a: Willy Harris, Walter's partner, runs off with it, including Beneatha's school money.

weeks.assessment_key: Theme essay rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper connects the title to 'Harlem,' analyzes at least two characters' deferred dreams with quotations, and explains how Walter's final choice answers Hughes. Play test key: Willy Harris steals $6,500; Walter refuses Lindner; Mama's plant; Asagai's proposal; 'manhood' line; the family moves.

weeks.prep: King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (full text at the King Institute, Stanford), Malcolm X's 'The Ballot or the Bullet' (excerpt), and JFK's Inaugural Address (text and video at jfklibrary.org).
misconceptions: Seeing King's approach as passive. He defends direct action and calls himself an 'extremist for love.'
Seeing Malcolm X as only calling for violence. The speech centers on voting rights and self-defense if the ballot fails.

days.guide: Listen to the JFK Inaugural while reading. The student marks antimetabole and parallel structure. Today's task from the plan: Read/listen to the Inaugural Address; mark antimetabole and parallel structure. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give JFK's best-known antimetabole.
questions.a: 'Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country.'

questions.q: Find another example.
questions.a: 'Let us never negotiate out of fear. But let us never fear to negotiate.'

days.guide: Read the first half of the Letter. The student outlines each criticism and King's rebuttal. Today's task from the plan: Read the first half of 'Letter from Birmingham Jail'; outline how King rebuts each criticism from the clergymen. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does King answer being called an 'outsider'?
questions.a: He was invited and says 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.'

questions.q: How does King respond to 'wait'?
questions.a: 'Wait' has almost always meant 'Never'; 'justice too long delayed is justice denied.'

days.guide: Finish the Letter. Have the student explain just vs. unjust laws and King's appeal to the Founders. Today's task from the plan: Finish the Letter; analyze King's definition of just and unjust laws and his appeal to Founders. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does King define just and unjust laws?
questions.a: A just law 'squares with the moral law or the law of God'; an unjust law 'degrades human personality' and is out of harmony with moral law.

days.guide: Read the Malcolm X excerpt. The student compares purpose, audience, and tone with King. Today's task from the plan: Read 'The Ballot or the Bullet' excerpt; compare purpose and audience with King. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does 'the ballot or the bullet' mean?
questions.a: Black Americans must gain full voting rights, or else be prepared to defend themselves.

days.guide: Timed rhetorical analysis (40 min) on an excerpt from the Letter. Today's task from the plan: Timed rhetorical analysis essay (40 min) on an excerpt from the Letter. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why is the long 'when you have seen' sentence effective?
questions.a: Its accumulating examples of injustice overwhelm the reader and make 'wait' feel impossible.

weeks.assessment_key: Timed analysis rubric (4-point): identifies audience (eight clergymen and white moderates), purpose (justify direct action), analyzes at least three choices (allusion, anaphora, long periodic sentence) with quotations and effect.

weeks.prep: Print the eight UC Personal Insight Questions (universityofcalifornia.edu/apply). Amy Tan's 'Mother Tongue' as a model of voice plus one model student personal essay (many universities post examples). Sticky notes or paper for a memory map.
misconceptions: Writing a list of accomplishments (a résumé in paragraphs). Focus on one specific scene and reflect on what it reveals about the writer.
Using clichés ('hard work pays off,' 'I stepped out of my comfort zone'). Replace each with a concrete detail only this writer could include.

days.guide: Read 'Mother Tongue' and one model essay. Have the student mark where each writer narrates a scene and where they reflect, and note the ratio. Discuss what makes the voice sound like a real person.

questions.q: What makes Tan's 'Mother Tongue' a model of personal voice?
questions.a: She builds the essay on specific anecdotes (the stockbroker call, the hospital) and honest reflection on how language shaped her and her mother, in a conversational but precise style.

days.guide: Read all eight UC prompts. The student makes a memory map (people, places, challenges, turning points) and chooses two prompts that fit real stories. Today's task from the plan: Read the UC Personal Insight Questions; brainstorm with a memory map and choose two prompts. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How many UC Personal Insight Questions must applicants answer, and how long can each be?
questions.a: Four of the eight, up to 350 words each.

days.guide: Model opening a draft inside a scene ('The smoke alarm went off just as...'). The student drafts a 350-word response: about one third scene, the rest reflection and what they learned or did next.

questions.q: What should a strong personal insight response focus on?
questions.a: One specific moment or experience that shows a quality, followed by reflection on what it reveals and how it shaped later actions.

days.guide: Read the draft aloud together. The student circles vague phrases and clichés and replaces each with specific detail; cut any sentence that doesn't reveal something new.

questions.q: Revise: 'I learned a lot from volunteering.'
questions.a: Name the specific lesson and moment, e.g., 'Teaching Mr. Ruiz to video-call his granddaughter taught me to slow down and explain one step at a time.'

days.guide: Collect the polished essay; the student starts a second prompt using the same process. Today's task from the plan: Submit a polished personal insight essay and write a second draft for another prompt. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the difference between telling and showing in a personal essay?
questions.a: Telling states a trait ('I am persistent'); showing gives actions and details that let the reader see it ('I rewrote the code eleven times before the robot turned left').

weeks.assessment_key: Personal narrative rubric (4-point per row): Focus (one clear experience that answers the prompt); Specificity (concrete details, no clichés); Reflection (insight into growth and what it shows about the writer); Voice and conventions (sounds authentic, error-free, within 350 words). Proficient = a focused scene with genuine reflection and only minor wordiness.

weeks.prep: Tim O'Brien's The Things They Carried (library): the title story, 'On the Rainy River,' and 'How to Tell a True War Story'; also skim the short chapter 'Good Form.' Choose one interview from the Library of Congress Veterans History Project. Parent note: graphic war violence and strong profanity; preview.
misconceptions: Assuming every event happened to the real Tim O'Brien. The book is fiction with a narrator who shares the author's name; O'Brien deliberately blurs fact and invention.
Reading 'On the Rainy River' as a story about cowardice in combat. The narrator says going to war was his act of cowardice, because he was too embarrassed not to go.

days.guide: Read the title story. The student charts tangible burdens (weights, weapons, letters) against intangible ones (fear, grief, love, shame) with quotations.

questions.q: What does Lt. Jimmy Cross carry, and how does Ted Lavender's death change him?
questions.a: Letters and a pebble from Martha, a girl he loves; after Lavender is shot while Cross daydreams about her, he blames himself and burns her letters, resolving to be a stricter leader.

questions.q: What does 'They carried all they could bear, and then some' suggest?
questions.a: The soldiers carried emotional weight—fear, grief, shame—that exceeded even their heavy physical loads.

days.guide: Read 'On the Rainy River.' Discuss the scene in the boat with Elroy Berdahl near the Canadian shore. Today's task from the plan: Read 'On the Rainy River'; analyze the choice between courage and shame. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does the narrator say 'I was a coward. I went to the war'?
questions.a: He could not bear the shame of being seen as a draft dodger, so he chose war over his convictions; giving in to embarrassment was his cowardice.

days.guide: Read 'How to Tell a True War Story,' then 'Good Form.' Define the two kinds of truth with examples. Today's task from the plan: Read 'How to Tell a True War Story'; define story-truth vs. happening-truth. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is the difference between story-truth and happening-truth?
questions.a: Happening-truth is what literally occurred; story-truth is an invented version that conveys the emotional reality more truly. O'Brien says 'story-truth is truer sometimes than happening-truth' (in 'Good Form').

days.guide: Watch a 15–20 minute veteran interview. The student compares how the veteran and O'Brien convey experience. Today's task from the plan: Watch a veteran interview from the Library of Congress Veterans History Project; compare oral history to fiction. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does an oral history differ from O'Brien's fiction?
questions.a: An oral history aims to record one person's actual memories as accurately as possible; O'Brien shapes and invents events to make readers feel the experience.

days.guide: The student writes a 500-word analysis of how O'Brien's structure blurs fact and fiction. Today's task from the plan: Write a 500-word response analyzing how O'Brien's structure blurs fact and fiction. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Name two techniques O'Brien uses to blur fact and fiction.
questions.a: A narrator named Tim O'Brien who comments on his own storytelling, and retelling the same event in different versions (e.g., Curt Lemon's death), so readers question what really happened.

weeks.assessment_key: Analytical response rubric (4-point): 4 = clear thesis about how structure blurs fact and fiction; evidence from at least two stories (e.g., the narrator's direct addresses, repeated retellings, the story-truth idea); analysis of WHY O'Brien does this (to convey emotional truth); controlled conventions. 3 = sound thesis, less developed analysis. 2 = summary dominates. 1 = off-topic or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Amy Tan's 'Mother Tongue'; six vignettes from Sandra Cisneros' The House on Mango Street (e.g., 'The House on Mango Street,' 'My Name,' 'Hairs,' 'Four Skinny Trees,' 'Those Who Don't,' 'Bums in the Attic'); excerpts from Richard Rodriguez's 'Aria' and Gloria Anzaldúa's 'How to Tame a Wild Tongue.'
misconceptions: Assuming all four writers agree. Rodriguez argues that learning public English, though painful, was necessary; Anzaldúa insists on keeping her home language as part of her identity.
Treating vignettes as unfinished stories. They are compressed, image-rich snapshots that build meaning across the collection.

days.guide: Read 'Mother Tongue.' The student lists the 'Englishes' and evaluates Tan's argument about how language shapes others' judgments. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Mother Tongue'; list the 'Englishes' she describes and evaluate her argument about language and judgment. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What 'Englishes' does Tan describe?
questions.a: The formal English of her writing and speeches, the simpler English she uses with her mother, and her mother's 'broken' or 'limited' English, which she says is vivid and full of meaning.

questions.q: What evidence does Tan give that her mother is judged by her English?
questions.a: Stores, banks, and a hospital ignored or dismissed her mother until Tan called pretending to be her (as with the stockbroker); she got results only with 'perfect' English.

days.guide: Read six vignettes. The student analyzes how short form conveys identity in two of them. Today's task from the plan: Read six Mango Street vignettes; analyze how compressed form conveys identity. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Esperanza say about her name in 'My Name'?
questions.a: 'In English my name means hope. In Spanish it means too many letters'; she inherited it from her great-grandmother, 'a wild horse of a woman,' but does not want to inherit her place by the window.

days.guide: Read the Rodriguez and Anzaldúa excerpts. The student makes a T-chart of their positions on public and private language. Today's task from the plan: Read excerpts; compare positions on public and private language. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is Rodriguez's position in 'Aria'?
questions.a: Speaking English in public (encouraged when nuns asked his parents to speak English at home) gave him a public identity and belonging, though it cost the intimacy of family Spanish.

questions.q: What does Anzaldúa mean by 'I am my language'?
questions.a: Her identity is inseparable from her languages; 'Until I can take pride in my language, I cannot take pride in myself.'

days.guide: The student writes two Cisneros-style vignettes about their own neighborhood or name (150–250 words each). Today's task from the plan: Write two Cisneros-style vignettes about your own neighborhood or name. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What makes a vignette effective?
questions.a: A single moment or image, concrete sensory details, figurative language, and an ending that implies meaning rather than stating it.

days.guide: The student writes an 800-word analytical essay comparing two authors' views on language and identity. Today's task from the plan: Write an 800-word analytical essay comparing two authors' views on language and identity. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Give a comparative thesis example.
questions.a: Tan and Anzaldúa both show how society judges people by their English, but while Tan learns to value her mother's English as a writer's resource, Anzaldúa demands that society accept her many languages on her own terms.

weeks.assessment_key: Analytical comparison essay rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper states a comparative thesis, quotes both authors at least twice, analyzes their purposes and techniques (anecdote, code-switching, imagery), and explains a genuine similarity and difference.

weeks.prep: Poetry Foundation pages for Joy Harjo's 'Remember' and 'Perhaps the World Ends Here,' Li-Young Lee's 'Persimmons,' Rita Dove's 'Testimonial,' and Natalie Diaz's 'The Facts of Art.' Read the short poet biographies. Phone to record performance.
misconceptions: Treating repetition as filler. In Harjo, repetition works like a chant or prayer, building rhythm and meaning.
Ignoring the poet's background. Harjo (Muscogee Nation, former U.S. Poet Laureate) and Diaz (Mojave) write from Native histories that shape the poems' meanings.

days.guide: Read both Harjo poems aloud. The student marks repetition and connections between land and identity. Today's task from the plan: Read two Harjo poems; analyze repetition and the connection between land and identity. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is repeated in 'Remember' and why?
questions.a: The command 'Remember' begins line after line (the sky, the moon, the earth, your mother); like a ritual, it ties personal identity to land, ancestors, and all living things ('you are all people and all people are you').

questions.q: What does the kitchen table represent in 'Perhaps the World Ends Here'?
questions.a: The center of human life: 'The world begins at a kitchen table'; births, grief, celebration, and survival happen there, and perhaps the world will end there too.

days.guide: Read 'Persimmons' and 'Testimonial.' The student traces images of fruit, memory, and language. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Persimmons' and 'Testimonial'; trace imagery of fruit, memory, and language. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What happened in sixth grade in 'Persimmons'?
questions.a: Mrs. Walker slapped the speaker for not knowing the difference between 'persimmon' and 'precision'; the poem shows she didn't know persimmons as he and his family do.

days.guide: Read 'The Facts of Art' with its epigraph. Discuss how humor and history combine. Today's task from the plan: Read 'The Facts of Art'; discuss how humor and history combine in the poem. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does Diaz combine humor and history?
questions.a: She uses irony and dark humor to retell a historical episode of government officials imposing their ideas on Native people, exposing condescension while making readers laugh uncomfortably.

days.guide: The student chooses a contemporary American poem and prepares an oral interpretation and a written introduction (poet, context, why chosen). Today's task from the plan: Choose a contemporary American poem and prepare an oral interpretation with a written introduction. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What makes an oral interpretation strong?
questions.a: Accurate reading, pauses that follow punctuation and line breaks purposefully, tone that matches the poem's shifts, and eye contact.

days.guide: Record the performance. Collect a 300-word explication. Today's task from the plan: Perform the poem (recorded) and submit a 300-word explication. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does an explication do?
questions.a: It explains how a poem's devices (imagery, sound, form, line breaks) create its meaning, moving line by line or by section with quotations.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (4-point): accuracy, pacing and pauses, expressive tone, introduction (poet and context). Explication rubric (4-point): central idea stated; at least three devices analyzed with quotations; explanation of how form supports meaning; conventions.

weeks.prep: Two op-eds on the American Dream with differing views; a short report on economic mobility (Pew Research Center, or Opportunity Insights' finding that about 90% of children born in 1940 out-earned their parents vs. about 50% of those born in 1980); a TED talk or podcast segment.
misconceptions: Treating op-eds as neutral reporting. Op-eds argue; evaluate their evidence and bias.
Cherry-picking a statistic without context. Check the source, date, and what the number actually measures.

days.guide: Read the two op-eds and the data report. The student annotates claims, evidence, and evidence quality. Today's task from the plan: Read two op-eds and a data report on economic mobility; annotate claims and evidence quality. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What is the difference between a claim and evidence?
questions.a: A claim is the arguable assertion; evidence is the data, examples, or expert testimony that supports it.

days.guide: Watch or listen to the talk. The student completes an SL.3 checklist (reasoning, evidence, rhetoric, exaggeration). Today's task from the plan: Watch or listen to a talk; evaluate the speaker's evidence and rhetoric with an SL.3 checklist. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does SL.3 ask you to evaluate?
questions.a: The speaker's point of view, reasoning, use of evidence and rhetoric, and whether any evidence is exaggerated or distorted.

days.guide: The student outlines a synthesis argument using at least four sources, including one literary text from the year. Today's task from the plan: Outline a synthesis argument using at least four sources, including one literary text from the year. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Which literary texts from the year fit this prompt?
questions.a: The Great Gatsby, A Raisin in the Sun, 'Harlem,' and Franklin's Autobiography all address the American Dream.

days.guide: The student drafts the 900-word synthesis essay. Today's task from the plan: Write a 900-word synthesis essay: 'Is the American Dream still achievable?'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is synthesis in writing?
questions.a: Combining several sources in your own argument, putting them in conversation rather than summarizing each separately.

days.guide: The student revises and submits; give the usage, hyphenation, and punctuation test. Today's task from the plan: Revise and submit; Unit 9 vocabulary and grammar test (usage, hyphenation, punctuation). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Correct: 'Its a twenty year old dream, and its fading.'
questions.a: 'It's a twenty-year-old dream, and it's fading.'

weeks.assessment_key: Synthesis essay rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper takes a position, uses at least four sources (one literary) put in conversation, evaluates evidence, and addresses a counterclaim. Grammar test key: its/it's; compound modifiers (well-known author, twenty-year-old dream); semicolon between independent clauses; colon after a complete clause; comma splice corrections.

weeks.prep: All the year's texts and essays; a free site builder (Google Sites). Theme-map template.
misconceptions: Choosing only favorite pieces. Include work that shows range and growth.
Writing a vague reflection ('I improved a lot'). Point to specific evidence from pieces.

days.guide: The student chooses a theme and maps it across six texts from at least four periods. Today's task from the plan: Choose a theme (freedom, identity, the frontier, dissent) and map it across six texts from different periods. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give a sample theme map for 'dissent.'
questions.a: Paine and Henry (political revolution), Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience,' Douglass' Fourth of July speech, Miller's The Crucible (Proctor's refusal), and King's 'Letter from Birmingham Jail.'

days.guide: The student selects four best pieces and revises one substantially. Today's task from the plan: Select four best pieces and revise one substantially. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What counts as substantial revision?
questions.a: Changes to thesis, structure, or evidence—not just corrections.

days.guide: The student writes a 600-word reflective letter on growth. Today's task from the plan: Write a 600-word reflective letter on growth as reader and writer. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What should the letter include?
questions.a: Specific evidence of growth from two or more pieces, a challenge overcome, and goals for next year.

days.guide: The student builds the portfolio site. Today's task from the plan: Build a digital portfolio site with pieces, reflection, and a reading list. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What belongs in the portfolio?
questions.a: Four pieces (one revised), the reflection, the theme map, and a reading list.

days.guide: The student presents a 10-minute talk. Today's task from the plan: Present portfolio and thematic map to family in a 10-minute talk. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should the talk include?
questions.a: The theme map, one piece read aloud or summarized, and the main growth insights.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio rubric (4-point): selection shows range; revision is substantial; reflection cites evidence; site is organized and complete. Presentation: clear, 10 minutes, answers questions.

weeks.prep: Final exam packet: two unseen passages (one poem and one nonfiction), multiple-choice and short answer, plus an argument prompt (e.g., 'What does it mean to be American?').
misconceptions: Cramming the night before. Spread review across Days 1–2 and use flashcards.
Starting the essay without a plan. Spend 5–8 minutes on thesis and outline.

days.guide: The student builds a study guide of periods (traits, authors, quotation) and rhetorical terms. Today's task from the plan: Review literary periods and key rhetorical terms with a self-made study guide and flashcards. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Match: Edwards, Emerson, Twain, Fitzgerald to periods.
questions.a: Edwards—Puritan; Emerson—Transcendentalism; Twain—Realism; Fitzgerald—Modernism.

days.guide: Practice an unseen poem and nonfiction passage with timed responses. Today's task from the plan: Practice an unseen poem and a nonfiction passage with timed responses. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Strategy for an unseen passage?
questions.a: Read twice, mark shifts and key words, paraphrase, then answer using exact lines.

days.guide: Final exam I. Today's task from the plan: Reading comprehension: unseen literary and informational passages with multiple-choice and short answers. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How should multiple choice be approached?
questions.a: Return to the passage for evidence and eliminate wrong answers.

days.guide: Final exam II: 60-minute argument essay using three texts. Today's task from the plan: Timed 60-minute argument essay drawing on at least three texts from the year. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How should the essay be planned?
questions.a: Thesis, three reasons each tied to a text, and a counterclaim.

days.guide: Review results; set summer reading goals. Today's task from the plan: Review exam results, set summer reading goals, and choose three books for senior year. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What makes good summer reading goals?
questions.a: Three specific books with a plan (e.g., one classic, one contemporary, one nonfiction).

weeks.assessment_key: Exam I: score multiple choice by key; short responses 2 points each (answer + evidence). Exam II rubric (4-point): thesis, evidence from three texts, analysis, organization and conventions.

ELEC.overview: Introduction to Engineering Design is taught in 55-minute, hands-on lessons: a short demonstration, guided practice, then the student builds, sketches or models while recording everything in a bound engineering notebook. Free tools carry the course (Onshape for Education and Tinkercad for CAD, TeachEngineering activities), so a parent without an engineering background can teach by following the steps and worked answers here and asking the student to explain each decision. Insist on safety glasses and safe tool habits, measurable criteria and repeated trials, and finish the year with a nine-week capstone project (weeks 28–36) with a real user that ends in a technical report, portfolio and panel presentation.

weeks.prep: Buy a bound grid-paper notebook (pages numbered, not spiral) and a pen. Bookmark the Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook (bls.gov/ooh) for career data. Find a short video interview with a practicing engineer (e.g. 'Engineer Your Life', TryEngineering or a company career video), or arrange a call with an engineer you know.
misconceptions: Thinking engineers mostly fix engines or only do math. Engineers design solutions to problems — products, structures, systems, processes — and spend much of their time communicating and testing.

Treating the engineering notebook like a scratch pad. It is a legal, permanent record: bound, numbered pages, dated entries in pen, mistakes crossed out with one line (not erased), and no torn-out pages.
Confusing science and engineering. Scientists ask 'why does this happen?'; engineers use that knowledge to ask 'how can we make something that solves this problem?'
weeks.assessment_key: Notebook format check (pass when all present): numbered pages; table of contents on the first pages; each entry dated and titled; written in pen; errors struck through with a single line and initialed; blank space crossed out; entries signed (and witnessed on key pages). Career reflection rubric (300 words, 4 levels): 4 = compares at least two disciplines using the researched data (typical tasks, education — usually a bachelor's degree in engineering — and salary), connects to the student's interests and takeaways from the engineer interview, and names a next step; 3 = data and personal connection but little comparison; 2 = general opinions with little evidence; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Have the student research five disciplines in the Occupational Outlook Handbook, filling a table: what they design, typical education (bachelor's in that engineering field; licensure as a PE later for some), median pay, and a California employer (e.g. mechanical — Tesla; civil — Caltrans; electrical — PG&E; biomedical — Medtronic or Edwards Lifesciences; industrial — a manufacturing plant or Amazon fulfillment). Discuss which surprised them.

questions.q: What does a civil engineer design? A biomedical engineer?
questions.a: Civil: infrastructure such as roads, bridges, water systems and buildings. Biomedical: medical devices, equipment and technologies, such as prosthetics, implants and imaging machines.

questions.q: What education do most engineering jobs require?
questions.a: A bachelor's degree in an engineering field (usually ABET-accredited); some roles require a Professional Engineer (PE) license or a graduate degree.

days.guide: Model the notebook rules: write the table of contents on pages 1–2, number every page, date and title each entry, use pen, cross out mistakes with one line, and sign at the bottom. Have the student set it up and make the first entry (today's career table).

questions.q: Why must an engineering notebook be bound, in pen, with no torn-out pages?
questions.a: It is a permanent, trustworthy record of the design process and can serve as evidence of when ideas were created (for patents or legal disputes).

questions.q: How do you correct a mistake in the notebook?
questions.a: Draw a single line through it so it's still readable, and initial/date it — never erase or white it out.

days.guide: Have the student read about one innovation — e.g. the Golden Gate Bridge (opened 1937; chief engineer Joseph Strauss with key design work by Charles Ellis and Leon Moisseiff) or the iPhone (2007) — and summarize the problem, constraints and solution in the notebook.

questions.q: What problem did the Golden Gate Bridge solve, and what made it hard?
questions.a: It connected San Francisco to Marin County across the Golden Gate strait, replacing slow ferries; challenges included strong currents, deep water, fog, high winds and earthquakes.

questions.q: What problem did the original iPhone address?
questions.a: Combining a phone, music player and internet device into one easy-to-use touchscreen device, replacing small physical keyboards.

days.guide: Watch the interview (or hold one). The student records five takeaways, focusing on what the engineer does day to day and how they got there.

questions.q: What is one skill besides math and science that engineers say they use daily?
questions.a: Communication — writing, presenting and teamwork (also problem solving and project management).

days.guide: The student writes the 300-word reflection; check the notebook format against the list in the assessment key and score the reflection with the rubric.

questions.q: Which engineering discipline interests you most, and why?
questions.a: Answers vary; a strong answer cites specific tasks and data from the week's research.

weeks.prep: Gather printer paper (e.g. 10 sheets), tape (limit to 30 cm), scissors, about 200 pennies and a small cup. Set two books 20 cm apart as bridge supports. Copy a decision matrix template into the notebook.
misconceptions: Thinking the design process is a straight line. Real design loops back — testing often sends you back to research or ideation.
Mixing up criteria and constraints. Criteria are goals used to judge success (holds the most pennies); constraints are limits (span 20 cm, only 10 sheets).
Picking a favorite idea before evaluating. Use the decision matrix honestly; it's a tool to compare against the criteria, not to justify a choice already made.
weeks.assessment_key: Paper bridge challenge rubric (4 levels): 4 = design brief states problem, criteria and constraints; five sketches; decision matrix with weighted criteria; build meets all constraints; load test recorded in a data table (pennies held before failure, failure location); redesign based on observed failure; reflection explains what changed and why the result improved or not; 3 = all parts, reflection thin; 2 = missing matrix or redesign; 1 = incomplete. Load results are not graded on size — process documentation is.

days.guide: Teach the steps: define the problem, research, ideate (brainstorm), select, prototype, test, iterate, communicate. Have the student draw it as a cycle with arrows back from 'test' to earlier steps.

questions.q: Why is the design process drawn as a cycle?
questions.a: Testing reveals problems, so engineers loop back to redesign and improve (iterate) rather than finishing after one try.

questions.q: What happens in the 'define' step?
questions.a: The problem is clearly stated, including who it's for, the criteria for success, and constraints.

days.guide: Model a design brief: client, problem statement, criteria (e.g. holds as many pennies as possible at midspan; uses fewest sheets), constraints (spans a 20 cm gap, only paper and 30 cm of tape, built in 30 minutes). The student writes their own.

questions.q: Is 'must span 20 cm' a criterion or a constraint?
questions.a: A constraint — it's a required limit.

questions.q: Write one criterion for the bridge.
questions.a: Example: holds the most pennies in a cup at the center before collapsing (or uses the least paper).

days.guide: Set a 15-minute timer for five quick sketches (folded beams, tubes, arches, trusses). Then build a decision matrix: criteria in rows (strength, material use, ease of building), score 1–5, multiply by weights, total.

questions.q: Idea A scores 4 strength (weight 3) and 2 ease (weight 1); Idea B scores 3 strength and 5 ease. Which wins?
questions.a: A: 4×3 + 2×1 = 14; B: 3×3 + 5×1 = 14 — a tie; break it with another criterion or reconsider weights.

questions.q: Why does folding paper into a channel or tube make it stronger?
questions.a: Folding moves material away from the center (neutral axis), increasing stiffness in bending — the same reason I-beams work.

days.guide: Build, place the cup at midspan, and add pennies one at a time until failure. Record the count and where/how it failed.

questions.q: Why record how the bridge failed, not just how many pennies it held?
questions.a: The failure mode (buckling, tearing, slipping off supports) tells you what to improve in the redesign.

days.guide: The student redesigns once to fix the failure, retests and writes a reflection; score with the rubric in the assessment key.

questions.q: Your bridge sagged in the middle and folded. What redesign might help?
questions.a: Increase stiffness at midspan — e.g. deeper folds, a tube or truss shape, or an arch — so it resists bending.

weeks.prep: Get safety glasses for everyone, 20 sticks of uncooked spaghetti, 1 m of tape, 1 m of string and one marshmallow per team, and a timer (18 minutes). Print a shop-safety list. Prepare the safety quiz and Unit 1 quiz from the key below.
misconceptions: Thinking safety glasses are only needed for power tools. Wear eye protection whenever cutting, snapping, hammering, drilling, hot gluing or working near someone who is.
Planning so long that there's no time to build. The marshmallow challenge shows that early prototyping and testing beat one big final attempt.
Writing test procedures that are vague ('test if it is strong'). Procedures must be repeatable: exact steps, tools, measurements and number of trials.
weeks.assessment_key: Safety quiz (pass = 100%, retake missed items): 1) Safety glasses must be worn whenever tools are used or anything can fly. 2) Tie back long hair, remove dangling jewelry, no loose sleeves. 3) Cut away from your body, using a cutting mat. 4) Report any injury immediately. 5) Unplug tools before changing blades/bits. 6) Know where the first-aid kit is. Unit 1 quiz: 1) Steps of the design process in order (define, research, ideate, select, prototype, test, iterate, communicate). 2) Criteria = measurable goals; constraints = limits. 3) A design brief states client, problem, criteria and constraints. 4) Decision matrix compares ideas against weighted criteria. 5) Notebook rules (bound, dated, pen, single-line cross-outs). 6) Name two engineering disciplines and what they design. 7) A Gantt chart shows tasks against a timeline. 8) PPE = personal protective equipment. Score 7–8 = mastery.

days.guide: Go over shop rules: PPE (safety glasses, closed-toe shoes, gloves when appropriate), tidy workspace, tool handling (cut away from body, carry tools pointed down), first-aid location. Give the safety quiz.

questions.q: What does PPE stand for? Give two examples.
questions.a: Personal protective equipment — e.g. safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection, closed-toe shoes.

questions.q: Which direction should you cut with a craft knife?
questions.a: Away from your body and hands, on a cutting mat, keeping fingers behind the blade.

days.guide: Run the marshmallow challenge: 18 minutes to build the tallest free-standing tower with the marshmallow on top. Afterward discuss roles, communication and why testing early matters.

questions.q: Why do kindergartners often beat business students at the marshmallow challenge?
questions.a: They build and test small prototypes quickly and adjust, rather than planning one perfect tower and discovering at the end that the marshmallow's weight makes it collapse.

questions.q: What is the 'hidden assumption' that sinks many teams?
questions.a: That the marshmallow is light; it's actually heavy enough to make tall spaghetti structures buckle.

days.guide: Show a Gantt chart: tasks listed down the side, time across the top, bars for task duration, and dependencies. The student makes one for a hypothetical project (e.g. building a birdhouse in 3 weeks).

questions.q: What does a Gantt chart show?
questions.a: Each task as a bar across a timeline showing when it starts and ends, the order of tasks and dependencies.

questions.q: What is a dependency?
questions.a: A task that can't start until another task is finished (e.g. painting must wait until assembly is done).

days.guide: Model a repeatable test procedure: numbered steps, equipment, what is measured, number of trials, and an empty data table with units. The student writes one for testing a paper bridge.

questions.q: What makes a test procedure 'repeatable'?
questions.a: Anyone could follow the exact steps with the same equipment and get comparable results — steps, measurements, units and number of trials are specified.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 quiz in the assessment key.

questions.q: Put in order: test, define, prototype, ideate.
questions.a: Define, ideate, prototype, test.

weeks.prep: Gather grid paper, soft pencils (HB/2H), and an eraser. Choose 3–4 household objects with simple shapes (mug, box, tape dispenser, stapler).
misconceptions: Pressing hard on construction lines. Construction lines should be light so they can be left or erased; darken only final object lines.
Drawing lines by moving only the wrist. Move the whole arm and use short, overlapping strokes for straighter lines.
Guessing size instead of comparing. Use the pencil as a measuring stick to compare proportions (e.g. the mug is 1½ times as tall as wide).
weeks.assessment_key: Sketch portfolio rubric (4 levels): 4 = clean line practice sheet (straight lines, light construction lines, dark object lines); circles/arcs built from boxes and diagonals; household objects in correct proportion (within about 10% by eye); 10 thumbnails showing different views; all labeled and dated; 3 = mostly accurate with some uneven lines; 2 = proportions noticeably off or missing parts; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Demonstrate light construction lines versus dark object lines. Have the student fill a page with horizontal, vertical and angled lines, marking endpoints first and sketching between them.

questions.q: What's the difference between a construction line and an object line?
questions.a: Construction lines are light guidelines used to lay out the sketch; object lines are dark, thick lines showing the visible edges of the object.

questions.q: Tip for drawing a long straight line freehand?
questions.a: Mark both endpoints, keep your eye on the end point, and use your whole arm in light overlapping strokes.

days.guide: Show the box method: draw a square, its diagonals and center lines, mark the radius on each line, then connect with arcs. Practice circles and arcs of different sizes.

questions.q: How do you sketch a circle using a box?
questions.a: Draw a light square the size of the diameter, add diagonals and center lines, mark points at the radius along them, then connect the points with smooth arcs.

days.guide: Teach proportion: hold a pencil at arm's length to compare an object's height to its width. Sketch 3–4 household objects in proportion.

questions.q: A mug is 10 cm tall and 8 cm wide. If your sketch is 5 cm tall, how wide should it be?
questions.a: 4 cm (scale factor 0.5).

days.guide: Have the student make 10 small, quick 'thumbnail' sketches of one object from different angles (front, top, side, angled views).

questions.q: What is the purpose of thumbnail sketches?
questions.a: Quickly explore views and ideas without detail, to decide which view or design is best to develop further.

days.guide: Collect the sketch portfolio and score with the rubric in the assessment key; have the student redo the weakest sketch.

questions.q: Which sketch in your portfolio best shows correct proportion, and how do you know?
questions.a: Answers vary; a strong answer cites a measured comparison (e.g. height-to-width ratio matches the object).

weeks.prep: Get isometric grid paper (printable free online), wooden blocks or LEGO, and a coffee mug. Practice the four-center ellipse once yourself.
misconceptions: Drawing isometric receding lines at 45°. Isometric axes are vertical plus two lines at 30° from horizontal (all three 120° apart).
Drawing circles as circles on isometric faces. Circles on isometric faces appear as ellipses.
Drawing full depth in cabinet oblique. Cabinet oblique uses half depth along the receding axis; cavalier uses full depth (which looks too deep).
weeks.assessment_key: Pictorial sketch quiz rubric (each sketch scored 0–4): isometric — 4 = correct 30° axes, all parallel edges parallel, correct proportions, holes/curves drawn as ellipses, construction lines light and object lines dark; oblique — 4 = front face true shape, receding lines at a consistent angle (often 45°), depth scale stated (cavalier full, cabinet half). Proficient = 3+ on each sketch. Written items: 1) Isometric axes are 120° apart. 2) Cavalier = full depth; cabinet = half depth. 3) In oblique, the front face shows its true shape, so circles there can be drawn as true circles.
