questions.a: Pass if a first-time user opens it in less than 10 s in at least 4 of 5 trials (or mean < 10 s); fail otherwise.

days.guide: Run five or more trials per test; compute mean and SD in the spreadsheet.

questions.q: Times: 8, 9, 7, 12, 9 s. Mean?

days.guide: The user tries the prototype while the student observes and records quotes and pain points.

questions.q: Why stay silent while the user tests?
questions.a: Explaining hides real usability problems the user would face alone.

days.guide: Make at least one evidence-based improvement.

questions.q: What makes an improvement 'evidence-based'?
questions.a: It addresses a specific failure seen in test data or user observations.

days.guide: Retest and summarize which specifications are met.

questions.q: Why retest after changing the design?
questions.a: To confirm the change fixed the problem without creating new ones.

weeks.prep: Have a word processor and a free website builder (Google Sites works well). Collect renderings, drawings, build photos and test graphs into one folder.
misconceptions: Writing the executive summary first. Write it last, as a short summary of the whole report.
Using vague words ('pretty strong'). Use technical terms and data ('held 3.2 kg, SD 0.2 kg').
Missing citations for research, images or patents.
weeks.assessment_key: Technical report and portfolio rubric: 4 = report of 2,000+ words with executive summary, problem, research, concept selection, design (drawings/renderings), build, testing (tables and graphs with data), conclusions/recommendations and citations; correct technical vocabulary; figures numbered and captioned; portfolio page publicly viewable with renderings, drawings, build photos, test graphs and a short project summary; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing sections or data; 1 = incomplete.

days.guide: Outline the report sections.

questions.q: What belongs in an executive summary?
questions.a: A brief overview of the problem, solution, key test results and conclusions — readable on its own by a busy reader.

days.guide: Write the full draft with figures and data tables.

questions.q: How should figures be labeled?
questions.a: Numbered with a caption (e.g. 'Figure 3. Load test results over five trials'), and referred to in the text.

days.guide: Build the digital portfolio page.

questions.q: What should a portfolio show a college or employer?
questions.a: The problem, process, visuals of the design and build, test evidence, and what the student learned.

days.guide: Revise for clarity and terminology; check every source is cited.

questions.q: Replace 'the stand was pretty strong' with technical language.
questions.a: 'The stand supported a 300 g load with no measurable deflection across five trials.'

days.guide: Submit the report and publish the portfolio.

questions.q: Why put test data in an appendix?
questions.a: Full raw data supports the report's claims while keeping the main text readable.

weeks.prep: Invite a panel (family, community members, ideally an engineer). Prepare the room with a screen and table for the prototype. Prepare a written final exam covering the course from the key below. Bookmark California community college engineering pathways (ASSIST.org for transfer) and UC/CSU engineering program pages.
misconceptions: Reading slides aloud. Slides show visuals and data; the presenter explains.
Defensive answers in Q&A. Treat questions as feedback; it's fine to say 'I didn't test that — here's how I would.'
Assuming there is one path to engineering. Community college transfer (ASSIST.org, transfer agreements) and 4-year admission are both strong routes.
weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (4 levels): 4 = about 10 minutes; covers problem, user, research, concept selection, design, build, test data and next steps; live prototype demo; clear visuals; confident Q&A; 3 = complete but uneven; 2 = missing test data or demo; 1 = unprepared. Final exam representative key: 1) Design process steps. 2) Criteria vs. constraints. 3) Isometric axes at 30°. 4) Third-angle view placement (top above front, right side to right). 5) Tolerance 12 ± 0.05 → 11.95–12.05. 6) Accuracy vs. precision. 7) Mean/SD calculation (e.g. 4, 6, 8 → mean 6, SD 2). 8) Density = mass/volume. 9) Extrude, revolve, shell definitions. 10) Revolute mate leaves 1 DOF. 11) Injection molding for high volume; 3D printing for prototypes. 12) Stiffness vs. strength. 13) 5th–95th percentile design. 14) First NSPE canon. 15) Patent vs. trademark vs. copyright. Mastery 12+/15. Pathway plan: complete if it names at least one community college and one university program, required math/science courses (calculus, physics, chemistry), and transfer or admission steps.

days.guide: Build a 10-minute slide deck; rehearse twice with a timer.

questions.q: What should the first minute of the presentation cover?
questions.a: The problem and the user — why the project matters.

days.guide: Present to the panel and demonstrate the prototype.

questions.q: What should you do if the prototype fails during the demo?
questions.a: Stay calm, explain what failed and why, and show test data or a video of it working.

days.guide: Write responses to panel questions and list next steps for development.

questions.q: Name two next steps if the product were developed further.
questions.a: Examples: test with more users, choose materials for manufacturing, reduce cost, file a provisional patent.

days.guide: Research California engineering pathways and write a plan.

questions.q: What website shows which community college courses transfer to UC/CSU?
questions.a: ASSIST.org.

questions.q: Which high school courses best prepare for engineering?
questions.a: Math through calculus, physics, chemistry, and courses in CAD/programming.

days.guide: Give the written final in the key.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a factor of safety?
questions.a: To make sure a design can carry more than the expected load, covering uncertainty in loads, materials and manufacturing.

HSS.overview: U.S. History runs about 60 minutes a day built around primary sources: introduce context briefly, read or view the day's documents together, have the student analyze them with SOAPS or a sourcing routine, then write. Weekly checks alternate quizzes, paragraphs and DBQ essays; teach thesis, contextualization, sourcing and corroboration explicitly and reuse the DBQ rubric all year. Emphasize California connections, multiple perspectives and cause-and-effect, and preview sensitive sources (racist language in court opinions, war and Holocaust materials) before sharing them.

weeks.prep: Print the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution (archives.gov), an excerpt of Locke's Second Treatise (chapters on the state of nature and the ends of government), Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws (Book XI, ch. 6 on separation of powers), Federalist No. 10 and Brutus No. 1 excerpts. Make a SOAPS organizer (Subject, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Speaker).
misconceptions: Students think the Declaration created the U.S. government. It announced independence and justified it; the Constitution (1787, effective 1789) set up the federal government (after the Articles of Confederation).
Students think 'separation of powers' and 'checks and balances' are the same. Separation divides power among three branches; checks and balances give each branch ways to limit the others.
Students think the Anti-Federalists opposed any constitution. They feared a strong central government and a large republic, and demanded a bill of rights.

days.guide: Read the Locke and Montesquieu excerpts together, pausing to paraphrase. The student builds a chart: idea → thinker → where it appears in the Declaration.

questions.q: What did Locke say government is for, and what may people do if it fails?
questions.a: Government exists to protect natural rights (life, liberty and property) with the consent of the governed; if it violates those rights, the people may alter or abolish it.

questions.q: Which Declaration phrase echoes Locke?
questions.a: 'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' and 'deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed'.

days.guide: Model SOAPS on the preamble, then the student analyzes the list of grievances, grouping them (taxation without consent, standing armies, trial by jury, dissolving legislatures).

questions.q: Who is the audience of the Declaration?
questions.a: The world ('a decent respect to the opinions of mankind'), the colonists, and King George III/Britain; it sought foreign support (e.g., France).

questions.q: Name two grievances against the King.
questions.a: Imposing taxes without consent; keeping standing armies in peacetime; depriving colonists of trial by jury; dissolving representative houses.

days.guide: The student maps Articles I–III (Congress, President, courts) and lists at least six checks.

questions.q: How can Congress check the President?
questions.a: Override a veto by two-thirds of both houses, reject appointments and treaties in the Senate, control funding, and impeach and remove.

questions.q: How do the courts check the other branches?
questions.a: Through judicial review — declaring laws or actions unconstitutional (established in Marbury v. Madison, 1803).

days.guide: Compare Federalist No. 10 (Madison) and Brutus No. 1 on the size of the republic in a T-chart.

questions.q: How did Madison argue a large republic would control factions?
questions.a: A large republic includes many factions and interests, making it hard for any single majority faction to dominate and oppress others.

questions.q: What was Brutus's concern?
questions.a: A large, diverse republic could not truly represent the people; a distant, powerful national government would swallow the states and threaten liberty.

days.guide: The student writes a paragraph explaining how the Constitution put Enlightenment ideas into practice. Score with the rubric and revise.

questions.q: What does federalism mean?
questions.a: Power is divided between the national government and the state governments.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric (4 levels): 4 = clear claim; at least three specific connections with evidence — Locke's natural rights and consent of the governed (Declaration: 'Governments are instituted among Men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed'; Constitution's Preamble 'We the People'), Montesquieu's separation of powers (Articles I, II, III), checks and balances (presidential veto and two-thirds override, Senate confirmation of appointments and two-thirds treaty ratification, impeachment by the House and trial in the Senate), federalism dividing power between national and state governments, and the Bill of Rights protecting natural rights; explains how each puts an idea into practice. 3 = two connections with evidence. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Print Jefferson's letter to the Danbury Baptists (1802) and the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom (drafted 1777, enacted 1786). Choose case summaries: Engel v. Vitale (1962, Establishment) and Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972, Free Exercise) from Oyez or the U.S. Courts site. Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments (1848).
misconceptions: Students think the First Amendment originally applied to states. It originally limited only Congress; the Fourteenth Amendment's incorporation later applied most protections to states.

Students think 'separation of church and state' is in the Constitution's text. The phrase comes from Jefferson's Danbury letter; the text says 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'.
Students think suffrage expanded steadily to everyone. By 1860 most states had removed property requirements for white men, but women, most Black men and Native Americans remained excluded.

days.guide: Read about the First and Second Great Awakenings; the student charts leaders, dates, beliefs and effects on reform.

questions.q: How did the Second Great Awakening encourage reform?
questions.a: It stressed that individuals could choose salvation and improve society, inspiring abolition, temperance, prison and education reform.

days.guide: Analyze the Danbury letter and the Virginia Statute.

questions.q: What did Jefferson mean by a 'wall of separation between Church & State'?
questions.a: The government should neither establish a religion nor interfere with the free exercise of religion; religious belief is a matter between a person and God.

days.guide: The student reads one Establishment and one Free Exercise case summary and explains the reasoning.

questions.q: Why did the Court strike down school prayer in Engel v. Vitale?
questions.a: A state-composed prayer recited in public schools was a government establishment of religion, even if voluntary and nondenominational.

questions.q: Why did the Amish win in Wisconsin v. Yoder?
questions.a: Compulsory schooling beyond eighth grade substantially burdened their religious practice, and the state's interest wasn't strong enough to override it.

days.guide: Trace suffrage expansion 1789–1860 on a timeline and read excerpts of the Declaration of Sentiments.

questions.q: How did the Declaration of Sentiments use the Declaration of Independence?
questions.a: It copied its structure and language — 'all men and women are created equal' — and listed grievances against men's denial of women's rights, including the vote.

days.guide: Give the quiz on founding principles and religious liberty.

questions.q: Quote the two religion clauses of the First Amendment.
questions.a: 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.'

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Founding principles — natural rights, consent of the governed, limited government, separation of powers, federalism. 2) The two religion clauses — Establishment and Free Exercise. 3) 'Wall of separation' — Jefferson's 1802 letter to the Danbury Baptists. 4) Virginia Statute — no one compelled to support or attend any church; religious opinions don't affect civil rights; authored by Jefferson, passed with Madison's leadership in 1786. 5) Engel v. Vitale — state-sponsored school prayer violates the Establishment Clause. 6) Wisconsin v. Yoder — Amish families could not be compelled to send children to school past eighth grade (Free Exercise). 7) First Great Awakening (1730s–40s) — Edwards, Whitefield; emotional revivals, challenged authority. 8) Second Great Awakening (c. 1790s–1840s) — Finney; inspired abolition, temperance and other reforms. 9) Jacksonian democracy — expansion of white male suffrage, end of property requirements, rise of party politics. 10) Seneca Falls (1848) — Stanton and Mott; Declaration of Sentiments: 'all men and women are created equal'; demanded voting rights.

weeks.prep: Print the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments; Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) excerpts (Chief Justice Taney); Library of Congress photos of Freedmen's Bureau schools; a summary of the Compromise of 1877; examples of Black Codes (Mississippi 1865). Parental note: Taney's opinion contains racist language; discuss its historical context. Build the Unit 1 test with a short DBQ (6 documents) on the meaning of freedom.
misconceptions: Students think Reconstruction failed completely. It brought real gains — Black voting and officeholding, public schools, the 14th and 15th Amendments — before being rolled back.
Students think the 13th Amendment ended all forced labor. It allows involuntary servitude 'as a punishment for crime', a loophole exploited by convict leasing.
Students think Black Codes came only after 1877. Southern states passed Black Codes in 1865–66; after 1877, Jim Crow laws and disfranchisement spread.

days.guide: Read Dred Scott excerpts and explain how the decision intensified sectional conflict leading to war.

questions.q: Why did Dred Scott enrage Northerners?
questions.a: It said Congress could not ban slavery in any territory, opening the West to slavery and invalidating the Missouri Compromise; it also denied Black citizenship.

days.guide: Analyze the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments clause by clause.

questions.q: What does the Equal Protection Clause say?
questions.a: No state shall 'deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.'

questions.q: Which amendment overturned the Dred Scott citizenship ruling?
questions.a: The 14th Amendment: all persons born or naturalized in the U.S. are citizens.

days.guide: Examine Freedmen's Bureau school photos and letters; list gains of Reconstruction.

questions.q: Name two achievements of Reconstruction.
questions.a: Public schools and Black colleges founded; Black men voting and holding office (e.g., Hiram Revels in the Senate); the Reconstruction Amendments.

days.guide: Study the Compromise of 1877, Black Codes and sharecropping; build a cause-effect chain.

questions.q: What did the Compromise of 1877 do?
questions.a: Settled the disputed 1876 election by making Rutherford B. Hayes president in exchange for withdrawing federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction.

questions.q: Why did sharecropping trap families?
questions.a: Tenants owed a share of the crop plus debts for seed and supplies on credit at high interest, so they rarely got ahead.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test with a short DBQ.

questions.q: What is the main loophole in the 13th Amendment?
questions.a: 'Except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted.'

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key (sample): 1) Locke's natural rights; 2) separation of powers (Montesquieu); 3) Federalist No. 10 argument; 4) First Amendment religion clauses; 5) Dred Scott (1857) — Black Americans were not citizens; Congress could not ban slavery in the territories; Missouri Compromise unconstitutional. 6) 13th (1865) — abolished slavery except as punishment for crime. 7) 14th (1868) — birthright citizenship, due process, equal protection. 8) 15th (1870) — vote can't be denied by race. 9) Freedmen's Bureau (1865) — schools, labor contracts, aid. 10) Compromise of 1877 — Hayes became president; federal troops withdrawn from the South, ending Reconstruction. 11) Sharecropping — tenant farming that trapped families in debt. DBQ rubric: thesis on what freedom meant (e.g., legal citizenship, education, land and fair labor, voting — partly achieved then undermined); uses 4+ documents with sourcing; outside evidence (Black Codes, KKK, Hiram Revels as first Black senator, 1870).

weeks.prep: Print a map of railroads and natural resources c. 1890; Carnegie's 'The Gospel of Wealth' (1889) excerpt; William Graham Sumner and Walter Rauschenbusch excerpts; three trust cartoons from the Library of Congress (e.g., 'The Bosses of the Senate', 1889; Standard Oil octopus, 'Next!', 1904).
misconceptions: Students think vertical and horizontal integration are the same. Vertical controls every stage of production (Carnegie: mines, railroads, mills); horizontal buys up competitors at the same stage (Rockefeller: refineries).
Students see industrialists as all heroes or all villains. Use evidence for both innovation and philanthropy and for harsh labor practices and monopoly.
Students think Social Darwinism is Darwin's idea. It was a misapplication of 'survival of the fittest' (Herbert Spencer's phrase) to society to justify inequality.

days.guide: Map railroads and resources; the student explains geographic advantages (coal, iron, oil, timber, rivers, transcontinental railroad 1869, immigrant labor).

questions.q: Give two geographic advantages that fueled U.S. industry.
questions.a: Abundant natural resources (coal, iron ore, oil) and a large connected market linked by railroads and waterways.

days.guide: Diagram Carnegie's vertical and Rockefeller's horizontal integration.

questions.q: Which strategy did Rockefeller use, and how?
questions.a: Horizontal integration — buying or driving out competing refineries until Standard Oil controlled about 90% of U.S. refining by 1880.

days.guide: Read 'The Gospel of Wealth' and debate captains of industry vs. robber barons.

questions.q: What did Carnegie argue the rich should do with their wealth?
questions.a: Use it during their lifetimes for the public good (e.g., libraries, universities) rather than leave it to heirs.

days.guide: Compare Sumner (Social Darwinism) and Rauschenbusch (Social Gospel).

questions.q: How did the Social Gospel respond to industrial poverty?
questions.a: It argued Christians should apply ethics to society, reforming conditions like child labor and slums.

days.guide: The student analyzes three trust cartoons in writing.

questions.q: What federal law in 1890 targeted trusts?
questions.a: The Sherman Antitrust Act.

weeks.assessment_key: Cartoon analysis rubric: for each of three cartoons — identifies symbols and labels, caption, artist/date, the message (e.g., 'The Bosses of the Senate' shows huge money-bag trusts looming over senators, arguing that monopolies control government), the point of view, and the historical context (Sherman Antitrust Act 1890, trust-busting). 4 = all elements with accurate context for all three.

weeks.prep: Print an excerpt of Upton Sinclair's The Jungle (1906) — preview, it's graphic about meatpacking — and Lewis Hine child labor photos (LOC); summaries of the Homestead (1892) and Pullman (1894) strikes; the Omaha Platform (1892); Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' speech (1896).
misconceptions: Students think unions were widely accepted. Courts, employers and often government opposed them; strikes were frequently broken by force or injunctions.
Students think 'free silver' means free money. It meant unlimited coinage of silver at 16:1 with gold, expanding the money supply to raise prices and ease farm debts.
Students think the Populists failed completely. They lost elections but many demands later became law.

days.guide: Read The Jungle excerpt and study Hine photos; record working conditions.

questions.q: What reforms did The Jungle help produce?
questions.a: The Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act (both 1906).

days.guide: Compare the Knights of Labor and the AFL; study Homestead and Pullman.

questions.q: How did the AFL differ from the Knights of Labor?
questions.a: The AFL (Gompers, 1886) organized skilled craft workers and focused on wages, hours and conditions; the Knights accepted nearly all workers and had broad reform goals.

questions.q: How was the Pullman Strike ended?
questions.a: A federal injunction and federal troops sent by President Cleveland; Eugene Debs was jailed.

days.guide: Analyze the Omaha Platform's demands.

questions.q: List three Omaha Platform demands.
questions.a: Free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, government ownership of railroads and telegraphs, direct election of senators, secret ballot, eight-hour day.

days.guide: Read Bryan's speech and explain the silver vs. gold debate.

questions.q: Why did indebted farmers favor free silver?
questions.a: More money in circulation would cause inflation, raising crop prices and making debts easier to repay.

questions.q: What is the famous line of the speech?
questions.a: 'You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.'

days.guide: The student writes a paragraph on which Populist demands later became law.

questions.q: Which amendment created the federal income tax?
questions.a: The 16th Amendment (1913).

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = claim identifies which demands became law with evidence — graduated income tax (16th Amendment, 1913), direct election of senators (17th Amendment, 1913), secret ballot (adopted by states in the 1880s–90s), eight-hour day (Adamson Act 1916 for railroads; Fair Labor Standards Act 1938), initiative and referendum (many states, including California 1911), regulation of railroads (ICC strengthened) — and notes those that did not (free silver, government ownership of railroads); explains why (Progressive reformers adopted them). 3 = two or three examples. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Print Angel Island poems (Calisphere or the Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation), Jacob Riis photos and text from How the Other Half Lives (1890), Plunkitt of Tammany Hall excerpt ('honest graft', 1905), Thomas Nast cartoons of Boss Tweed, and a Jane Addams/Hull House reading. Build the Unit 2 test with a DBQ on the immigrant experience.
misconceptions: Students think Angel Island was 'the Ellis Island of the West' in the same way. Ellis Island processed most immigrants in hours; Angel Island, shaped by the Chinese Exclusion Act, detained many Chinese immigrants for weeks or months with interrogations.
Students think political machines did only harm. They traded services (jobs, help for immigrants) for votes while engaging in corruption.
Students think nativism targeted only one group. It targeted Chinese, Japanese, Southern and Eastern Europeans, Catholics and Jews in different ways.

days.guide: Compare Ellis Island and Angel Island using Angel Island wall poetry.

questions.q: Why were Chinese immigrants often detained at Angel Island?
questions.a: The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred most Chinese laborers; officials interrogated detainees to test claims of exempt status (e.g., 'paper sons').

days.guide: Analyze Riis's photographs and text.

questions.q: How did Riis use photography as reform?
questions.a: He used flash photography to show crowded, unsanitary tenements to middle-class readers, building pressure for housing laws like New York's 1901 Tenement House Act.

days.guide: Study Tammany Hall and Plunkitt's 'honest graft'.

questions.q: What did Plunkitt mean by 'honest graft'?
questions.a: Using insider knowledge for profit (e.g., buying land he knew the city would need) rather than outright theft — 'I seen my opportunities and I took 'em.'

days.guide: Read about Hull House and Americanization programs.

questions.q: What services did settlement houses provide?
questions.a: English and citizenship classes, childcare, health care, job training and recreation for immigrants.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: What was the Chinese Exclusion Act?
questions.a: An 1882 federal law that banned Chinese laborers from immigrating; it was the first major U.S. law to bar a specific ethnic group.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key (sample): 1) Vertical vs. horizontal integration. 2) Gospel of Wealth. 3) Social Darwinism vs. Social Gospel. 4) Sherman Antitrust Act (1890). 5) Homestead and Pullman strikes. 6) Omaha Platform. 7) Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) — first law banning immigration by a specific ethnic group; repealed 1943. 8) Ellis Island (1892) vs. Angel Island (1910). 9) Jacob Riis exposed tenement conditions. 10) Tammany Hall/Boss Tweed and political machines. 11) Settlement houses — Jane Addams's Hull House (Chicago, 1889). DBQ rubric: thesis about immigrant experience (opportunity and hardship; discrimination; community building; Americanization pressures); 4+ documents with sourcing; outside evidence.

weeks.prep: Print Ida Tarbell's History of the Standard Oil Company (1904) or Lincoln Steffens's The Shame of the Cities excerpt; Meat Inspection Act summary; a reform chart template; Calisphere sources on Hiram Johnson, the 1911 special election and suffrage posters.
misconceptions: Students think Progressives were one party. Progressivism was a movement with Republicans (TR), Democrats (Wilson) and the 1912 Progressive ('Bull Moose') Party.
Students confuse initiative, referendum and recall. Initiative: citizens propose laws; referendum: voters approve or reject laws; recall: voters remove officials.

Students think all women got the vote in 1920. California women voted from 1911; the 19th Amendment (1920) barred sex discrimination in voting nationally, but many women of color still faced barriers.

days.guide: Read Tarbell or Steffens excerpts and identify targets.

questions.q: What did Ida Tarbell expose?
questions.a: Standard Oil's ruthless and unfair business practices (rebates, crushing competitors).

days.guide: Chart reforms of TR, Taft and Wilson.

questions.q: What did the Federal Reserve Act (1913) create?
questions.a: A central banking system of 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks to manage the money supply and stabilize banks.

days.guide: Study Hiram Johnson and California's 1911 reforms.

questions.q: Why did California reformers want the initiative and referendum?
questions.a: To let voters bypass a legislature they saw as controlled by the Southern Pacific Railroad.

days.guide: Analyze suffrage posters and California's 1911 vote.

questions.q: How close was California's 1911 suffrage vote?
questions.a: Very close — it passed by about 3,600 votes, carried by rural and small-town voters.

days.guide: Give the Progressive reforms quiz.

questions.q: What is a recall election?
questions.a: A vote by citizens to remove an elected official from office before the term ends.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Muckrakers — journalists exposing corruption (Tarbell: Standard Oil; Steffens: city corruption; Sinclair: meatpacking). 2) TR — Square Deal, trust-busting (Northern Securities, 1904), Meat Inspection and Pure Food and Drug Acts (1906), conservation. 3) Taft — more antitrust suits (Standard Oil broken up 1911). 4) Wilson — Federal Reserve Act (1913), Clayton Antitrust Act and FTC (1914), Underwood Tariff with income tax. 5) 16th Amendment — income tax (1913). 6) 17th — direct election of senators (1913). 7) 18th — Prohibition (1919). 8) 19th — women's suffrage (1920). 9) Hiram Johnson — elected governor 1910, broke Southern Pacific Railroad's political power. 10) California 1911 — initiative, referendum, recall adopted; women's suffrage (Proposition 4) passed narrowly, making California the sixth state with full women's suffrage.

weeks.prep: Print excerpts: Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890); Queen Liliuokalani's protest (1893 or 1897); Hearst's New York Journal and Pulitzer's New York World headlines on the Maine (Feb. 1898); McKinley's reported rationale for the Philippines (1899, published 1903); the Anti-Imperialist League platform (1899).
misconceptions: Students think the Maine was proven to be sunk by Spain. The cause was never proven; a 1976 U.S. Navy study concluded an internal coal-bunker fire likely caused it.

Students think Hawaii's annexation was requested by Hawaiians. American planters and businessmen overthrew Queen Liliuokalani in 1893 with U.S. Marines present; many Native Hawaiians petitioned against annexation (1897).
Students think the war ended in 1898 for the Philippines. Filipinos fought U.S. rule in the Philippine-American War (1899–1902, with fighting continuing later).

days.guide: Analyze Mahan's argument and list motives for expansion (economic markets, naval bases, Social Darwinism/racial ideas, missionary goals, closing of the frontier).

questions.q: What did Mahan argue?
questions.a: Great nations need a strong navy, overseas coaling stations and bases, and access to trade; sea power builds national greatness.

days.guide: Read Liliuokalani's protest and the annexation debate.

questions.q: How was Hawaii's monarchy overthrown?
questions.a: In 1893 American and European planters and businessmen, backed by U.S. Marines from the USS Boston, forced Queen Liliuokalani from power; the U.S. annexed Hawaii in 1898.

days.guide: Analyze yellow journalism headlines about the Maine.

questions.q: What is yellow journalism?
questions.a: Sensational, exaggerated news to attract readers — used by Hearst and Pulitzer to inflame opinion against Spain.

days.guide: Compare McKinley's rationale and the Anti-Imperialist League platform.

questions.q: What territories did the U.S. gain from the 1898 Treaty of Paris?
questions.a: Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines (paying Spain $20 million); Cuba became nominally independent.

questions.q: How did the Anti-Imperialist League use the Declaration of Independence?
questions.a: It argued governing Filipinos without their consent violated the principle that governments derive power from the consent of the governed.

days.guide: The student writes a short argument on whether U.S. expansion was consistent with founding ideals.

questions.q: What was the Open Door Policy (1899)?
questions.a: Secretary of State John Hay's call for equal trading rights for all nations in China.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument rubric: 4 = clear claim on whether expansion was consistent with founding ideals (consent of the governed, self-determination); uses at least three pieces of evidence (Liliuokalani's protest, annexation without a Hawaiian vote, Philippine-American War, Anti-Imperialist League's quoting of the Declaration, McKinley's 'uplift' rationale, Puerto Ricans' limited rights under the Insular Cases, Cuba's Platt Amendment); addresses a counterargument (spreading democracy, strategic or economic needs); clear organization. 3 = claim with two pieces of evidence. 2 = general. 1 = unsupported.

weeks.prep: Print the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) text, Panama Canal photos, quotes for Big Stick, Dollar Diplomacy and Moral Diplomacy, a blank Latin America map, and the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Students think the U.S. simply bought Panama. The U.S. backed Panama's 1903 independence from Colombia after Colombia rejected a canal treaty, then signed a canal treaty with the new government.

Students confuse the Monroe Doctrine and Roosevelt Corollary. Monroe (1823) warned Europe not to colonize; the Corollary (1904) claimed a U.S. right to intervene in Latin American nations as an 'international police power'.
Students think Moral Diplomacy meant no intervention. Wilson intervened often (Mexico, Haiti, Dominican Republic) claiming to promote democracy.

days.guide: Study the canal's construction and the U.S. role in Panama's independence.

questions.q: What problems did canal builders overcome?
questions.a: Tropical diseases (yellow fever and malaria, controlled by Dr. William Gorgas's mosquito eradication), mountainous terrain (the Culebra Cut) and massive engineering with locks.

days.guide: Compare TR, Taft and Wilson's diplomacy using quotes.

questions.q: What did the Roosevelt Corollary claim?
questions.a: That the U.S. could act as an 'international police power' and intervene in Latin American countries to prevent European intervention.

days.guide: Examine the Mexican Revolution and Pershing's expedition.

questions.q: Why did Wilson send Pershing into Mexico in 1916?
questions.a: To capture Pancho Villa after Villa's raid on Columbus, New Mexico; Pershing failed to catch him.

days.guide: Map U.S. interventions in Latin America 1898–1920.

questions.q: Name three countries the U.S. occupied militarily between 1898 and 1920.
questions.a: Examples: Cuba, Nicaragua, Haiti, Dominican Republic, Mexico (Veracruz).

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: When did the Panama Canal open?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key (sample): 1) Mahan's sea-power argument. 2) Hawaii overthrow (1893) and annexation (1898). 3) Yellow journalism and the Maine. 4) Treaty of Paris (1898) gains. 5) Philippine-American War. 6) Open Door Policy. 7) Panama — U.S. supported independence (1903); canal opened 1914. 8) Big Stick (TR) — 'speak softly and carry a big stick'; Roosevelt Corollary (1904). 9) Dollar Diplomacy (Taft) — using investment to gain influence. 10) Moral Diplomacy (Wilson) — support for democratic governments; interventions in Mexico (Veracruz 1914; Pershing's expedition 1916–17), Haiti (1915–34), Dominican Republic (1916–24). 11) Map interventions: Cuba, Puerto Rico, Panama, Nicaragua, Haiti, Dominican Republic, Mexico, Honduras.

weeks.prep: Print the Zimmermann Telegram (DocsTeach) with its decoded translation, four WWI propaganda posters (e.g., 'I Want You', 'Destroy This Mad Brute', 'Food Will Win the War', a Liberty Bond poster), Schenck v. United States (1919) excerpt, and a Fourteen Points summary.
misconceptions: Students think the U.S. entered WWI right after the Lusitania (1915). The U.S. entered in April 1917, after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram was revealed.
Students think 'clear and present danger' is today's free-speech standard. It was later replaced; since Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969), speech can be punished only if it incites imminent lawless action.
Students think the Senate rejected the Treaty because of the war's outcome. Opposition centered on the League of Nations (Article X) and fears of entangling commitments.

days.guide: Analyze the Zimmermann Telegram and unrestricted submarine warfare.

questions.q: What did the Zimmermann Telegram propose?
questions.a: A German-Mexican alliance if the U.S. entered the war, with Mexico regaining Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

days.guide: Analyze four WWI posters for persuasion techniques.

questions.q: Name two propaganda techniques in WWI posters.
questions.a: Appeals to patriotism, fear (dehumanizing the enemy as a brute), guilt, and calls to action like buying Liberty Bonds.

days.guide: Read Schenck v. U.S. and debate 'clear and present danger'.

questions.q: What analogy did Holmes use in Schenck?
questions.a: Free speech would not protect someone 'falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.'

days.guide: Study the Great Migration, women's war work and the 1918 flu.

questions.q: Why did many Black Southerners move North during WWI?
questions.a: Factory jobs opened as immigration fell and men went to war; they also sought to escape Jim Crow segregation and violence.

days.guide: Give the quiz and a paragraph on the Fourteen Points and Versailles debate.

questions.q: What was the main objection to the League of Nations in the Senate?
questions.a: Article X's collective-security pledge might commit the U.S. to war without Congress's approval.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Zimmermann Telegram (Jan. 1917) — Germany proposed a military alliance with Mexico, promising Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. 2) Unrestricted submarine warfare resumed Feb. 1917. 3) U.S. declared war April 1917. 4) Espionage Act (1917) and Sedition Act (1918) limited speech. 5) Schenck (1919) — Justice Holmes: 'clear and present danger'; distributing anti-draft leaflets not protected in wartime. 6) Great Migration — Black Southerners moved North for war jobs and to escape Jim Crow. 7) 1918 influenza killed about 675,000 Americans. 8) Fourteen Points — open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, arms reduction, self-determination, League of Nations. Paragraph rubric: explains why the Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles (Lodge's reservations, Article X collective security, Wilson's refusal to compromise) with evidence.

weeks.prep: Print 1920s advertisements (cars, appliances, radios), a Langston Hughes poem ('The Negro Speaks of Rivers' or 'I, Too'), Coolidge's 1925 speech excerpt ('the chief business of the American people is business'), and a Louis Armstrong recording (e.g., 'West End Blues').
misconceptions: Students think everyone prospered in the 1920s. Farmers struggled with low prices, and wealth was highly unequal.
Students think installment buying is harmless. It drove consumer debt and demand that couldn't last.
Students think the Harlem Renaissance was only music. It included poetry, fiction, art, theater and scholarship.

days.guide: Analyze Harding and Coolidge policies and the boom (tax cuts under Treasury Secretary Mellon, high tariffs, limited regulation).

questions.q: What did Harding mean by a 'return to normalcy'?
questions.a: A return to peace, prosperity and less government activism after the war and Progressive reforms.

days.guide: Study the automobile, radio and electricity's effect on daily life.

questions.q: How did Ford's assembly line change car ownership?
questions.a: It cut production time and price (Model T fell below $300), making cars affordable to many families.

days.guide: Analyze 1920s ads and the role of mass media.

questions.q: What technique do 1920s ads use?
questions.a: Linking products to status, youth, modernity and anxiety, and offering installment payment plans.

days.guide: Analyze Harlem Renaissance music, art and poetry.

questions.q: What themes does Langston Hughes explore?
questions.a: Black identity, pride, heritage, and the struggle for equality (e.g., 'I, too, am America').

days.guide: The student writes about how technology changed life in the 1920s.

questions.q: What was the first commercial radio station and year?
questions.a: KDKA in Pittsburgh, 1920.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = claim about how technology changed life; at least three specific technologies with effects (automobile/Model T and assembly line — mobility, suburbs, gas stations, tourism; radio — mass culture, national advertising, news, sports; electricity and appliances — less household labor, consumer debt; movies — shared culture); evidence from ads or data; mentions who was left out (rural areas lacked electricity). 3 = two technologies. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Print the Immigration Act of 1924 quota tables, summaries of the Palmer Raids and the Sacco and Vanzetti case, the 18th Amendment, and Scopes trial transcript excerpts (Darrow's examination of Bryan). Build the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Students think the 1924 quotas treated all nations equally. Quotas were set at 2% of each nationality in the 1890 census, favoring Northern and Western Europe and barring most Asian immigration.
Students think Prohibition stopped drinking. Consumption fell at first, but bootlegging, speakeasies and organized crime grew; it was repealed by the 21st Amendment (1933).
Students think Scopes was acquitted. He was convicted and fined $100; the verdict was overturned on a technicality.

days.guide: Study the Palmer Raids and Sacco and Vanzetti.

questions.q: What caused the first Red Scare?
questions.a: Fear of communism after the 1917 Russian Revolution, a wave of strikes in 1919 and anarchist bombings.

days.guide: Analyze the 1924 quota tables and the KKK revival.

questions.q: Why did the 1924 Act use the 1890 census?
questions.a: Fewer Southern and Eastern Europeans lived in the U.S. in 1890, so their quotas would be small.

days.guide: Examine the 18th Amendment and its consequences.

questions.q: Name two unintended consequences of Prohibition.
questions.a: Growth of organized crime (e.g., Al Capone), speakeasies, corruption of police, and loss of tax revenue.

days.guide: Read Scopes trial excerpts and analyze the modernist vs. traditionalist conflict.

questions.q: Who were the opposing lawyers in the Scopes trial?
questions.a: Clarence Darrow for the defense and William Jennings Bryan for the prosecution.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test.

questions.q: Which amendment repealed Prohibition?
questions.a: The 21st Amendment (1933).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test key (sample): 1) Zimmermann Telegram. 2) Schenck and 'clear and present danger'. 3) Fourteen Points and League of Nations. 4) Coolidge pro-business policies. 5) Installment buying. 6) Harlem Renaissance figures (Hughes, Hurston, Armstrong, Ellington). 7) Palmer Raids (1919–20) — mass arrests of suspected radicals; hundreds deported. 8) Sacco and Vanzetti — Italian anarchists convicted of murder in 1921, executed 1927 amid doubts about fairness. 9) Immigration Act of 1924 — 2% of 1890 census; Asian exclusion. 10) KKK revival in the 1920s — millions of members, nativist and anti-Black, anti-Catholic, antisemitic. 11) 18th Amendment and Volstead Act; repealed by the 21st. 12) Scopes trial (1925) — Tennessee's Butler Act banned teaching evolution; Darrow vs. Bryan; modernism vs. traditionalism.

weeks.prep: Print 1920s–30s stock market data (Dow Jones: peak about 381 in Sept. 1929, low about 41 in July 1932), a margin-buying example, unemployment data (about 25% in 1933), and Hoover speech excerpts (e.g., 1928 'rugged individualism'; 1931–32 statements).
misconceptions: Students think the 1929 crash alone caused the Depression. The crash was a trigger; deeper causes included overproduction, unequal income, farm debt, bank failures, Federal Reserve policy and falling world trade.
Students think Hoover did nothing. He pushed voluntarism and later created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932), but opposed direct federal relief to individuals.
Students think buying on margin meant buying cheap stock. It meant borrowing most of the price from a broker; when prices fell, margin calls forced selling.

days.guide: Learn the origins of the Federal Reserve and monetary debates.

questions.q: Why was the Federal Reserve created?
questions.a: To prevent banking panics like 1907 by providing a central bank that could lend to banks and manage the money supply.

days.guide: Analyze 1929 market data and buying on margin with a worked example.

questions.q: You buy $1,000 of stock with $100 down on margin. The price falls 20%. What happens?
questions.a: The stock is worth $800, but you still owe $900; your $100 is wiped out and you owe $100 more — the broker issues a margin call.

days.guide: The student ranks the causes with evidence.

questions.q: How did bank failures worsen the Depression?
questions.a: Depositors lost savings (no deposit insurance), credit dried up, and the money supply shrank, cutting spending and investment.

days.guide: Read Hoover's speeches and evaluate his response.

questions.q: What was Hoover's philosophy of relief?
questions.a: Voluntarism and 'rugged individualism' — local and private charity, not direct federal aid to individuals.

days.guide: Give the quiz on causes.

questions.q: What was the Smoot-Hawley Tariff's effect?
questions.a: Other countries retaliated with their own tariffs and world trade collapsed, deepening the Depression.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Federal Reserve (1913) — 12 regional banks after the Panic of 1907. 2) Buying on margin — paying as little as 10% and borrowing the rest. 3) Black Thursday (Oct. 24) and Black Tuesday (Oct. 29, 1929). 4) Dow fell about 89% from 1929 peak to 1932 low. 5) Bank runs and failures — about 9,000 banks failed 1930–33. 6) Money supply fell about one-third; the Fed did not act as lender of last resort. 7) Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) — raised tariffs, other nations retaliated, trade collapsed. 8) Overproduction/underconsumption and unequal income. 9) Hoover's RFC (1932). 10) Bonus Army (1932) — WWI veterans demanding early bonus payment were driven out by the Army.

weeks.prep: Print Dorothea Lange photographs (Migrant Mother, 1936, Nipomo, California; others from Calisphere/LOC), Woody Guthrie's 'Dust Bowl Blues' lyrics, excerpts of Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath (1939), and a reading on Mexican repatriation (including California's 2005 Apology Act).
misconceptions: Students think the Dust Bowl was purely natural. Drought combined with plowing up native grasslands (wheat boom of the 1910s–20s) left soil exposed to wind.
Students think 'Okies' were welcomed in California. Many faced hostility, low wages, migrant camps and a 1936 Los Angeles 'bum blockade' at the state border.
Students think repatriation was voluntary emigration. Many Mexicans and Mexican Americans, including U.S. citizens, were deported or pressured to leave.

days.guide: Study causes of the Dust Bowl and farming practices.

questions.q: How did farming practices contribute to the Dust Bowl?
questions.a: Farmers plowed up deep-rooted prairie grasses to plant wheat; when drought came, the loose topsoil blew away in massive dust storms.

days.guide: Analyze Lange's photographs of migrants in California.

questions.q: What does Migrant Mother show and why is it powerful?
questions.a: Florence Owens Thompson, a pea picker in Nipomo, California, with her children; her worried face became a symbol of Depression suffering.

days.guide: Analyze Woody Guthrie's 'Dust Bowl Blues' lyrics.

questions.q: What does Guthrie's music reveal about Dust Bowl migrants?
questions.a: Their losses, hardship on the road and in California, and resilience.

days.guide: Learn about Mexican repatriation in the 1930s.

questions.q: Why were Mexicans and Mexican Americans targeted?
questions.a: Officials blamed them for taking jobs and using relief during high unemployment; raids and pressure drove hundreds of thousands to Mexico.

days.guide: The student writes a short essay on the human toll in California.

questions.q: What did California's 2005 Apology Act do?
questions.a: It formally apologized for the state's role in the unconstitutional removal of Mexicans and Mexican Americans during the 1930s.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric: 4 = thesis on the human toll in California; evidence from at least three sources (Lange's photos of migrant families; Guthrie's lyrics; Steinbeck; data — about 300,000–400,000 Dust Bowl-era migrants to California; estimates of 400,000 to over a million people repatriated to Mexico nationally, many of them U.S. citizens); analysis of discrimination and labor conditions; conclusion on significance. 3 = two sources. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Get audio of FDR's First Inaugural (March 4, 1933) and the first fireside chat on banking (March 12, 1933); WPA posters; a chart template for relief/recovery/reform; critic excerpts (Huey Long 'Share Our Wealth', Father Coughlin, American Liberty League); the Wagner Act summary. Assemble DBQ documents (unemployment data 1929–1941, programs, critics).
misconceptions: Students think the New Deal ended the Depression. Unemployment fell from about 25% (1933) to about 14% (1937), then rose again in the 1937–38 recession; full recovery came with WWII spending.
Students think all New Deal programs survived. The Supreme Court struck down the NRA (Schechter, 1935) and the first AAA (Butler, 1936).
Students think critics were only conservatives. Critics came from the left (Long, Coughlin, Townsend) and the right (Liberty League).

days.guide: Listen to FDR's First Inaugural and a fireside chat.

questions.q: What is FDR's most famous line from his First Inaugural?
questions.a: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself.'

questions.q: What was the purpose of the first fireside chat?
questions.a: To explain the bank holiday and restore confidence so people would redeposit money.

days.guide: Chart programs by relief, recovery and reform.

questions.q: Classify: CCC, FDIC, Social Security, NRA.
questions.a: CCC — relief; NRA — recovery; FDIC — reform; Social Security — reform (and relief).

days.guide: Analyze critiques from Long, Coughlin and the Liberty League.

questions.q: What did Huey Long's 'Share Our Wealth' propose?
questions.a: Heavy taxes on the rich to guarantee every family a basic income and home.

days.guide: Study the Wagner Act and the CIO.

questions.q: What did the Wagner Act (1935) do?
questions.a: Guaranteed workers' right to organize and bargain collectively and created the National Labor Relations Board.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 DBQ.

questions.q: What was FDR's court-packing plan?
questions.a: A 1937 proposal to add up to six justices to the Supreme Court; Congress rejected it.

weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric (Did the New Deal end the Depression?): 4 = defensible thesis (e.g., it provided relief and lasting reform but didn't fully end the Depression, which ended with WWII mobilization); uses 4+ documents with sourcing (e.g., unemployment data, FDR's speeches, critics); outside evidence (FDIC, SEC, Social Security Act 1935, Wagner Act 1935, 1937 recession, court-packing plan 1937); complexity (distinguishes relief/recovery/reform). 3 = thesis with some evidence. 2 = partial. 1 = no thesis.

weeks.prep: Print a map of aggression 1931–1939; FDR's 'Arsenal of Democracy' fireside chat (Dec. 29, 1940); Lindbergh's America First speech excerpt (Des Moines, Sept. 11, 1941 — parental note: contains antisemitic statements; discuss how it was condemned at the time); FDR's Four Freedoms speech (Jan. 6, 1941); Norman Rockwell's Four Freedoms paintings (1943); FDR's 'Day of Infamy' draft with handwritten edits (DocsTeach). Build the quiz with a sourcing question.
misconceptions: Students think appeasement was cowardice. Leaders sought to avoid another catastrophic war; it failed because Hitler's aims were unlimited.
Students think the U.S. was fully neutral until Pearl Harbor. The U.S. aided Britain through cash-and-carry (1939), destroyers-for-bases (1940) and Lend-Lease (1941).
Students think isolationists were all pro-Nazi. Most opposed involvement because of WWI's costs; some leaders like Lindbergh also used antisemitic rhetoric.

days.guide: Map aggression by Japan, Italy and Germany 1931–1939 and explain appeasement at Munich.

questions.q: What happened at the Munich Conference (1938)?
questions.a: Britain and France agreed to let Germany annex the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia in hopes of avoiding war; Chamberlain claimed 'peace for our time'.

days.guide: Compare Lindbergh's America First speech with FDR's 'Arsenal of Democracy' in a T-chart.

questions.q: What did FDR mean by 'arsenal of democracy'?
questions.a: The U.S. should supply Britain and other democracies with weapons to fight the Axis, without sending troops.

days.guide: Read the Four Freedoms speech, analyze Rockwell's paintings, and explain Lend-Lease.

questions.q: List the Four Freedoms.
questions.a: Freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, freedom from fear.

days.guide: Examine FDR's 'Day of Infamy' draft edits and explain word changes.

questions.q: Why change 'world history' to 'infamy'?
questions.a: 'Infamy' conveys shame and outrage, framing the attack as treacherous and unifying Americans for war.

days.guide: Give the quiz with a sourcing question.

questions.q: What was Lend-Lease?
questions.a: A 1941 law letting the U.S. lend or lease war supplies to Britain and other Allies.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and China (1937). 2) Italy invaded Ethiopia (1935). 3) Germany remilitarized the Rhineland (1936), annexed Austria (1938), took the Sudetenland after Munich (Sept. 1938), the rest of Czechoslovakia (March 1939), invaded Poland (Sept. 1, 1939). 4) Neutrality Acts (1935–37) banned arms sales to warring nations; cash-and-carry (1939). 5) Lend-Lease (March 1941) — the U.S. could lend or lease war supplies to nations vital to U.S. defense. 6) Four Freedoms — speech, worship, from want, from fear. 7) Pearl Harbor — Dec. 7, 1941. 8) Sourcing item: FDR changed 'a date which will live in world history' to 'a date which will live in infamy' and 'simultaneously' to 'suddenly' — to make the attack sound more shocking and treacherous to rally the nation.

weeks.prep: Print rationing coupons and war bond posters, a map of wartime migration to the West Coast, Executive Order 8802 (1941), the 1942 Bracero agreement summary, Executive Order 9066 (DocsTeach), Dorothea Lange and Ansel Adams Manzanar photographs (Calisphere/LOC), Korematsu v. United States (1944) majority and Murphy dissent excerpts, and the Civil Liberties Act of 1988.
misconceptions: Students think most incarcerated Japanese Americans were noncitizens. About two-thirds of the roughly 120,000 people removed were U.S. citizens.

Students think Korematsu was overruled at the time. The Court upheld it 6–3 in 1944; his conviction was vacated in 1983, and the Court said in Trump v. Hawaii (2018) that Korematsu was 'gravely wrong'.
Students think the Bracero Program ended with the war. It ran from 1942 to 1964.

days.guide: Study rationing, war bonds and the growth of California shipyards and aircraft plants; map wartime migration.

questions.q: How did WWII change California's economy?
questions.a: Massive federal spending built shipyards (e.g., Kaiser in Richmond) and aircraft plants (Douglas, Lockheed), drawing hundreds of thousands of workers, including many Black and women workers.

days.guide: Analyze Randolph's threatened march, EO 8802 and the Bracero agreement.

questions.q: What did Executive Order 8802 do?
questions.a: Banned discrimination in defense industries and government based on race, creed, color or national origin, and created the Fair Employment Practices Committee.

questions.q: What was the Bracero Program?
questions.a: A 1942–1964 agreement bringing Mexican workers on short-term contracts to fill U.S. farm and railroad labor shortages.

days.guide: Read EO 9066 and compare Lange's (censored) and Adams' Manzanar photographs.

questions.q: Why were Lange's photographs impounded?
questions.a: They showed the injustice and hardship of incarceration too clearly for the Army's liking.

days.guide: Read Korematsu excerpts and the 1988 Civil Liberties Act; discuss in a recorded conversation.

questions.q: What did Justice Murphy argue in his dissent?
questions.a: That the exclusion order fell 'into the ugly abyss of racism' and was based on racial prejudice, not real military necessity.

questions.q: What did the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 provide?
questions.a: A formal apology and $20,000 to each surviving incarcerated Japanese American.

days.guide: The student writes a 400-word response.

questions.q: About how many Japanese Americans were incarcerated, and what share were citizens?
questions.a: About 120,000; roughly two-thirds were U.S. citizens.

weeks.assessment_key: Civil liberties response rubric (400 words): 4 = clear position on when government may limit civil liberties in wartime; uses EO 9066, Korematsu majority (military necessity) and Murphy's dissent ('legalization of racism'), the 1988 apology and redress ($20,000 per surviving person), and at least one other example (Schenck, Patriot Act); addresses a counterargument; precise language. 3 = position with some evidence. 2 = general. 1 = unsupported.

weeks.prep: Print the semester review packet, a 5-document set on women's suffrage (e.g., Seneca Falls Declaration 1848, an anti-suffrage poster, California 1911 results, the 19th Amendment, a suffrage parade photo 1913), DBQ thesis prompts and rubric, and the semester exam (50 multiple-choice/stimulus questions plus a DBQ document set on the federal government's role 1900–1945).
misconceptions: Students write a thesis that restates the prompt. A thesis must take a position and preview reasons.
Students summarize documents instead of using them as evidence. Use documents to support a claim and explain how.
Students skip sourcing. Explain how the author's point of view, purpose, audience or context affects the document.

days.guide: Build an illustrated timeline (1877–1945) with 25 events and cause-effect arrows.

questions.q: Connect two events with cause and effect.
questions.a: Example: the Zimmermann Telegram (1917) → U.S. entry into WWI.

days.guide: Practice sourcing, contextualizing and corroborating with the suffrage document set.

questions.q: What does 'corroborate' mean?
questions.a: Check whether other sources agree with or contradict a document.

days.guide: Write three DBQ thesis statements for practice prompts and self-score.

questions.q: Strengthen: 'The New Deal changed America.'
questions.a: 'The New Deal permanently expanded the federal government's role by regulating banks and stocks, creating Social Security and protecting labor unions, though it did not end the Depression.'

days.guide: Give semester exam part 1 (50 questions).

questions.q: (Exam day) Which unit felt hardest?
questions.a: Answers vary.

days.guide: Give the timed 50-minute DBQ.

questions.q: Name one way the federal role expanded under the New Deal.
questions.a: Social Security (1935), FDIC deposit insurance, SEC regulation, Wagner Act labor protections.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam part 1: score multiple choice using your answer key built from Units 1–6 (sample items: 14th Amendment's equal protection; Sherman Act 1890; 17th Amendment direct election; Zimmermann Telegram; 1924 quotas; buying on margin; FDIC; EO 9066). DBQ rubric (How did the federal government's role change between 1900 and 1945?): Thesis (1 pt) — e.g., it expanded from limited regulation to managing the economy, providing social welfare and mobilizing society for war; Contextualization (1); Evidence from documents (up to 3: uses 4+ documents to support the argument); Outside evidence (1: e.g., Federal Reserve, FDIC, Social Security, WPA, War Production Board); Sourcing (1); Complexity (1: continuity, such as limits on civil rights enforcement).

weeks.prep: Print Eisenhower's D-Day order of the day and his 'in case of failure' note (DocsTeach), Truman's statement on Hiroshima (Aug. 6, 1945), Veterans History Project interviews (LOC), and six atomic-bomb DBQ documents (Stimson memo April 1945, Szilard petition July 1945, Truman statement, a Hiroshima survivor account, casualty estimates for invading Japan, Stimson's 1947 Harper's article). Parental note: Holocaust and atomic-bomb sources include disturbing descriptions and images; preview.
misconceptions: Students think the U.S. did nothing about the Holocaust. The U.S. responded slowly and restricted refugees (e.g., the St. Louis, 1939), but created the War Refugee Board in 1944, which helped rescue tens of thousands.
Students think the atomic bomb decision was simple or universally supported. Some scientists (Szilard petition) urged a demonstration or warning; historians still debate alternatives.
Students think Japanese American soldiers didn't serve. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, mostly Nisei, became one of the most decorated units for its size and length of service.

days.guide: Map Midway, Normandy, the Bulge, Iwo Jima and Okinawa; explain 'Europe first' and island hopping.

questions.q: Why was Midway a turning point?
questions.a: The U.S. sank four Japanese aircraft carriers, ending Japan's ability to launch major offensives.

days.guide: Watch a Veterans History Project interview and write a one-page profile of the Tuskegee Airmen, the 442nd or the Navajo Code Talkers.

questions.q: Why were the Navajo Code Talkers valuable?
questions.a: They transmitted messages in a code based on the Navajo language that the Japanese never broke.

days.guide: Examine U.S. responses to the Holocaust and liberators' testimony.

questions.q: What happened to the St. Louis in 1939?
questions.a: Over 900 mostly Jewish refugees from Germany were refused entry to Cuba and the U.S. and returned to Europe; about 254 later died in the Holocaust.

days.guide: Analyze six atomic-bomb documents and write a thesis.

questions.q: What did the Szilard petition ask Truman to do?
questions.a: Not to use the bomb against Japan without first giving warning and a chance to surrender, citing moral responsibility.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test with a constructed response.

questions.q: What was the Manhattan Project?
questions.a: The secret U.S. program to build the atomic bomb, with sites including Los Alamos, Oak Ridge and Hanford.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key (sample): 1) 'Europe first' strategy — defeat Germany first while holding in the Pacific. 2) Midway (June 1942) — turning point in the Pacific. 3) D-Day (June 6, 1944) — Allied invasion of Normandy. 4) Battle of the Bulge (Dec. 1944–Jan. 1945) — last major German offensive. 5) Island hopping — capture key islands, bypass others. 6) Iwo Jima and Okinawa (1945) — costly battles that shaped invasion estimates. 7) Tuskegee Airmen, 442nd, Navajo Code Talkers. 8) St. Louis (1939) — Jewish refugees turned away from Cuba and the U.S.; War Refugee Board (1944). 9) Manhattan Project. 10) Hiroshima (Aug. 6) and Nagasaki (Aug. 9, 1945); Japan surrendered Aug. 15 (formal Sept. 2). Constructed response rubric: thesis on the decision; uses at least three documents with sourcing; considers alternatives (invasion, blockade, demonstration, modifying surrender terms, Soviet entry Aug. 8).

weeks.prep: Print the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) excerpts, Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech (Fulton, Missouri, March 5, 1946), a summary of Kennan's Long Telegram (Feb. 1946), the Truman Doctrine speech (March 12, 1947), Marshall Plan aid by country, Berlin Airlift photos, and a map for the quiz.
misconceptions: Students think the Cold War was a direct war between the U.S. and USSR. It was a rivalry fought through arms races, alliances, propaganda and proxy wars.
Students think the Marshall Plan was purely charity. It rebuilt Western Europe to resist communism and to create markets for U.S. goods.
Students think NATO and the Warsaw Pact formed at the same time. NATO formed in 1949; the Warsaw Pact in 1955.

days.guide: Read the UDHR; explain the purposes of the UN, IMF and World Bank.

questions.q: Who led the drafting of the UDHR?
questions.a: Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights that drafted it.

days.guide: Analyze Churchill's speech and Kennan's Long Telegram summary.

questions.q: What did Churchill mean by an 'iron curtain'?
questions.a: A division across Europe from the Baltic to the Adriatic, with Eastern Europe under Soviet control.

days.guide: Read the Truman Doctrine; map Marshall Plan aid and explain why a rebuilt Europe mattered.

questions.q: Why did a rebuilt Europe matter to the U.S. economy?
questions.a: Prosperous European nations would buy American goods and be less likely to turn to communism.

days.guide: Analyze Berlin Airlift photos and explain NATO and the Warsaw Pact.

questions.q: How did the U.S. respond to the Berlin blockade?
questions.a: With the Berlin Airlift — flying in food and fuel for about 11 months until the USSR lifted the blockade in May 1949.

days.guide: Give the early Cold War quiz with a map section.

questions.q: What is collective security in NATO?
questions.a: Article 5: an attack on one member is an attack on all.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) UN founded 1945 (Charter signed in San Francisco). 2) UDHR (1948) — Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting commission. 3) IMF and World Bank — created at Bretton Woods (1944) to stabilize currencies and fund reconstruction/development. 4) 'Iron curtain' — Churchill's image of Soviet control dividing Europe. 5) Kennan — Soviet expansion must be contained. 6) Containment — prevent the spread of communism. 7) Truman Doctrine — aid to Greece and Turkey ($400 million) to resist communism. 8) Marshall Plan (1948–52) — about $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe; largest recipients Britain, France, West Germany, Italy. 9) Berlin blockade/airlift (1948–49). 10) NATO (1949) and Warsaw Pact (1955). Map section: identify Berlin, East/West Germany, Greece, Turkey, NATO members (U.S., Canada, UK, France, Italy, etc.), Warsaw Pact members (USSR, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Albania).

weeks.prep: Print a Korean War phases map, Truman's statement on firing MacArthur (April 1951), McCarthy's Wheeling speech excerpt (Feb. 9, 1950), Margaret Chase Smith's 'Declaration of Conscience' (June 1, 1950), Hollywood Ten statements, and the film 'Duck and Cover' (1951).
misconceptions: Students think the Korean War ended with a peace treaty. It ended with an armistice (July 27, 1953); technically the war never formally ended.

Students think McCarthy found many spies. Some Soviet espionage was real (e.g., the Rosenbergs, revealed by Venona), but McCarthy's accusations were largely unsupported and ruined many innocent people.
Students think 'Duck and Cover' was scientifically sound. It offered limited protection and also served to reduce panic and build support for civil defense.

days.guide: Map the phases of the Korean War and analyze Truman's firing of MacArthur.

questions.q: Why did Truman fire MacArthur?
questions.a: MacArthur publicly challenged Truman's limited-war policy, urging attacks on China; Truman upheld civilian control of the military.

questions.q: What were the main phases of the war?
questions.a: North Korean invasion to the Pusan Perimeter (1950), Inchon landing and UN advance to the Yalu, Chinese intervention and retreat, stalemate near the 38th parallel until the 1953 armistice.

days.guide: Read excerpts from McCarthy's Wheeling speech and Smith's 'Declaration of Conscience'.

questions.q: What did McCarthy claim at Wheeling?
questions.a: That he had a list of communists working in the State Department (he cited 205 names).

questions.q: What was Margaret Chase Smith's main point?
questions.a: McCarthy's smear tactics threatened Americans' right to criticize, hold unpopular beliefs and protest — 'the right to independent thought'.

days.guide: Study the Hollywood Ten and the blacklist.

questions.q: Who were the Hollywood Ten?
questions.a: Screenwriters and directors who refused to answer HUAC's questions about communist ties in 1947, were cited for contempt, jailed and blacklisted.

days.guide: Watch 'Duck and Cover', evaluate it as propaganda; explain the arms race and SEATO.

questions.q: What was brinkmanship?
questions.a: Secretary of State Dulles's policy of pushing to the edge of war to force the other side to back down.

days.guide: The student writes a comparison of the first and second Red Scares.

questions.q: When did McCarthy's influence collapse?
questions.a: After the televised Army-McCarthy hearings (1954) and his Senate censure in December 1954.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison essay rubric: 4 = compares the first Red Scare (1919–20: Palmer Raids, deportations of immigrant radicals, fear after the Russian Revolution) and second (late 1940s–1950s: HUAC, McCarthy, loyalty oaths, Hollywood blacklist, Rosenbergs); similarities (fear of communism, civil liberties violations, targeting of dissent) and differences (scale, Cold War nuclear context, role of television, federal loyalty programs); thesis and evidence. 3 = solid with fewer specifics. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Print the GI Bill (Servicemen's Readjustment Act, 1944) summary, Levittown advertisements and a restrictive covenant example, an HOLC redlining map of a California city (Mapping Inequality site), California population data (1940: 6.9 million; 1950: 10.6 million; 1960: 15.7 million; 1970: 20.0 million), and a summary of the 1960 California Master Plan for Higher Education.
misconceptions: Students think the GI Bill benefited all veterans equally. Black veterans often were denied loans and admission because of segregation, discrimination and redlining.
Students think covenants were illegal from the start. They were legal until Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) made them unenforceable; the Fair Housing Act (1968) banned housing discrimination.
Students think the Master Plan created the UC system. UC existed since 1868; the Master Plan defined roles for UC, CSU and community colleges.

days.guide: Analyze the GI Bill and Levittown ads; examine exclusion through redlining and covenants.

questions.q: How did redlining shape suburbs?
questions.a: Federal mortgage agencies rated minority neighborhoods as risky, so residents couldn't get loans, while new suburbs restricted sales to white buyers.

days.guide: Graph California's population 1940–1970; study aerospace, defense spending and freeways.

questions.q: Calculate California's percent population growth from 1940 to 1970.

days.guide: Read the Master Plan summary and explain the three tiers.

questions.q: What share of high school graduates was UC to admit under the Master Plan?
questions.a: The top one-eighth (12.5%).

days.guide: Analyze rock and roll's origins, television and California car and surf culture.

questions.q: Name a California band that spread surf culture nationally.
questions.a: The Beach Boys (from Hawthorne).

days.guide: Give the postwar society quiz.

questions.q: What did Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) decide?
questions.a: Courts could not enforce racially restrictive covenants.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) GI Bill — college tuition, low-interest home and business loans, unemployment pay for veterans. 2) Levittown (1947) — mass-produced suburb that barred Black buyers. 3) Redlining — HOLC/FHA maps rating minority neighborhoods hazardous, denying loans. 4) Baby boom — high birth rates 1946–1964. 5) Interstate Highway Act (1956). 6) California population grew from about 6.9 million (1940) to about 20 million (1970). 7) Aerospace/defense growth in Southern California. 8) Master Plan tiers — UC: top 12.5% of high school graduates, research, doctoral degrees; CSU: top one-third, bachelor's and master's; community colleges: open to all, transfer and vocational. 9) Rock and roll grew from rhythm and blues, gospel and country. 10) Television ownership soared in the 1950s.

weeks.prep: Get JFK's Cuban Missile Crisis address (Oct. 22, 1962), the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (Aug. 1964, DocsTeach), U.S. troop levels in Vietnam (end of year: 1960 ~900; 1963 ~16,300; 1965 ~184,300; 1967 ~485,600; 1968 ~536,100; 1970 ~334,600; 1972 ~24,200), Walter Cronkite's Feb. 27, 1968 commentary, and protest photos (Berkeley, Kent State). Build the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Students think the Cuban Missile Crisis ended with a pure U.S. win. Khrushchev removed missiles in exchange for a U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba and a secret promise to remove U.S. Jupiter missiles from Turkey.
Students think Tet was a military victory for North Vietnam. Militarily the offensive failed, but it shattered U.S. public confidence that the war was being won.
Students think the 26th Amendment came long after Vietnam. It was ratified in 1971, driven partly by the argument 'old enough to fight, old enough to vote'.

days.guide: Listen to JFK's address and role-play ExComm options (invasion, air strike, blockade/quarantine, diplomacy).

questions.q: Why did Kennedy choose a 'quarantine'?
questions.a: It showed resolve without immediately attacking, leaving time for diplomacy and avoiding a likely escalation to nuclear war.

days.guide: Read the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and graph troop levels 1960–1973.

questions.q: What power did the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution give LBJ?
questions.a: Authority 'to take all necessary measures' to repel attacks and prevent aggression in Southeast Asia, without a declaration of war.

days.guide: Analyze Cronkite's 1968 commentary and its effect.

questions.q: What did Cronkite conclude in February 1968?
questions.a: That the U.S. was 'mired in stalemate' and should negotiate an honorable exit.

days.guide: Study antiwar protests and the 26th Amendment.

questions.q: What happened at Kent State on May 4, 1970?
questions.a: Ohio National Guard troops fired on student protesters, killing four and wounding nine.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

questions.q: What was the domino theory?
questions.a: The belief that if one nation fell to communism, neighboring nations would follow.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test key (sample): 1) Containment and domino theory. 2) Bay of Pigs (April 1961) — failed CIA-backed invasion by Cuban exiles. 3) Cuban Missile Crisis (Oct. 1962) — quarantine; missiles removed; no-invasion pledge; secret Turkey deal; hotline 1963. 4) Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) — gave LBJ broad power to use force (passed 416–0 in the House, 88–2 in the Senate). 5) Troop peak about 536,000 (1968–69). 6) Tet Offensive (Jan. 1968). 7) Cronkite's 'mired in stalemate'. 8) Berkeley Free Speech Movement (1964). 9) Kent State (May 4, 1970) — Ohio National Guard killed four students. 10) 26th Amendment (1971) — voting age 18. Essay rubric: evaluates containment's successes and limits with evidence.

weeks.prep: Print Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) majority and Justice Harlan's dissent excerpts, Jim Crow photographs (LOC), Executive Order 9981 (1948), summaries of Murray v. Pearson (1936), Missouri ex rel. Gaines (1938), Sweatt v. Painter (1950), Mendez v. Westminster (1946–47) and Brown v. Board of Education (1954).
misconceptions: Students think Brown immediately desegregated schools. Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation 'with all deliberate speed', and Southern resistance delayed real integration for years.

Students think Mendez was a Supreme Court case. It was decided by a federal district court (1946) and affirmed by the Ninth Circuit (1947); it led California to repeal school segregation laws in 1947.
Students think the NAACP attacked school segregation all at once. It strategically began with graduate and law schools where inequality was easiest to prove.

days.guide: Analyze Plessy and Harlan's dissent alongside Jim Crow photos.

questions.q: What did Plessy v. Ferguson decide?
questions.a: Racial segregation laws were constitutional as long as facilities were 'separate but equal'.

questions.q: What did Harlan argue in dissent?
questions.a: 'Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.'

days.guide: Read Executive Order 9981 and explain its significance.

questions.q: What did EO 9981 (1948) do?
questions.a: Ordered equality of treatment and opportunity in the armed forces, leading to desegregation of the military.

days.guide: Trace the NAACP strategy from Murray and Gaines to Sweatt and Brown.

questions.q: Why did Sweatt v. Painter matter?
questions.a: The Court ruled Texas's hastily created Black law school was not equal to UT Law in faculty, reputation and opportunities — intangible factors counted.

days.guide: Compare Mendez v. Westminster and Brown v. Board.

questions.q: How was Mendez connected to Brown?
questions.a: Mendez struck down segregation of Mexican American students in California; Thurgood Marshall filed a brief in the appeal, and Governor Earl Warren signed the repeal of California's segregation law — Warren later wrote the Brown decision.

days.guide: The student writes a paragraph explaining how Brown overturned Plessy.

questions.q: What was the key holding of Brown?
questions.a: 'In the field of public education the doctrine of separate but equal has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.'

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = explains that Plessy (1896) upheld 'separate but equal'; the NAACP Legal Defense Fund (Houston, Marshall) chipped away with graduate-school cases (Gaines, Sweatt, McLaurin) showing separate facilities were not equal; Brown (1954, unanimous, Chief Justice Warren) held that 'separate educational facilities are inherently unequal' and violate the Equal Protection Clause, citing psychological harm (doll studies); notes Mendez as precedent and Harlan's dissent ('Our Constitution is color-blind'). 3 = accurate but fewer details. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Print Rosa Parks's arrest record and the Montgomery Improvement Association leaflet (National Archives), Freedom Riders' mugshots (Mississippi Department of Archives), excerpts of 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (April 16, 1963), Birmingham campaign photos, 'I Have a Dream' (Aug. 28, 1963) and a Malcolm X excerpt ('The Ballot or the Bullet', April 1964).
misconceptions: Students think Rosa Parks was simply tired. She was an experienced NAACP activist and secretary of the Montgomery branch who made a deliberate choice.
Students think the movement was led only by King. Local organizers, students (SNCC), women (Ella Baker, Fannie Lou Hamer, Diane Nash) and many others led.
Students think King and Malcolm X were simple opposites. They differed on integration and nonviolence, but both fought racism, and their views evolved.

days.guide: Analyze Parks's arrest record and the MIA leaflet.

questions.q: Why was the bus boycott effective?
questions.a: Black riders were the majority of Montgomery's bus customers; a sustained boycott with car pools cost the company revenue and drew national attention.

days.guide: Study Greensboro, SNCC and the Freedom Rides; analyze mugshots.

questions.q: What did the Freedom Riders test?
