questions.a: Whether Southern states would obey Supreme Court rulings desegregating interstate buses and terminals.

days.guide: Read 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' excerpts and connect to campaign photos.

questions.q: How did King distinguish just and unjust laws?
questions.a: A just law squares with moral law; an unjust law degrades human personality, and segregation laws are unjust.

days.guide: Compare 'I Have a Dream' with a Malcolm X excerpt.

questions.q: How did Malcolm X's approach differ from King's in 1964?
questions.a: He emphasized Black nationalism, self-defense and the ballot 'or the bullet', rather than nonviolent integration.

days.guide: Give the quiz on civil rights strategies and leaders.

questions.q: What is a sit-in?
questions.a: A nonviolent protest where people occupy seats in a segregated place and refuse to leave.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Montgomery Bus Boycott (Dec. 1955–Dec. 1956, 381 days); ended by Browder v. Gayle. 2) Montgomery Improvement Association — led by Martin Luther King Jr. 3) Greensboro sit-in (Feb. 1, 1960) — four NC A&T students at Woolworth's. 4) SNCC founded 1960 with Ella Baker's help. 5) Freedom Rides (1961) — CORE tested desegregation of interstate bus terminals (Boynton v. Virginia); riders attacked in Anniston and Birmingham. 6) Birmingham campaign (1963) — Bull Connor's dogs and fire hoses on children. 7) 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' — 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere'; just vs. unjust laws; criticism of the white moderate. 8) March on Washington (Aug. 28, 1963). 9) Malcolm X — Black nationalism, self-defense, 'by any means necessary'. 10) SCLC — founded 1957, King president.

weeks.prep: Print the Civil Rights Act of 1964 key titles (DocsTeach), Freedom Summer and Selma materials, voter registration data (Mississippi Black registration about 6.7% in 1964 → about 59.8% in 1967; Alabama about 19.3% → 51.6%), and LBJ's 'We Shall Overcome' speech (March 15, 1965). Rubric for the short argument.
misconceptions: Students think the 1964 Act protected voting fully. Voting protections came mainly in the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Students think the 24th Amendment banned poll taxes everywhere. It banned them in federal elections (1964); Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966) banned them in state elections.
Students think laws alone changed things. Grassroots pressure (Freedom Summer, Selma) created the political will for laws.

days.guide: Read key titles of the Civil Rights Act and explain their effects.

questions.q: What does Title VII of the Civil Rights Act do?
questions.a: Bans employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin and created the EEOC.

days.guide: Study Freedom Summer and the Selma marches.

questions.q: What happened on 'Bloody Sunday'?
questions.a: On March 7, 1965, state troopers and deputies beat marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma; televised images shocked the nation.

days.guide: Analyze registration data before and after 1965.

questions.q: Mississippi Black voter registration rose from about 6.7% (1964) to about 59.8% (1967). By how many percentage points?
questions.a: About 53 percentage points.

days.guide: Listen to LBJ's 'We Shall Overcome' speech; analyze the Great Society.

questions.q: Name three Great Society programs.
questions.a: Medicare and Medicaid (1965), Head Start, the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965), the War on Poverty.

days.guide: The student writes a short argument on the movement's most effective strategy.

questions.q: What did the 24th Amendment do?
questions.a: Banned poll taxes in federal elections (1964).

weeks.assessment_key: Short argument rubric: 4 = defensible claim on the most effective strategy (e.g., nonviolent direct action that produced media coverage, legal challenges through the courts, voter registration drives, federal legislation) supported by at least three specific examples (Brown, Montgomery, Birmingham, Selma, Civil Rights Act, Voting Rights Act, registration data); addresses a counterargument. 3 = claim with two examples. 2 = general. 1 = unsupported. Key facts: Civil Rights Act (July 2, 1964) — Title II public accommodations, Title VI federal funds, Title VII employment (race, color, religion, sex, national origin; EEOC). Voting Rights Act (Aug. 6, 1965) — banned literacy tests, federal examiners, preclearance. Freedom Summer (1964) — Chaney, Goodman and Schwerner murdered. Selma — 'Bloody Sunday', March 7, 1965.

weeks.prep: Calisphere Delano grape strike documents (photos, UFW flyers), sources on the 1968 East L.A. walkouts, Third World Liberation Front strike materials (SF State 1968–69), the Alcatraz proclamation (1969), the NOW Statement of Purpose (1966), and summaries of Title IX (1972), the ADA (1990) and Stonewall (1969). A comparison chart template.
misconceptions: Students think Chávez started the Delano strike. Filipino workers of the AWOC, led by Larry Itliong, struck first on Sept. 8, 1965; the mostly Mexican American NFWA (Chávez, Huerta) joined days later.
Students think the ERA became law. Congress passed it in 1972, but it was not ratified by 38 states before the deadline.
Students treat movements as separate. Many shared tactics (boycotts, walkouts, occupations, lawsuits) and inspired one another.

days.guide: Study Chávez, Huerta and Itliong and the Delano grape strike using Calisphere.

questions.q: What tactic made the grape strike succeed?
questions.a: A national consumer boycott of table grapes, which pressured growers to sign union contracts in 1970.

days.guide: Analyze the 1968 East L.A. walkouts.

questions.q: What did East L.A. students demand in 1968?
questions.a: Better schools: bilingual education, Mexican American teachers and history, smaller classes and an end to punishing students for speaking Spanish.

days.guide: Study the TWLF strikes and the Alcatraz occupation.

questions.q: What resulted from the SF State TWLF strike?
questions.a: The nation's first College of Ethnic Studies (1969).

questions.q: Why did Indians of All Tribes occupy Alcatraz?
questions.a: To claim the surplus federal land under treaty, protest federal policies like termination, and demand Native self-determination.

days.guide: Read the NOW Statement of Purpose; study Title IX, the ADA and Stonewall.

questions.q: What does Title IX prohibit?
questions.a: Sex discrimination in any education program receiving federal funds.

days.guide: The student creates a comparison chart of five movements.

questions.q: What did the ADA (1990) do?
questions.a: Banned discrimination against people with disabilities in employment, public accommodations, transportation and government services.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart rubric: five movements (farmworkers/UFW, Chicano Movement, Asian American/TWLF, American Indian Movement/Red Power, women's movement, and optionally disability rights or LGBTQ rights) with goals, leaders, key events, tactics and results — e.g., UFW: Chávez, Huerta, Itliong; Delano strike and grape boycott (1965–70); contracts in 1970; California Agricultural Labor Relations Act (1975). Chicano: East L.A. walkouts (1968), Sal Castro, demands for bilingual education and Mexican American history. TWLF: SF State strike (1968–69) → first College of Ethnic Studies. Red Power: Alcatraz occupation (1969–71), AIM, Wounded Knee (1973). Women: NOW (1966), Title IX (1972), ERA. Disability: ADA (1990). 4 = accurate in all columns.

weeks.prep: Print Justice Powell's opinion excerpts in Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978), the 1996 Proposition 209 ballot text and arguments for and against (California Secretary of State voter guide), and eight DBQ documents for 'How successful was the civil rights movement in achieving its goals by 1975?' (e.g., Brown, Civil Rights Act, VRA registration data, Kerner Commission excerpt 1968, Black Panther Ten-Point Program 1966, income/poverty data, Swann busing case 1971, a UFW contract photo). Build the Unit 8 test.
misconceptions: Students think Bakke banned affirmative action. It struck down UC Davis's racial quota (16 of 100 seats) but allowed race as one factor among many to pursue diversity.

Students think Prop 209 is federal law. It amended California's constitution to ban preferences in public employment, education and contracting; a 2020 repeal attempt (Prop 16) failed. Nationally, SFFA v. Harvard (2023) later ended race-conscious college admissions.
Students think 'success' must be all or nothing. Evaluate legal, political, economic and social goals separately.

days.guide: Read Powell's opinion and chart what the Court allowed and prohibited.

questions.q: What did Bakke prohibit and allow?
questions.a: Prohibited fixed racial quotas (UC Davis set aside 16 of 100 seats); allowed race as one 'plus' factor among many to achieve a diverse student body.

days.guide: Read the Prop 209 ballot arguments and summarize each side's strongest evidence.

questions.q: What did Prop 209 ban?
questions.a: Preferential treatment based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in California public employment, education and contracting.

days.guide: Source and group eight documents and draft a thesis.

questions.q: Suggest three groupings for the documents.
questions.a: Legal/political gains (Brown, CRA, VRA); economic and social limits (poverty data, Kerner Report); changing strategies (Black Power, busing).

days.guide: Write the 60-minute DBQ essay.

questions.q: What's the difference between a document summary and analysis?
questions.a: Summary repeats what it says; analysis explains how it supports your argument and considers its source.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What did the Kerner Commission (1968) conclude?
questions.a: 'Our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white — separate and unequal,' blaming white racism for urban unrest.

weeks.assessment_key: DBQ rubric (7 points): thesis with a line of reasoning (e.g., highly successful in ending legal segregation and securing voting rights, less successful in economic equality and housing); contextualization (Jim Crow, WWII, Cold War); evidence from 6+ documents; outside evidence (e.g., Fair Housing Act 1968, Loving v. Virginia 1967, Shelley v. Kraemer); sourcing for 2+ documents; complexity. Unit 8 test key (sample): Plessy and Harlan; EO 9981; Mendez; Brown; Montgomery; sit-ins; Freedom Rides; Birmingham letter; CRA Titles II/VI/VII; VRA; 24th Amendment; Delano strike; East L.A. walkouts; TWLF; Alcatraz; Title IX; Bakke — quotas unconstitutional, race may be one factor; Prop 209 (1996).

weeks.prep: Print Nixon's resignation speech (Aug. 8, 1974), United States v. Nixon (1974) excerpts, Earth Day 1970 photos, a summary of the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill, oil price and inflation/unemployment data for the 1970s, and Carter's 'Crisis of Confidence' (July 15, 1979) excerpt.
misconceptions: Students think Nixon was impeached and removed. The House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment, but Nixon resigned before a House vote.
Students think Nixon was hostile to all environmental laws. The EPA (1970), Clean Air Act (1970) and Endangered Species Act (1973) were created under Nixon.
Students think stagflation is just inflation. It is high inflation plus high unemployment and slow growth at the same time.

days.guide: Analyze Nixon's domestic and foreign policies including détente and China.

questions.q: Why was Nixon's 1972 trip to China significant?
questions.a: It opened relations with the People's Republic of China and used the China–Soviet split to pressure the USSR.

days.guide: Read U.S. v. Nixon and explain the constitutional crisis.

questions.q: What did U.S. v. Nixon decide?
questions.a: Unanimously, that executive privilege does not shield evidence needed in a criminal trial; Nixon had to release the tapes.

days.guide: Study the EPA, Clean Air Act and the Santa Barbara oil spill.

questions.q: How did the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill affect environmental policy?
questions.a: Images of oiled beaches and wildlife built public support for Earth Day and federal laws like NEPA and the Clean Air Act.

days.guide: Analyze stagflation and the oil crisis; read Carter's speech excerpt.

questions.q: What caused the 1973 oil crisis?
questions.a: Arab members of OPEC embargoed oil shipments to the U.S. for supporting Israel in the Yom Kippur War.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What did Gerald Ford do that hurt his popularity?
questions.a: He pardoned Nixon in September 1974.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Détente — easing tensions with the USSR (SALT I, 1972). 2) Nixon visited China (1972). 3) Vietnamization. 4) Watergate break-in (June 17, 1972) and cover-up. 5) U.S. v. Nixon (1974, 8–0) — executive privilege is not absolute; Nixon must turn over the tapes. 6) Nixon resigned Aug. 9, 1974; Ford pardoned him. 7) Santa Barbara oil spill (1969) — helped spark Earth Day (April 22, 1970) and environmental laws. 8) EPA (1970), Clean Air Act (1970). 9) 1973 OPEC oil embargo — prices roughly quadrupled. 10) Stagflation. 11) Carter's 'Crisis of Confidence' speech.

weeks.prep: Print Reagan's First Inaugural excerpt (Jan. 20, 1981), data for 1980–1990 (top marginal income tax rate 70% → 50% in 1982 → 28% in 1988; unemployment 7.1% in 1980, peak 10.8% late 1982, 5.3% in 1989; federal debt about $0.9 trillion in 1980 → about $2.9 trillion in 1989), 'Tear Down This Wall' (June 12, 1987), nuclear freeze rally photos, and debate sources.
misconceptions: Students think Reagan's tax cuts balanced the budget. Deficits and debt grew sharply in the 1980s because of tax cuts and increased defense spending.
Students think the Cold War ended because of a single speech. Many factors combined: Soviet economic stagnation, Gorbachev's reforms, U.S. pressure and diplomacy, and Eastern European movements.
Students confuse glasnost and perestroika. Glasnost = openness (more free speech); perestroika = restructuring of the economy.

days.guide: Read Reagan's First Inaugural and explain the rise of modern conservatism.

questions.q: Which groups formed the New Right coalition?
questions.a: Evangelical Christians, fiscal conservatives, anti-communists and many suburban and Sunbelt voters.

days.guide: Graph tax rates, deficits and unemployment 1980–1990; evaluate supply-side economics.

questions.q: What happened to the federal debt during the 1980s?
questions.a: It roughly tripled, from about $0.9 trillion to about $2.9 trillion.

days.guide: Read 'Tear Down This Wall'; study Gorbachev's reforms and the fall of the Wall.

questions.q: What did glasnost and perestroika mean?
questions.a: Glasnost: openness and freer speech; perestroika: restructuring the Soviet economy.

days.guide: Hold a structured debate on what ended the Cold War.

questions.q: Give one argument for each side.
questions.a: U.S. pressure: defense buildup and SDI strained the Soviet economy. Internal collapse: economic stagnation, the Afghanistan war, nationalism and Gorbachev's reforms unraveled the system.

days.guide: Give the quiz with a stimulus-based short answer.

questions.q: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.a: November 9, 1989.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) New Right — evangelicals, anti-tax and anti-communist conservatives. 2) 'Government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.' 3) Reaganomics — tax cuts, deregulation, reduced domestic spending, defense buildup. 4) Supply-side theory — lower taxes boost investment and growth. 5) Deficits/debt rose. 6) Gorbachev (1985) — glasnost and perestroika. 7) INF Treaty (1987). 8) Berlin Wall fell Nov. 9, 1989. 9) USSR dissolved Dec. 1991. 10) Nuclear freeze movement. Debate rubric: clear position, two cited sources each side, rebuttal, respectful delivery.

weeks.prep: Print LBJ's remarks signing the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 (Oct. 3, 1965, Statue of Liberty), Census data on immigrant origins before and after 1965, California demographic data 1970–2020 (non-Hispanic white about 77% in 1970 → about 35% in 2020; Hispanic about 40% in 2020; Asian about 15–16%; Black about 5–6%), IRCA (1986) and NAFTA (1994) overviews, and an oral history release form and recording device.
misconceptions: Students think the 1965 Act was expected to change demographics dramatically. LBJ called it 'not a revolutionary bill'; ending national-origin quotas and emphasizing family reunification led to large immigration from Latin America and Asia.
Students think IRCA only increased enforcement. It legalized about 2.7 million undocumented immigrants and created employer sanctions.
Students think NAFTA's effects were all positive or all negative. Trade increased; some U.S. manufacturing jobs and many small Mexican farmers were hurt; migration pressures grew.

days.guide: Read LBJ's signing remarks and compare immigration sources before and after 1965 using Census data.

questions.q: What did the 1965 Immigration Act end?
questions.a: The national-origins quota system from the 1920s.

days.guide: Graph California's demographics 1970–2020 and map Sunbelt migration.

questions.q: What is the Sunbelt?
questions.a: Southern and Southwestern states that grew rapidly after WWII from migration, air conditioning, defense and new industries.

days.guide: Study IRCA and NAFTA and their effects on agriculture and border communities.

questions.q: What two main things did IRCA (1986) do?
questions.a: Legalized about 2.7 million undocumented immigrants and penalized employers who knowingly hired unauthorized workers.

days.guide: Interview a family member or neighbor about migration or moving; record and transcribe 10 minutes.

questions.q: Turn 'Did you like moving?' into an open-ended question.
questions.a: 'What do you remember about your first months after moving, and what surprised you?'

days.guide: The student writes a 400-word explanation of how immigration has reshaped California since 1965.

questions.q: What was Prop 187 (1994)?
questions.a: A California ballot measure to deny public services to undocumented immigrants; it passed but was largely blocked by courts and never took effect.

weeks.assessment_key: Oral history: 10 minutes recorded and transcribed with consent; open-ended questions; context paragraph. Explanation rubric (400 words): 4 = explains how the 1965 Act ended national-origins quotas and favored family reunification and skills, with evidence of shifting sources (Europe → Latin America and Asia); uses California data (California became majority-minority around 1999–2000; Latino the largest group by 2014); IRCA, NAFTA and refugee flows (e.g., Southeast Asians after 1975); effects on culture, economy and politics (Prop 187, 1994); integrates the oral history. 3 = solid. 2 = general. 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Print a Middle East map with oil reserves and the 1991 Gulf War coalition, trade data (U.S. imports/exports, WTO founding 1995), George H. W. Bush's address on the Gulf War (Jan. 16, 1991), George W. Bush's address to Congress (Sept. 20, 2001), 9/11 Memorial & Museum oral histories (preview — emotional content), and a Patriot Act provisions summary.
misconceptions: Students think the Gulf War and Iraq War are the same. The Gulf War (1991) expelled Iraq from Kuwait; the Iraq War began in 2003 and toppled Saddam Hussein.
Students think globalization only means trade. It includes the movement of people, capital, technology, culture and ideas.
Students think the Patriot Act is unchanged. Some provisions expired or were amended; the USA FREEDOM Act (2015) ended the NSA's bulk collection of phone records.

days.guide: Map U.S. strategic and oil interests and the 1991 coalition.

questions.q: Why did the U.S. lead a coalition against Iraq in 1991?
questions.a: To reverse Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, protect Saudi Arabia and oil supplies, and uphold international law under U.N. resolutions.

days.guide: Analyze trade data and the role of the WTO and multinationals.

questions.q: What does the WTO do?
questions.a: Sets and enforces rules for international trade and settles trade disputes among members.

days.guide: Read Bush's address to Congress and listen to an oral history.

questions.q: What was the main goal Bush announced on Sept. 20, 2001?
questions.a: A war on terror against al-Qaeda and those who harbor terrorists, starting with the Taliban in Afghanistan.

days.guide: Analyze Patriot Act provisions and debate security vs. civil liberties.

questions.q: Name one Patriot Act provision that raised civil liberties concerns.
questions.a: Section 215 access to business records (later used for bulk phone data collection) or delayed-notice 'sneak and peek' searches.

days.guide: Give the quiz on post-1990 foreign policy.

questions.q: When did the Iraq War begin?
questions.a: March 2003.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Iraq invaded Kuwait Aug. 2, 1990; Operation Desert Storm Jan.–Feb. 1991 with a U.N.-backed coalition of about 35 nations. 2) U.S. interests — oil, regional stability, allies. 3) Globalization — interconnected economies; WTO (1995), NAFTA (1994). 4) Multinational corporations. 5) 9/11 — al-Qaeda attacks killed nearly 3,000 people. 6) 'Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.' 7) War in Afghanistan (Oct. 2001). 8) Patriot Act (Oct. 2001) — expanded surveillance and information sharing (roving wiretaps, business records, delayed-notice searches). 9) Department of Homeland Security (2002). 10) Debate of security vs. liberty.

weeks.prep: Print a computing timeline (ENIAC 1945–46; transistor 1947; integrated circuit 1958–59; Intel 1968; Apple 1976; IBM PC 1981; World Wide Web 1989–91; iPhone 2007), Pew/BLS data on women's labor-force participation (about 34% in 1950, 43% in 1970, 58% in 1990, peak 60% in 1999, about 56% in 2020), local government data on homelessness and housing costs for a California city, and a summary of the California Environmental Quality Act (1970) and state climate laws (AB 32, 2006; SB 32, 2016). Build the Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Students think Silicon Valley began with personal computers. It grew from defense-funded electronics, Stanford, and semiconductor firms (Fairchild, Intel) in the 1950s–60s.
Students think homelessness has one cause. Housing costs, income, mental illness, addiction and policy all interact; California's high housing costs are a major driver.
Students think women's labor participation rose steadily without limits. It rose sharply from 1950 to the late 1990s, then plateaued.

days.guide: Trace the computer revolution from ENIAC to the smartphone and analyze effects on work.

questions.q: How did the transistor and integrated circuit change computing?
questions.a: They replaced bulky vacuum tubes, making computers smaller, cheaper, faster and more reliable.

days.guide: Graph women's labor-force participation 1950–2020 and explain changing family structures.

questions.q: Give two reasons women's labor participation rose after 1950.
questions.a: Expanded education, the women's movement and anti-discrimination laws, economic need, service-sector growth, access to contraception.

days.guide: Research homelessness, housing costs and drug policy in a California city using local data.

questions.q: Why is housing so expensive in many California cities?
questions.a: High demand with limited new construction due to zoning, land costs, regulations and slow permitting.

days.guide: Trace environmental laws from the EPA to California's climate policies and evaluate controversies.

questions.q: What does CEQA require?
questions.a: Public agencies must study and disclose significant environmental impacts of projects and mitigate them where feasible.

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test.

questions.q: What triggered the Great Recession?
questions.a: The collapse of a housing bubble fueled by risky mortgages, causing a financial crisis in 2008.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test key (sample): 1) 1965 Immigration Act. 2) IRCA. 3) NAFTA. 4) Gulf War (1991). 5) 9/11 and Patriot Act. 6) Silicon Valley origins (Stanford, defense funding, semiconductors). 7) Women's labor-force participation roughly 34% (1950) to about 60% (1999). 8) Great Recession (2007–09) — housing bubble and financial crisis. 9) CEQA (1970) requires environmental review of projects. 10) AB 32 (2006) — cut GHG to 1990 levels by 2020; SB 32 (2016) — 40% below 1990 by 2030. 11) Income inequality trends since the 1980s.

weeks.prep: Open the National History Day theme page (nhd.org), Calisphere, LOC and DocsTeach. Arrange library database access (public library card) for secondary sources. Annotated bibliography template (Chicago or MLA style per NHD rules).
misconceptions: Students choose topics too broad ('World War II'). Narrow to a specific person, event or decision connected to California and the theme.
Students treat any old source as primary. A primary source is created at the time by participants or witnesses; a later history book is secondary.
Students write annotations that only summarize. NHD annotations explain how the source was used and why it is credible.

days.guide: Choose a 20th-century California topic tied to the NHD theme and write a research question.

questions.q: Narrow 'immigration' into a researchable question.
questions.a: Example: 'How did detention at Angel Island shape Chinese immigrants' communities in San Francisco, 1910–1940?'

days.guide: Find at least six primary sources.

questions.q: Is a 1936 Dorothea Lange photograph primary or secondary?
questions.a: Primary — created at the time by a witness.

days.guide: Find three secondary sources and summarize historians' interpretations.

questions.q: What is historiography?
questions.a: The study of how historians' interpretations of an event have changed over time.

days.guide: Write the annotated bibliography.

questions.q: What should an NHD annotation include?
questions.a: A brief description of the source, how you used it, and why it's credible.

days.guide: Submit research question, thesis and bibliography for review.

questions.q: What makes a working thesis strong?
questions.a: It makes an arguable claim that answers the research question and can change as evidence is found.

weeks.assessment_key: Bibliography rubric: research question connected to the NHD theme and California; working thesis; at least 6 primary sources (Calisphere, LOC, DocsTeach) and 3 secondary sources (scholarly books or articles); correct citation format; annotations (2–3 sentences each) describing the source and how it was used; separated into primary and secondary. 4 = all criteria met; 3 = minor citation errors; 2 = too few sources or weak annotations; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Poster board or a website builder (NHDWebCentral) or video tools; slides; the NHD rule book for word limits (exhibits 500 student-composed words; papers 1,500–2,500 words; process paper up to 500 words); a project rubric.
misconceptions: Students build first, argue later. Outline thesis, context, evidence and significance before building.
Students fill projects with quotes. Balance primary-source evidence with the student's own analysis.
Students forget the 'so what'. Explain the topic's significance and connection to the theme.

days.guide: Outline the argument with context, thesis, evidence and significance.

questions.q: What belongs in the context section?
questions.a: Background events and conditions needed to understand the topic.

days.guide: Build the exhibit, website, documentary or paper.

questions.q: How should primary sources be used in the project?
questions.a: As evidence that directly supports specific claims, with captions or analysis explaining their meaning.

days.guide: Write the 500-word process paper.

questions.q: What four things does a process paper explain?
questions.a: How you chose the topic, how you researched, how you created the project, and how it connects to the theme.

days.guide: Rehearse a 5-minute presentation and answer mock judge questions.

questions.q: Example judge question?
questions.a: 'Which source changed your thinking the most, and why?'

days.guide: Present the project and receive feedback.

questions.q: How should you respond to critical feedback?
questions.a: Listen, thank them, ask a clarifying question, and note what to revise.

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric (NHD-style): Historical quality 60% (accurate, analysis and interpretation, historical context, wide research, balanced primary/secondary sources); Relation to theme 20% (clear connection, significance); Clarity of presentation 20% (organized, follows rules, original and clear). Process paper: how the topic was chosen, research conducted, project created, and connection to the theme (≤500 words). 4 = strong in all categories.

weeks.prep: Final review packet, a decade-by-decade chart template (1900–2000), practice documents, the final exam (multiple choice and stimulus questions covering all units), and a DBQ document set on continuity and change in the federal government's role in civil rights (e.g., 14th Amendment, Plessy, EO 9981, Brown, Civil Rights Act 1964, VRA 1965, Bakke, Shelby County v. Holder 2013).
misconceptions: Students treat continuity-and-change prompts as only change. Address what stayed the same as well as what changed.
Students list events without analysis. Connect each event to the argument.
Students skip reflection as unimportant. Reflection consolidates learning.

days.guide: Create a decade-by-decade chart (1900–2000) with political, economic, social and foreign policy columns.

questions.q: Fill one row: the 1930s.
questions.a: Political: New Deal, FDR; Economic: Great Depression; Social: Dust Bowl migration, repatriation; Foreign: neutrality, rising aggression abroad.

days.guide: Practice document analysis and a timed thesis for a continuity-and-change prompt.

questions.q: Write a continuity-and-change thesis on the federal role in the economy, 1900–1945.
questions.a: 'Although the federal government shifted from limited regulation to active management of the economy through the New Deal, it continued to rely on private enterprise and left many workers, such as farm and domestic laborers, outside new protections.'

days.guide: Give final exam part 1.

questions.q: (After the exam) Which era do you understand best now?
questions.a: Answers vary.

days.guide: Give the timed DBQ on the federal government's role in civil rights.

questions.q: What did Shelby County v. Holder (2013) decide?
questions.a: It struck down the Voting Rights Act's coverage formula, effectively ending preclearance unless Congress updates it.

days.guide: The student writes a reflection on how the course changed their understanding of America.

questions.q: What makes a reflection strong?
questions.a: Specific examples of events or sources that changed your thinking, and how.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam part 1: score with your key built from all unit keys. Part 2 DBQ rubric (7 points): thesis on continuity and change (e.g., the federal role shifted from tolerating segregation — Plessy — to actively enforcing civil rights — Brown, CRA, VRA — while continuity appears in limits and backlash, such as slow enforcement, Bakke and Shelby County weakening VRA preclearance); contextualization; evidence from 6 documents; outside evidence; sourcing; complexity. Reflection: specific examples of changed understanding.

MATH.overview: Algebra II runs about 60 minutes a day: 10–15 minutes of you modeling one worked example aloud, 25–30 minutes of the student working problems while you circulate and ask 'how do you know?', and 10 minutes of checking answers (Desmos is the referee for graphs). Insist on written steps, not just answers, and have the student correct every missed quiz item with a one-line explanation of the error. Pacing is one unit roughly every three to four weeks; if a quiz score is below 80%, spend an extra day on Khan Academy practice before moving on.

weeks.prep: Bookmark Desmos and set up a notebook with a 'function gallery' page. Print or draw six blank coordinate grids. Preview Khan Academy 'Transformations of functions'.
misconceptions: Thinking f(x−3) moves the graph LEFT 3. Show with a table: the output f(0) now happens at x = 3, so the graph moves RIGHT. Inside changes act 'opposite' to what they look like.
Confusing a vertical stretch a·f(x) with a horizontal change f(bx). Have the student plot both y = 2x² and y = (2x)² in Desmos and compare which points move.

days.guide: Model graphing y = x² and recording a table of domain, range, and intercepts. The student then graphs the other five parents (linear, absolute value, square root, cube root, cubic) in Desmos and fills the table. Check each row against the graphs before moving on.

questions.q: State the domain and range of y = √x.
questions.a: Domain x ≥ 0; range y ≥ 0. You cannot take the real square root of a negative, and the outputs are never negative.

questions.q: Which parent functions have domain AND range of all real numbers?
questions.a: Linear y = x, cube root y = ∛x, and cubic y = x³.

days.guide: Show the slider for y = (x − h)² + k in Desmos and ask the student to predict before dragging each slider. Then have them write rules for the 10 pictured graphs, saying the shift in words first ('right 2, down 5').

questions.q: Describe how g(x) = (x + 4)² − 3 is related to f(x) = x².
questions.a: Shift left 4 and down 3; the vertex moves from (0, 0) to (−4, −3).

questions.q: Write the rule for y = |x| shifted right 2 and up 5.

days.guide: Graph y = x², 3x², ½x², and −x² together and have the student describe each change. Then explore f(bx) with y = √(4x) and y = √x. Student matches the 12 cards and explains two matches aloud.

questions.q: Describe y = −½x² compared with y = x².
questions.a: Reflected over the x-axis and vertically compressed by a factor of ½ (it opens down and is wider).

questions.q: Show that √(4x) is the same as a vertical stretch of √x.
questions.a: √(4x) = √4·√x = 2√x, so it is a vertical stretch by 2 (equivalently a horizontal compression by ¼).

days.guide: Model g(x) = −2|x − 3| + 1 by transforming key points of |x|: (−1,1), (0,0), (1,1) become (2,−1), (3,1), (4,−1). Student graphs three similar functions by hand, then checks each in Desmos.

questions.q: Give the vertex, direction, and range of g(x) = −2|x − 3| + 1.
questions.a: Vertex (3, 1); opens down; slopes −2 and 2 on each side; range y ≤ 1.

questions.q: Where does (2, 4) on f(x) = x² go under y = (x + 1)² − 5?
questions.a: (1, −1): left 1 and down 5.

days.guide: Give the 10-item quiz closed-book (Desmos off), about 25 minutes. Grade together, then let the student verify any missed graph in Desmos and write the corrected rule.

questions.q: Write the equation of an absolute value graph with vertex (−1, 4) that opens down with slopes ±1.

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested 10 items and answers: 1) y=(x−5)²: right 5. 2) y=x²+7: up 7. 3) y=−|x|: reflect over x-axis. 4) y=√(x+2)−1: left 2, down 1. 5) y=3x³: vertical stretch by 3. 6) y=|½x|: horizontal stretch by 2 (same as vertical compression by ½). 7) parabola vertex (2,−3) opening up, same shape as x²: y=(x−2)²−3. 8) square root starting at (−4,0): y=√(x+4). 9) V-shape vertex (0,6) opening down slopes ±2: y=−2|x|+6. 10) cubic x³ moved right 1, up 2: y=(x−1)³+2. Score 1 point each; 8+/10 is mastery.

weeks.prep: Find a current USPS price list or make a simple parking-garage table (e.g., $5 first hour, $3 each extra hour or part). Have Desmos ready (it graphs piecewise with braces).
misconceptions: Using a closed dot on both pieces at a boundary. A function has one output per input: check which piece's condition includes the boundary (≤ or ≥) and put the closed dot only there.
Solving |x + 3| = −4 and getting answers. An absolute value is never negative, so there is no solution; always isolate the absolute value first and check its sign.

days.guide: Model f(x) = {x + 2 if x < 1; 3x if x ≥ 1}: graph each piece only on its interval, open dot at (1, 3) on the first piece, closed dot at (1, 3) on the second. Student graphs three piecewise functions and evaluates at boundaries.

questions.q: For f(x) above, find f(1), f(0), and f(−3).

days.guide: Use the parking table: $5 for the first hour or part, $3 for each additional hour or part. Student builds the table, graphs the step function with open/closed dots, and explains what a jump means.

questions.q: Using that rate, what does 2.5 hours cost? What about exactly 2 hours?
questions.a: 2.5 hours: 5 + 3 + 3 = $11 (any part of the third hour counts). Exactly 2 hours: 5 + 3 = $8.

days.guide: Model: isolate the absolute value, then split into two equations (= +value and = −value). Student solves 6–8 equations and substitutes each answer back to check.

questions.q: Solve |2x − 5| = 9.
questions.a: 2x − 5 = 9 gives x = 7; 2x − 5 = −9 gives x = −2. Both check.
|x − 1| = −1, which is impossible: no solution.

days.guide: Teach 'less than = AND (between)', 'greater than = OR (outside)'. Model |x − 4| < 3, then the tolerance problem. Student graphs each solution on a number line.

questions.q: Solve |x − 4| < 3 and |2x + 1| ≥ 5.
A bolt must be 10 mm long with tolerance 0.05 mm. Write and solve the inequality.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Review the average rate of change as (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) on one piece before starting. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on piecewise evaluation, graphing, and absolute value solutions; average rate of change on each piece. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: For f(x) = 3x on [1, 3], what is the average rate of change?

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) For g(x) = {x² if x ≤ 0; 2x+1 if x > 0}: g(−2)=4, g(0)=0, g(3)=7. 2) Graph: parabola left of 0 with closed dot at (0,0), line from open dot (0,1). 3) |x+2|=6 → x=4 or x=−8. 4) |3x|−4=5 → x=±3. 5) |x−1|≤4 → −3≤x≤5. 6) |x+5|>2 → x>−3 or x<−7. 7) Average rate of change of x² on [−3,−1]: (1−9)/2 = −4. 8) Parking 3.2 h at $5 + $3/extra hour: $14. Full credit requires checked solutions and correctly drawn endpoints.

weeks.prep: Graph paper and Desmos. Prepare a ticket problem and a bakery profit problem (below). Review elimination yourself with one 3×3 example.
misconceptions: Forgetting to multiply every term (including the constant) when scaling an equation for elimination. Have the student draw arrows to each term as they multiply.
Assuming the maximum profit is at the 'middle' of the feasible region. The optimum of a linear objective always occurs at a vertex; have the student test every corner in a table.

days.guide: Solve x + y = 10, x − y = 4 three ways (graph, substitution, elimination) and compare. Then show a parallel system and an identical-line system. Student solves and classifies six systems.

questions.q: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
questions.a: Add: 2x = 14, x = 7, y = 3. Solution (7, 3).

questions.q: How many solutions does 2x + 4y = 8, x + 2y = 4 have?
questions.a: Infinitely many: the first equation is 2 times the second (same line).

days.guide: Model eliminating one variable from two different pairs to get a 2×2 system, then back-substitute. Student solves the ticket problem. Today's task from the plan: Solve three-variable systems by elimination; model a ticket-sales problem with three prices. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x + y − z = 1.
questions.a: Subtract eq 2 from eq 1: 2y = 4, y = 2. Then x + z = 4 and 2x − z = −1; add: 3x = 3, x = 1, z = 3. (1, 2, 3).

questions.q: 100 tickets sold for $720: adult $10, student $6, child $4, with as many adult as student tickets. How many of each?

days.guide: Model graphing each inequality, shading, and testing (0, 0). Student writes constraints for a budget-and-time problem and shades the feasible region. Today's task from the plan: Graph a feasible region for a budget-and-time constraint problem. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: With x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 8, 2x + y ≤ 12, is (3, 4) feasible? Is (5, 4)?

days.guide: Bakery: x cakes, y pies, constraints from yesterday, profit P = 5x + 3y. Model finding vertices by solving pairs of boundary lines, then evaluate P at each in a table.

questions.q: Find the vertices and maximum profit.
questions.a: Vertices (0,0), (6,0), (4,4), (0,8). P = 0, 30, 32, 24. Maximum $32 at 4 cakes and 4 pies.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test (about 50 minutes). Allow graph paper; no Desmos except for the final check after submitting. Today's task from the plan: Unit 1 test: transformations, piecewise functions, and systems. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Solve 3x + 2y = 16 and x − y = 2.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key (sample items): 1) y=−(x+2)²+1: reflect, left 2, up 1. 2) Write rule: |x| right 3 down 4 → y=|x−3|−4. 3) f(x)={−x if x<0; √x if x≥0}: f(−4)=4, f(9)=3. 4) |x−6|=2 → 4, 8. 5) |2x−1|>7 → x>4 or x<−3. 6) 2x+3y=12, x−3y=−3 → x=3, y=2. 7) x+y+z=4, 2x−y+z=6, x+2y−z=0 → (2, 0, 2). 8) Linear programming with P=4x+5y on vertices (0,0),(6,0),(3,4),(0,5): max 32 at (3,4). Grading: 4 = all correct with work; 3 = minor arithmetic slips; 2 = method right but several errors; 1 = method errors.

weeks.prep: Desmos; draw a few square-and-rectangle area models (or use algebra tiles). Find a short video of a ball being thrown for Day 4.
misconceptions: Reading the vertex of y = (x − 3)² + 2 as (−3, 2). The h value is the number that makes the inside zero: x = 3.
When completing the square with a ≠ 1, forgetting to multiply the added constant by a. Factor a out first and track it: 2(x² − 4x + 4) adds 8, not 4.

days.guide: Model y = −2(x − 1)² + 5 as transformations of x². Student graphs four vertex-form equations by hand and labels vertex, axis, and max/min. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = a(x−h)²+k using transformations; identify vertex, axis, and max/min. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: State the vertex, axis of symmetry, and max/min of y = −2(x − 1)² + 5.
questions.a: Vertex (1, 5); axis x = 1; opens down, so maximum value 5.

days.guide: Show that zeros come straight from factored form and the vertex x is their midpoint. Student graphs three factored-form quadratics. Today's task from the plan: Graph from zeros; find vertex via the midpoint of the zeros. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the zeros and vertex of y = (x − 2)(x + 6).

days.guide: Draw x² + 6x as a square plus two 3-by-x strips; the missing corner is 9. Model converting x² + 6x + 5, then 2x² − 8x + 3. Student converts five more.

questions.q: Write x² + 6x + 5 in vertex form.
Write 2x² − 8x + 3 in vertex form.

days.guide: Use h = −16t² + 32t + 48 (feet, seconds). Student writes it in factored and vertex form and says which form answers which question. Today's task from the plan: For one context (a launched ball), use each form to answer a different question. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: When does the ball land, what is its maximum height, and from what height was it launched?
questions.a: Factored: −16(t − 3)(t + 1), lands at t = 3 s. Vertex: −16(t − 1)² + 64, max 64 ft at 1 s. Standard: launched from 48 ft (the constant).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Afterwards, check graphs in Desmos. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on converting forms and graphing key features. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Write y = x² − 4x − 12 in vertex and factored form.
questions.a: Vertex form (x − 2)² − 16; factored (x − 6)(x + 2).

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) y=(x+1)²−9 → standard x²+2x−8, factored (x+4)(x−2). 2) y=x²−10x+21 → (x−5)²−4; zeros 3, 7. 3) y=3x²+12x+7 → 3(x+2)²−5. 4) y=−(x−4)(x+2): zeros 4, −2, vertex (1, 9). 5) Graph y=½(x−2)²−2: vertex (2,−2), zeros 0 and 4. 6) Which form shows the y-intercept? Standard form (c). Mastery = 5 of 6 with work shown.

weeks.prep: Index cards (one equation per card) for Day 5 sorting. Preview Khan Academy 'Quadratic formula proof'.
misconceptions: Dividing both sides by x (e.g., in x² = 5x) and losing the solution x = 0. Move everything to one side and factor: x(x − 5) = 0.
Mis-handling −b and the 2a in the quadratic formula (e.g., dividing only the radical by 2a). Write the formula with one long fraction bar and substitute b in parentheses.

days.guide: Model factoring 6x² + x − 2 by the ac method (ac = −12, use 4 and −3). Student solves 8 equations by factoring, setting each factor to zero. Today's task from the plan: Factor trinomials with a ≠ 1, difference of squares, and GCF; solve by zero-product property. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 6x² + x − 2 = 0.
Solve 4x² − 25 = 0.

days.guide: Model (x − 3)² = 20 by square roots (remember ±), then x² + 8x − 1 = 0 by completing the square. Student does six of each. Today's task from the plan: Solve equations by taking square roots and completing the square. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve (x − 3)² = 20.
Solve x² + 8x − 1 = 0 by completing the square.

days.guide: Walk through completing the square on ax² + bx + c = 0 symbolically, line by line, with the student writing each step. Then solve 8 equations with the formula.

questions.q: Solve 2x² − 3x − 5 = 0 with the quadratic formula.

days.guide: Explain b² − 4ac: positive = two real roots (two x-intercepts), zero = one repeated root (vertex on axis), negative = two complex roots (no x-intercepts). Student predicts for 8 equations, then checks in Desmos.

questions.q: Classify the solutions of x² + 4x + 7 = 0 and 9x² − 12x + 4 = 0.
questions.a: First: 16 − 28 = −12 < 0, two complex (non-real) solutions. Second: 144 − 144 = 0, one repeated real solution (x = 2/3).

days.guide: Student sorts the 12 cards by best method, solves, and writes a one-sentence justification for each. Discuss choices together. Today's task from the plan: Choose the most efficient method for 12 equations and justify each choice. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Which method is best for x² = 49, x² + 5x + 6 = 0, and 3x² + 7x − 2 = 0?
questions.a: Square roots (x = ±7); factoring ((x + 2)(x + 3), x = −2, −3); quadratic formula (doesn't factor nicely: x = (−7 ± √73)/6).

weeks.assessment_key: Score each item 1 pt for a reasonable method and 1 pt for correct solutions. Sample answers: x²=49 → ±7 (roots); (x−4)²=9 → 1, 7 (roots); x²−7x+12=0 → 3, 4 (factor); 2x²+5x−3=0 → 1/2, −3 (factor); x²+6x=2 → −3±√11 (complete square); x²−2x−1=0 → 1±√2 (formula or complete square); 3x²+7x−2=0 → (−7±√73)/6 (formula); x²+2x+10=0 → −1±3i accepted later or 'no real solution' (formula). Proficient = 20/24 or better with justifications that mention structure (no linear term, nice factors, a=1 and even b, etc.).

weeks.prep: Graph paper for a complex plane (horizontal real axis, vertical imaginary axis). Preview Khan Academy 'Intro to i'.
misconceptions: Writing √(−4)·√(−9) = √36 = 6. Convert first: 2i·3i = 6i² = −6.
Treating i like a variable and leaving i² in the answer. Always replace i² with −1 and write the result as a + bi.

days.guide: Ask: what number squared is −1? Define i, then build the cycle i, −1, −i, 1. Student simplifies powers of i by dividing the exponent by 4. Today's task from the plan: Explore why x²+1 = 0 has no real solutions; define i and simplify powers of i. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify i²³ and √(−49).

days.guide: Model adding like combining like terms and multiplying with FOIL, replacing i² with −1. Student practices and plots one sum as a vector on the complex plane.

questions.q: Compute (3 + 2i)(1 − 4i).
Compute (5 − i) + (−2 + 3i).

days.guide: Show that (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b² is real. Model dividing by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate. Today's task from the plan: Use conjugates to divide complex numbers and rationalize denominators. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Divide (2 + 3i)/(1 − i).

days.guide: Solve x² + 2x + 5 = 0 with the formula, simplifying √(−16) = 4i. Then factor sums of squares over the complex numbers. Today's task from the plan: Solve quadratics with negative discriminants; factor x²+4 as (x+2i)(x−2i). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve x² + 2x + 5 = 0.
Factor x² + 9.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes) without a calculator. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on complex arithmetic and complex solutions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Compute (4 − 3i)(4 + 3i).

weeks.prep: Tennis ball, phone that records video (slow-motion helps), a wall or doorframe with tape marks every foot (or meter), stopwatch. Desmos regression: type a table and y1 ~ ax1² + bx1 + c.
misconceptions: Thinking the parabola is the path in the air across the room. In the lab the graph is height vs TIME; a ball tossed straight up still produces a parabola in time.
Accepting a negative time or a negative length as an answer. Always state the domain that makes sense in context and reject nonviable solutions.

days.guide: Toss the ball straight up next to the taped wall while the phone records. Step through the video to record height every 0.1 s (or every few frames). Enter points in Desmos and fit y ~ ax² + bx + c.

questions.q: Why should the data be quadratic, and what should a be close to?
questions.a: Gravity gives constant downward acceleration, so height vs time is a parabola. In feet a ≈ −16 (half of −32 ft/s²); in meters a ≈ −4.9.

days.guide: Student uses the regression to find the vertex (max height) and positive zero (landing time) and compares the a-value to −16 (or −4.9). Today's task from the plan: Use the regression to find max height and landing time; compare to h = −16t² + v₀t + h₀. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: For h = −16t² + 48t + 6, find the maximum height and when it lands.
questions.a: Vertex at t = −48/(2·−16) = 1.5 s; h = −36 + 72 + 6 = 42 ft. Landing: −16t² + 48t + 6 = 0 → t = (48 + √2688)/32 ≈ 3.12 s (reject the negative root).

days.guide: Model solving y = x², y = x + 2 by substitution and showing the two crossing points in Desmos. Discuss 0, 1, or 2 intersections. Today's task from the plan: Solve algebraically and graphically (e.g., a line crossing a parabola). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve y = x² and y = x + 2.

days.guide: Model the fencing problem: 40 ft of fence, A = x(20 − x). Then revenue R = p(200 − 10p). Student finds each vertex and interprets. Today's task from the plan: Solve a fencing/area and a revenue (price × quantity) maximization problem. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What dimensions maximize the area with 40 ft of fence?
questions.a: A = x(20 − x) has vertex at x = 10: a 10 ft × 10 ft square, 100 sq ft.

questions.q: If quantity sold is 200 − 10p, what price maximizes revenue?
questions.a: R = 200p − 10p², vertex p = 10: price $10, revenue $1,000.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test (about 50 minutes) and collect the lab report. Today's task from the plan: Unit 2 test: forms, solving methods, complex numbers, and modeling. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Solve x² − 6x + 13 = 0.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric (4 pts each): data table and graph; regression equation stated; max height and landing time found and interpreted; comparison of a to −16 or −4.9 with a sentence on error sources. Unit 2 test sample answers: (x−1)²−9 → zeros −2, 4; 2x²+x−6=0 → 3/2, −2; x²+2x+3=0 → −1±i√2; (2−i)/(2+i) = (3−4i)/5; max of −5t²+20t+1 is 21 at t=2; y=2x+3 and y=x² meet at (3, 9) and (−1, 1).

weeks.prep: Algebra tiles or area-model templates. Have the student review exponent rules from Algebra I.
misconceptions: Writing (x + 2)² = x² + 4 (forgetting the middle term). Draw the area model: the two 2x rectangles are part of the square.
Subtracting only the first term of the second polynomial. Rewrite subtraction as adding the opposite and distribute the negative to every term.

days.guide: Model naming polynomials by degree and number of terms. Student classifies 10 polynomials and rewrites each in standard form. Today's task from the plan: Classify polynomials by degree and terms; write in standard form. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Classify 4x³ − 2x + 7 and write 5 − 3x² + x⁴ in standard form.
questions.a: 4x³ − 2x + 7: cubic trinomial (degree 3, three terms). 5 − 3x² + x⁴ = x⁴ − 3x² + 5, a quartic trinomial.

days.guide: Model combining like terms vertically. Discuss closure: integers + integers stay integers; polynomials ± and × stay polynomials. Today's task from the plan: Combine polynomials and discuss closure compared with integers. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (3x² − 2x + 5) − (x² + 4x − 1).
Are polynomials closed under division? Give an example.
questions.a: No. 1 ÷ x = 1/x (x⁻¹) is not a polynomial.

days.guide: Use an area grid to multiply (2x − 1)(x² + 3x − 4), then expand (x + 2)³ as (x + 2)(x + 2)². Today's task from the plan: Multiply polynomials with area models and distribution, including (x+2)³. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Expand (x + 2)³.
Multiply (2x − 1)(x² + 3x − 4).

days.guide: Prove an identity by expanding one side until it matches the other. Use (x² − y²)² + (2xy)² = (x² + y²)² to make Pythagorean triples. Today's task from the plan: Prove (a+b)² and a³−b³ identities; use x²+y² identity to generate Pythagorean triples. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Use x = 3, y = 2 in the identity to make a Pythagorean triple.
Verify a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
questions.a: (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³ = a³ − b³.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes) including one written proof. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on operations and a written proof of one identity. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Expand (x − 3)².

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) (4x³+x−2)+(x³−5x+9) = 5x³−4x+7. 2) (2x²−x)−(5x²+3x−4) = −3x²−4x+4. 3) (x−4)(x+4) = x²−16. 4) (3x+2)(x²−x+1) = 3x³−x²+x+2. 5) (2x−1)³ = 8x³−12x²+6x−1. Proof rubric (4 levels): 4 = expands one side completely, each step justified, ends with the other side; 3 = correct with a skipped step; 2 = partial expansion; 1 = substitutes numbers only (numbers check but do not prove).

weeks.prep: Practice set of division problems. Remind the student of numerical long division (divide, multiply, subtract, bring down).
misconceptions: Leaving out missing terms (e.g., dividing x³ − 7x + 6 without a 0x² placeholder). Always write every power with zeros as placeholders.
Using +3 instead of −3 in synthetic division for the divisor x + 3. The number in the box is the zero of the divisor: x + 3 = 0 → −3.

days.guide: Model (x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6) ÷ (x − 2) side by side with 1,452 ÷ 12. Student does five long divisions. Today's task from the plan: Divide polynomials by binomials using long division, connecting to numerical long division. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Divide (2x² + 5x − 1) ÷ (x + 3).
questions.a: 2x − 1 with remainder 2: (2x² + 5x − 1) = (x + 3)(2x − 1) + 2.

days.guide: Model synthetic division for the same problem as Day 1, comparing time. Student does eight synthetic divisions. Today's task from the plan: Use synthetic division for divisors of the form x−a; compare speed. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Divide (x³ − 7x + 6) ÷ (x + 3) synthetically.
questions.a: Use −3 with coefficients 1, 0, −7, 6: bottom row 1, −3, 2, 0 → x² − 3x + 2, remainder 0.

questions.q: Divide (x³ + 2x² − 5x − 6) ÷ (x − 2).
questions.a: Bottom row 1, 4, 3, 0 → x² + 4x + 3, remainder 0.

days.guide: Have the student compute p(3) directly and by synthetic division with 3; they match. State the Remainder Theorem. Today's task from the plan: Verify that p(a) equals the remainder; use it to evaluate p(3) quickly. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: For p(x) = x³ − 4x² + x + 5, find p(3) and the remainder of p(x) ÷ (x − 3).
questions.a: p(3) = 27 − 36 + 3 + 5 = −1, and the remainder is also −1.

days.guide: Remainder 0 means x − a is a factor. Model factoring x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 given root 1. Student factors four cubics. Today's task from the plan: Determine whether x−a is a factor and fully factor cubics given one root. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Factor x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6 given that x = 1 is a zero.
questions.a: Synthetic with 1 gives x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3).

questions.q: Is x + 1 a factor of x³ + 1?

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on division methods and theorems. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Find the remainder when x⁴ − 3x + 2 is divided by x − 2.

weeks.prep: Desmos for checking zeros. Make a reference card: a³ ± b³ = (a ± b)(a² ∓ ab + b²).
misconceptions: Factoring x³ − 27 as (x − 3)³. Expand (x − 3)³ to show it is different; use the difference-of-cubes pattern.
Listing only p/q with positive signs in the Rational Root Theorem. Every candidate needs ±.

days.guide: Model a³ − b³ and a³ + b³ (SOAP: Same, Opposite, Always Positive) and quadratic-form polynomials. Student factors eight. Today's task from the plan: Factor sums/differences of cubes and quadratic-form polynomials like x⁴−5x²+4. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Factor x³ − 27 and 8x³ + 1.
Factor x⁴ − 5x² + 4 completely.

days.guide: Model grouping the first two and last two terms and pulling out the common binomial. Student factors six. Today's task from the plan: Factor four-term polynomials by grouping. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Factor x³ + 3x² − 4x − 12.

days.guide: Model listing ±(factors of constant)/(factors of leading coefficient), testing with synthetic division, and factoring the quotient. Today's task from the plan: List possible rational roots and test with synthetic division. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Find the zeros of 2x³ − 3x² − 11x + 6.

days.guide: State the Fundamental Theorem: a degree-n polynomial has exactly n complex zeros counting multiplicity. Model finding complex zeros after factoring out real ones.

questions.q: Find all zeros of x³ − x² + 4x − 4.
Find all zeros of x⁴ − 16.

days.guide: Give the quiz: five polynomials, all zeros with multiplicities (about 35 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz: find all zeros of five polynomials and state multiplicities. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: State the zeros and multiplicities of f(x) = (x − 1)²(x + 3).
questions.a: x = 1 with multiplicity 2; x = −3 with multiplicity 1.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) x³−4x = x(x−2)(x+2): 0, 2, −2 (each mult. 1). 2) x³+2x²+x = x(x+1)²: 0 (1), −1 (2). 3) x³−2x²−9x+18 = (x−2)(x−3)(x+3): 2, 3, −3. 4) x⁴−13x²+36 = (x−2)(x+2)(x−3)(x+3): ±2, ±3. 5) x³+8 = (x+2)(x²−2x+4): −2, 1±i√3. Full credit requires all zeros (including complex) and multiplicities.

weeks.prep: Desmos and graph paper. Prepare a few printed polynomial graphs for Day 4 and the quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking a zero with multiplicity 2 crosses the axis. Even multiplicity touches and turns (bounces); odd crosses (multiplicity 3 flattens as it crosses).
Forgetting to use the y-intercept to find the leading coefficient when writing an equation from a graph.

days.guide: In Desmos, graph x², x³, −x⁴, −x⁵ and record end behavior in a 2×2 table (even/odd degree × positive/negative lead). Today's task from the plan: Investigate how degree and leading coefficient determine end behavior using Desmos. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Describe the end behavior of f(x) = −2x⁵ + 3x² − 1.
questions.a: Odd degree, negative leading coefficient: as x → ∞, f(x) → −∞; as x → −∞, f(x) → +∞.

days.guide: Graph y = (x − 1), (x − 1)², (x − 1)³ and compare behavior at x = 1. Today's task from the plan: Explore how even vs. odd multiplicity affects the graph at a zero. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does y = (x + 2)²(x − 3) behave at each zero?
questions.a: At x = −2 (multiplicity 2) it touches and turns; at x = 3 (multiplicity 1) it crosses.

days.guide: Model the sketch checklist: degree & end behavior, zeros & multiplicity, y-intercept, then a smooth curve. Student sketches y = (x + 2)(x − 1)²(x − 4) and two more.

questions.q: List the features of y = (x + 2)(x − 1)²(x − 4).
questions.a: Degree 4, leading coefficient positive: both ends up. Crosses at −2 and 4, bounces at 1. y-intercept (2)(1)(−4) = −8.

days.guide: Give one polynomial as a graph and one as an equation; student compares zeros, end behavior, and approximate maximum. Today's task from the plan: Compare a polynomial given by graph to one given by equation (max, zeros, end behavior). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Which has more real zeros: f(x) = x³ − x, or a graph that crosses the x-axis only once?
questions.a: f(x) = x(x − 1)(x + 1) has three real zeros (−1, 0, 1), so f has more.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 35 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz: sketch three polynomials and write equations from two graphs. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Write a cubic with zeros −3 (cross) and 2 (bounce) passing through (0, 12).

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: sketches graded on end behavior (1), zeros with correct cross/bounce (2), y-intercept (1). Sketch 1: y=x(x−3)² — starts low, crosses at 0, bounces at 3, ends high. Sketch 2: y=−(x+1)(x−2)(x−4) — up on left, down on right, crosses −1, 2, 4, y-int −8. Sketch 3: y=(x−1)³ — flattens and crosses at 1, y-int −1. Equations: graph with zeros −2, 1, 3 (all crossing) and y-int 6 → y=(x+2)(x−1)(x−3); quartic bouncing at ±2 with y-int 16 opening up → y=(x−2)²(x+2)².

weeks.prep: Cardstock (letter size 8.5 × 11 in), scissors, ruler, tape. Draw Pascal's triangle to row 6 yourself.
misconceptions: In the binomial expansion, forgetting to raise the coefficient (e.g., the 2 in 2x) to the power. Put each term in parentheses: (2x)³ = 8x³.
In the box problem, allowing x values that make a side negative. The domain is 0 < x < (shorter side)/2.

days.guide: Each corner square is x in; student builds boxes with x = 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5 in, measures volume, then models V(x) = x(11 − 2x)(8.5 − 2x) and finds the max in Desmos.

questions.q: What cut size maximizes volume for an 8.5 × 11 sheet, and what is the domain?
questions.a: Domain 0 < x < 4.25. Maximum at x ≈ 1.59 in, V ≈ 66.1 in³.

days.guide: Build Pascal's triangle (each entry = sum of two above). Expand (a + b)² and (a + b)³ and match coefficients. Today's task from the plan: Build Pascal's triangle and connect rows to (a+b)^n coefficients. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is row 4 of Pascal's triangle and what does it give?
questions.a: 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 — the coefficients of (a + b)⁴ = a⁴ + 4a³b + 6a²b² + 4ab³ + b⁴.

days.guide: Model (2x − 3)⁴ using C(4, k)(2x)^(4−k)(−3)^k. Then find one term of (x + 2)⁷ without expanding. Today's task from the plan: Expand (2x−3)⁴ and find a specific term using combinations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Expand (2x − 3)⁴.
Find the x³ term of (x + 2)⁷.

days.guide: Model profit = revenue − cost with function notation. Student adds/multiplies two functions and interprets. Today's task from the plan: Add and multiply functions (e.g., revenue minus cost = profit) and interpret. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: R(x) = 15x and C(x) = 5x + 2000. Write P(x) and find the break-even point.
questions.a: P(x) = 10x − 2000; break-even when P = 0: x = 200 units.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test (about 50 minutes) and collect the box lab write-up. Today's task from the plan: Unit 3 test on polynomial operations, zeros, graphs, and modeling. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Find the remainder of x³ + 2x² − x + 4 divided by x + 1.

weeks.assessment_key: Box lab rubric: measured volumes table (1), correct V(x) and domain (1), max found (x≈1.59 in, V≈66.1 in³ for letter paper) (1), comparison of physical boxes to the model (1). Unit 3 test sample answers: (x²−3x+2)(x+4) = x³+x²−10x+8; zeros of x³−7x−6 = −1, −2, 3; (x+1)⁵ coefficients 1,5,10,10,5,1; end behavior of −x⁴: both down; x²+4x+5 zeros −2±i.

weeks.prep: Practice set. Remind the student how to simplify numerical fractions and find LCDs.
misconceptions: Cancelling terms instead of factors, e.g., (x + 3)/(x + 5) → 3/5. Only common FACTORS cancel; factor first.
Forgetting excluded values from the original denominator after a factor cancels.

days.guide: Model factoring numerator and denominator, cancelling common factors, and listing excluded values from the ORIGINAL denominator. Today's task from the plan: Factor and simplify rational expressions, stating excluded values. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (x² − 9)/(x² + 5x + 6) and state excluded values.

days.guide: Model multiply = factor everything then cancel; divide = multiply by the reciprocal. Today's task from the plan: Multiply and divide rational expressions with factoring. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (x/3) ÷ (x²/6).

days.guide: Model finding the LCD from factored denominators and rewriting each fraction. Today's task from the plan: Find LCDs and add/subtract rational expressions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify 3/x + 2/(x + 1).
Simplify 1/(x − 2) − 4/(x² − 4).

days.guide: Method 1: simplify top and bottom then divide. Method 2: multiply top and bottom by the LCD of all small fractions. Compare. Today's task from the plan: Simplify complex fractions by two methods and compare. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify (1 + 1/x)/(1 − 1/x²).
questions.a: Multiply by x²: (x² + x)/(x² − 1) = x(x + 1)/((x − 1)(x + 1)) = x/(x − 1).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on rational expression operations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Simplify (2x + 6)/(x² − 9).

weeks.prep: Desmos. Look up Boyle's law (pressure × volume constant at fixed temperature).
misconceptions: Thinking a graph can never cross a horizontal asymptote. Horizontal asymptotes describe end behavior only; graph y = x/(x² + 1) to see it cross y = 0.
Calling every zero of the denominator a vertical asymptote. If the factor cancels, it is a hole.

days.guide: Introduce y = k/x. Model finding k from one data point. Graph and discuss why y never reaches 0. Today's task from the plan: Model Boyle's law-type inverse variation and graph y = k/x. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: y varies inversely with x and y = 6 when x = 4. Find y when x = 8.
A gas at 2 atm occupies 6 L. At constant temperature, what is its volume at 3 atm?
questions.a: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂: 12 = 3V, V = 4 L.

days.guide: Treat y = a/(x − h) + k like any transformation: asymptotes x = h and y = k. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = a/(x−h)+k and identify asymptotes. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give the asymptotes of y = 3/(x + 2) − 1.
questions.a: Vertical x = −2; horizontal y = −1.

days.guide: Model factoring, finding holes (cancelled factors), vertical asymptotes (remaining denominator zeros), and horizontal asymptote by comparing degrees. Today's task from the plan: Find vertical asymptotes, holes, and horizontal asymptotes from factored forms. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find holes and asymptotes of f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² − x − 2).
questions.a: (x − 1)(x + 1)/((x − 2)(x + 1)): hole at x = −1 (point (−1, 2/3)), vertical asymptote x = 2, horizontal asymptote y = 1.

days.guide: Model dividing (2x + 3) by (x − 1) to get 2 + 5/(x − 1), and read the graph as 5/x shifted right 1, up 2. Today's task from the plan: Use long division to rewrite (2x+3)/(x−1) as 2 + 5/(x−1) and interpret the graph. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Rewrite (2x + 3)/(x − 1) and name its asymptotes.
questions.a: 2 + 5/(x − 1) (since 2(x − 1) + 5 = 2x + 3). Vertical x = 1, horizontal y = 2.

days.guide: Give the quiz: graph three rational functions with all features labeled (about 35 minutes). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of y = 3x/(x² + 4)?
questions.a: Degree of denominator is greater, so y = 0.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) y=1/(x−3)+2: VA x=3, HA y=2, y-int 5/3, x-int 5/2. 2) y=(x+1)/(x−2): VA x=2, HA y=1, x-int −1, y-int −1/2. 3) y=(x²−4)/(x−2): hole at (2, 4), otherwise the line y = x+2, no asymptotes. Each graph: 1 pt each for VA, HA/hole, intercepts, correct branches.

weeks.prep: Practice set. Prepare one 'two pipes' and one boat-current problem. Calculator allowed.
misconceptions: Not checking solutions in the original equation. Any value that makes an original denominator zero is extraneous.
Averaging speeds (e.g., 60 and 40 → 50) for a round trip. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

days.guide: Model multiplying both sides by the LCD, solving, then checking each answer against excluded values. Today's task from the plan: Solve rational equations by multiplying by the LCD; check for extraneous solutions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 3/x + 1/2 = 2.
questions.a: Multiply by 2x: 6 + x = 4x, x = 2. Check: 1.5 + 0.5 = 2 ✓.
x = 3 + 2(x − 3) → x = 3, which makes a denominator zero: extraneous, so no solution.

days.guide: Model 'work rate = 1/time' and adding rates. Student solves four job problems. Today's task from the plan: Solve 'two pipes fill a tank' and shared-job problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 h, pipe B in 3 h. Together?
questions.a: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 tank per hour, so 2 hours.

days.guide: Model a d = rt table for upstream and downstream. Student solves three rate problems. Today's task from the plan: Solve upstream/downstream and average-speed problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A boat goes 12 mph in still water against a 3 mph current for 30 miles, then back. Total time?
questions.a: Upstream 30/9 = 3⅓ h, downstream 30/15 = 2 h; total 5⅓ h (5 h 20 min).

questions.q: Drive 120 miles at 60 mph and return at 40 mph. Average speed?
questions.a: Time 2 + 3 = 5 h for 240 miles: 48 mph.

days.guide: Model isolating f in the lens formula by multiplying through by the LCD. Today's task from the plan: Rearrange formulas like 1/f = 1/a + 1/b (lens formula) to isolate variables. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 1/f = 1/a + 1/b for f, then find b when a = 30 and f = 10.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test (about 50 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Unit 4 test on rational expressions, functions, and equations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 sample key: 1) simplify (x²−x−6)/(x²−9) = (x+2)/(x+3). 2) 1/x + 1/(2x) = 3/(2x). 3) y=(x−1)/(x+4): VA x=−4, HA y=1. 4) 5/x = 10/(x+3) → x=3. 5) x/(x−1) − 1/(x−1) = 1 → 1 = 1 for all x ≠ 1 (an identity; x = 1 is excluded). 6) Two painters, 4 h and 6 h: 2.4 h together. 7) Solve 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ for R₂: R₂ = RR₁/(R₁ − R). Rubric: method 2 pts, answer and check 1 pt each.

weeks.prep: Practice set. A calculator without radical simplification is fine; much of this is mental.
misconceptions: Thinking 27^(2/3) = 27·(2/3) = 18. The denominator is the root and the numerator is the power: (∛27)² = 9.
Adding unlike radicals: √2 + √3 ≠ √5. Only like radicals (same index and radicand) combine.

days.guide: Use the power rule: (8^(1/3))³ = 8¹ = 8, so 8^(1/3) must be ∛8 = 2. Student evaluates nth roots, including odd roots of negatives. Today's task from the plan: Evaluate nth roots and explain why 8^(1/3) = 2 using exponent properties. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate ⁴√81 and ⁵√(−32).
questions.a: 3 and −2.

questions.q: Why does 8^(1/3) = 2?
questions.a: (8^(1/3))³ = 8^((1/3)·3) = 8, and 2³ = 8, so 8^(1/3) is the cube root of 8, which is 2.

days.guide: Model converting x^(m/n) = (ⁿ√x)^m and applying exponent rules. Today's task from the plan: Convert and simplify expressions like 27^(2/3) and x^(3/4)·x^(1/2). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify x^(3/4) · x^(1/2).

days.guide: Model pulling out perfect powers, and multiplying different indices by converting to rational exponents. Today's task from the plan: Simplify and multiply radicals with different indices. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify √72 and ∛54.
Write √2 · ∛2 as a single radical.

days.guide: Model combining like radicals and rationalizing with a conjugate. Today's task from the plan: Add, subtract, and rationalize denominators with radicals. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify 3√12 + √27.
Rationalize 4/(3 − √5).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes, no calculator). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on rational exponents and radical simplification. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Simplify (x⁶y³)^(1/3).
questions.a: x²y.

weeks.prep: String and a washer (pendulum), a meter stick, stopwatch. Desmos.
misconceptions: Forgetting to check radical-equation answers. Squaring can introduce extraneous solutions; substitute back every time.
Writing f⁻¹(x) as 1/f(x). The inverse undoes f; it is not the reciprocal.

days.guide: Graph √x and ∛x, then transformations; student states domain/range for six. Today's task from the plan: Graph transformations of √x and ∛x and state domain and range. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: State domain and range of y = √(x − 2) + 3.
questions.a: Domain x ≥ 2; range y ≥ 3.

questions.q: What is the domain of y = ∛(x + 1)?
questions.a: All real numbers (cube roots of negatives exist).

days.guide: Model isolate the radical, square both sides, solve, CHECK. Student solves six. Today's task from the plan: Solve √(x+3) = x−3 type equations and identify extraneous roots. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve √(x + 3) = x − 3.
questions.a: x + 3 = x² − 6x + 9 → x² − 7x + 6 = 0 → x = 1 or 6. Check: x = 1 gives 2 = −2 ✗; x = 6 gives 3 = 3 ✓. Solution x = 6.

days.guide: Model f(g(x)) as 'do g first.' Use a currency chain: dollars → euros → yen with made-up rates. Today's task from the plan: Compose functions and evaluate f(g(x)) in context (currency conversions). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find f(g(3)) and g(f(3)).
