questions.a: f(g(3)) = f(9) = 19. g(f(3)) = g(7) = 49. Order matters.

questions.q: If E(d) = 0.9d converts dollars to euros and Y(e) = 160e converts euros to yen, what is Y(E(d))?
questions.a: Y(E(d)) = 160(0.9d) = 144d yen per d dollars.

days.guide: Model swap x and y, solve for y, verify f(f⁻¹(x)) = x. Then time 10 swings for three string lengths and compare to T = 2π√(L/g). Today's task from the plan: Find inverses algebraically, verify by composition, and graph reflections over y = x; model pendulum period T = 2π√(L/g) and invert to find length. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = 3x − 4 and of g(x) = x³ + 1.
How long should a pendulum be for a 2-second period (g = 9.8 m/s²)?

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on radical equations and inverses. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Solve √(2x + 1) = 5.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) √(x−4) = 3 → x=13. 2) √(x+7) = x+1 → x=2 (x=−3 extraneous). 3) ∛(x−2) = −3 → x=−25. 4) f(x)=2x+5, g(x)=x−1: f(g(x)) = 2x+3. 5) inverse of y=(x−1)/2 is y=2x+1. 6) inverse of y=√x (x≥0) is y=x², x≥0. 7) Verify inverses by showing f(g(x)) = x. Scoring 1 pt each plus 1 pt for checks shown.

weeks.prep: Print or assemble a semester review packet (Khan Academy unit tests work well) and a 25-problem non-calculator exam plus a calculator section. Clear two quiet 60-minute blocks for the exam.
misconceptions: Rushing the review by only re-reading notes. Have the student do mixed problems without knowing the topic first, which is what the exam requires.
Leaving answers unchecked under time pressure. Teach a 5-minute end-of-test check of extraneous solutions and signs.

days.guide: Student works a mixed set (transformations, systems, quadratics, complex numbers) for 40 minutes; you mark and they redo misses. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on transformations, systems, quadratics, and complex numbers. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve x² + 4x + 8 = 0.

days.guide: Mixed set on polynomial zeros, graphs, and rational functions; correct together. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on polynomial zeros, graphs, and rational functions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find all zeros of x³ − 2x² − 3x.
Name the asymptotes of y = (x + 1)/(x − 4).
questions.a: VA x = 4, HA y = 1.

days.guide: Mixed set on radicals and inverses; student builds a one-page formula sheet as study (not for use on exam unless you allow it). Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on radicals and inverses; make a one-page formula sheet. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the inverse of f(x) = (x − 2)³.

Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Simplify (3 − i)(2 + 5i).

days.guide: Exam part 2: calculator and two extended-response modeling tasks. Afterward, the student corrects errors for half credit back. Today's task from the plan: Calculator and modeling section with two extended-response tasks. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A ball's height is h = −16t² + 64t + 5. When is it highest and how high?

weeks.assessment_key: Score part 1 by item (1 pt each, 25 pts). Representative answers: (x+3)²−7 vertex (−3,−7); |x−2|<5 → −3<x<7; (2,−1) solves 2x+y=3, x−y=3; i³⁰=−1; x³−8 = (x−2)(x²+2x+4); (x²−x−2)/(x−2) = x+1; 8^(2/3)=4; √(x−1)=x−3 → x=5. Part 2 extended responses (4-point rubric each): 4 = correct model, correct answer with units, interpretation of domain/limits; 3 = minor error; 2 = correct setup, incomplete solution; 1 = some relevant work. Semester grade: 90%+ excellent, 75–89% proficient, below 75% reteach weak units in January.

weeks.prep: 100 coins (or M&Ms) and a cup. Desmos. Make a table template: round, number remaining.
misconceptions: Confusing growth factor and rate: a 6% increase is b = 1.06, not 0.06 or 6. A 15% decrease is b = 0.85.
Thinking an exponential function eventually reaches its asymptote. y = 100(0.5)^x gets closer to 0 but never equals 0.

days.guide: Show two tables (constant difference vs constant ratio). Student classifies six tables and writes each rule. Today's task from the plan: Compare constant difference vs. constant ratio in tables. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.a: First: ratio 2, exponential, y = 3·2^x. Second: difference 3, linear, y = 3x + 5.

days.guide: Graph y = ab^x and transformations; identify y-intercept and horizontal asymptote. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give the asymptote and y-intercept of y = 3(2)^x − 4.
questions.a: Asymptote y = −4; y-intercept 3 − 4 = −1.

days.guide: Shake coins, remove heads, record remaining each round until few left. Fit an exponential regression in Desmos. Today's task from the plan: Shake 100 coins, remove heads each round, record counts, and fit an exponential model. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Starting with 100 coins, what model do you expect, and about how many remain after 4 rounds?
questions.a: N ≈ 100(0.5)^n; after 4 rounds about 100/16 ≈ 6 coins.

days.guide: Model writing y = ab^x from (0, 5) and (2, 45), and from percent statements. Today's task from the plan: Write models from two points and from percent rate statements (population, depreciation). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Write the exponential through (0, 5) and (2, 45).
A $24,000 car loses 15% per year. Write a model and find its value after 3 years.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes) and collect the decay lab table and graph. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on graphs and writing exponential models. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Is y = 200(1.03)^t growth or decay, and by what percent?
questions.a: Growth, 3% per time period.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab rubric: data table (1), graph with regression (1), b-value compared to 0.5 (1), explanation of why the ratio is about one half (1). Quiz sample key: 1) y=2(3)^x → y-int 2, HA y=0, growth. 2) through (1, 6) and (3, 54): b=3, a=2, y=2·3^x. 3) population 50,000 growing 2%/yr: P=50000(1.02)^t. 4) 0.7^x decay by 30%. 5) table 80, 40, 20 → y = 80(0.5)^x.

misconceptions: Using r = 4 instead of 0.04. Always convert percent to decimal.
Mixing up n (compounds per year) with t (years). Label every variable before substituting.

Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the balance: $1,000 at 4% compounded monthly for 5 years.

days.guide: Spreadsheet: column of n = 1, 10, 100, 1000, … and (1 + 1/n)^n. Watch it level off. Today's task from the plan: Increase n in a spreadsheet to see (1 + 1/n)^n approach e. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What are (1 + 1/n)^n for n = 1 and n = 100, and what does it approach?
questions.a: 2 and about 2.7048; it approaches e ≈ 2.71828.

days.guide: Model A = Pe^(rt) and compare to monthly compounding. Then use it for bacteria growth. Today's task from the plan: Use A = Pe^(rt) for continuous compounding and bacterial growth. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: $500 compounded continuously at 3% for 10 years?

days.guide: Show that 1.15^t = (1.15^(1/12))^(12t) and compute 1.15^(1/12). Today's task from the plan: Rewrite 1.15^t as (1.15^(1/12))^(12t) to find monthly rates. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A quantity grows 15% per year. What is the equivalent monthly growth rate?

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on interest problems and equivalent forms. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Which is better: 5% compounded annually or 4.9% compounded continuously?
questions.a: Annual: 1.05 effective. Continuous: e^0.049 ≈ 1.0502. The continuous account is very slightly better (5.02% vs 5%).

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) $2,000 at 6% quarterly for 8 years: 2000(1.015)^32 ≈ $3,220.65. 2) $2,000 at 6% continuously for 8 years: 2000e^0.48 ≈ $3,232.15. 3) Monthly rate equivalent to 12% annual growth: 1.12^(1/12) ≈ 1.0095 (≈0.95%). 4) Bacteria 200e^(0.4t) at t=5: ≈1,478. 5) Explain why more frequent compounding helps but levels off (approaches e^r).

weeks.prep: Desmos. Make a small card: log_b(x) = y means b^y = x.
misconceptions: Thinking log(x + 2) = log x + log 2. Logs turn products into sums, not sums into anything.
Trying to take log of 0 or a negative number. The domain of log_b x is x > 0.

days.guide: Teach 'a log is an exponent.' Student converts 10 forms each way and evaluates mentally. Today's task from the plan: Convert between exponential and logarithmic form; evaluate log₂32 mentally. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate log₂32 and log₃(1/9).
Write 10³ = 1000 in log form.

days.guide: Use calculator log and ln; derive change of base as log_b x = ln x/ln b. Today's task from the plan: Evaluate log and ln with a calculator; use the change-of-base formula. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate log₅40.

days.guide: Graph y = 2^x and y = log₂x and y = x; show the reflection. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = log_b x as the inverse of y = b^x; identify asymptote and domain. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: State the domain, asymptote, and two points of y = log₂x.
questions.a: Domain x > 0, vertical asymptote x = 0; points (1, 0), (2, 1), (8, 3).

days.guide: Graph transformed logs in Desmos; student states features of four. Today's task from the plan: Graph transformed log functions in Desmos and state features. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give the domain, asymptote, and x-intercept of y = log₃(x + 2) − 1.
questions.a: Domain x > −2; VA x = −2; x-intercept: log₃(x + 2) = 1 → x = 1.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on log conversions and graphs. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Solve log_x 49 = 2.
questions.a: x² = 49 and the base must be positive: x = 7.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) log₄64 = 3. 2) log 0.01 = −2. 3) ln e⁵ = 5. 4) 2⁻³ = 1/8 ↔ log₂(1/8) = −3. 5) log₇20 ≈ 1.540. 6) y = log(x−3): domain x>3, VA x=3, x-int (4,0). 7) Sketch y=log₂x reflecting y=2^x over y=x.

weeks.prep: Practice set. Have the student review exponent rules (b^m·b^n = b^(m+n), etc.).
misconceptions: Writing log(M/N) = log M / log N. The quotient rule gives a difference: log M − log N.
Applying the power rule to (log x)² as 2 log x. The power must be on the argument: log(x²) = 2 log x.

days.guide: Let M = b^m, N = b^n. Then MN = b^(m+n), so log_b(MN) = m + n = log_b M + log_b N. Do the same for the quotient. Today's task from the plan: Derive the product and quotient properties from exponent rules. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Use the product rule to evaluate log 4 + log 25.

days.guide: Derive log_b(M^p) = p·log_b M from (b^m)^p = b^(mp). Today's task from the plan: Derive and apply the power property. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Simplify log₂(8³).

days.guide: Model expanding and condensing; student completes 10 items. Today's task from the plan: Expand and condense log expressions (10 items). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Expand log(x³y/z²).
questions.a: 3 log x + log y − 2 log z.

questions.q: Condense 2 ln x − ln y + ½ ln z.
questions.a: ln(x²√z / y).

days.guide: Given log 2 ≈ 0.301 and log 3 ≈ 0.477, estimate other logs using properties. Today's task from the plan: Estimate values like log 50 using known logs and properties. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Estimate log 50 and log 6.

days.guide: Give the quiz with one written proof (about 35 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz with a written proof of one property. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Condense log₃ 18 − log₃ 2.
questions.a: log₃ 9 = 2.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) log₂(4·8) = 5. 2) Expand ln(a²b) = 2 ln a + ln b. 3) Expand log(√x/y) = ½log x − log y. 4) Condense 3 log 2 + log 5 = log 40. 5) log 18 ≈ 0.301 + 2(0.477) = 1.255. Proof rubric: 4 = defines M=b^m, N=b^n, applies exponent rule, converts back correctly; 3 = small notation slip; 2 = idea present but steps missing; 1 = only numerical example.

weeks.prep: A mug of hot water, a kitchen or digital thermometer, timer. Desmos. Look up the pH and decibel definitions.
misconceptions: Forgetting to check log-equation solutions; arguments must be positive.
Treating log scales as linear: pH 3 is not 'a bit' more acidic than pH 5; it is 100 times more acidic.

days.guide: Model isolating the exponential, then taking ln of both sides. Doubling time and half-life examples. Today's task from the plan: Solve ab^(ct) = d using logarithms (doubling time, half-life). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: $500 grows at 6% per year. When does it double?
Carbon-14 half-life is 5,730 years. How old is a sample with 25% remaining?
questions.a: Two half-lives: 11,460 years.

days.guide: Model condensing to one log, rewriting in exponential form, solving, and checking. Today's task from the plan: Solve log equations and check extraneous solutions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve log₂x + log₂(x − 2) = 3.
questions.a: log₂(x(x − 2)) = 3 → x² − 2x − 8 = 0 → x = 4 or −2. Reject −2 (log of negative). x = 4.

days.guide: Record room temp, then the mug's temperature every 2 minutes for 30 minutes. Subtract room temp and fit an exponential to (T − T_room). Today's task from the plan: Record a cooling cup's temperature every 2 minutes and fit an exponential model. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why subtract room temperature before fitting the exponential?
questions.a: Newton's law says the DIFFERENCE from room temperature decays exponentially: T = T_room + (T₀ − T_room)e^(−kt); the water approaches room temp, not 0.

days.guide: Model pH = −log[H⁺], dB = 10 log(I/I₀), and magnitude comparisons with powers of 10. Today's task from the plan: Compute pH, decibel, and earthquake magnitude comparisons. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Compare pH 3 to pH 5.
questions.a: pH 3 has 10² = 100 times the hydrogen-ion concentration.

questions.q: How much more intense is 90 dB than 60 dB?
questions.a: 30 dB difference = 10³ = 1,000 times the intensity.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test (about 50 minutes) and collect the cooling lab. Today's task from the plan: Unit 6 test on exponential and logarithmic functions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

weeks.assessment_key: Cooling lab rubric: table (1), graph of T − T_room with exponential fit (1), model written in T form (1), prediction for when water reaches a chosen temperature with comment on accuracy (1). Unit 6 test sample answers: 2^x = 50 → x ≈ 5.644; e^(2x) = 7 → x ≈ 0.973; log(x+1) = 2 → x = 99; ln x + ln 3 = ln 12 → x = 4; earthquake 6.0 vs 4.0: 100 times the amplitude; half-life 8 days, 100 g after 24 days = 12.5 g.

weeks.prep: A paper plate, string, scissors, protractor, marker. Optional printed blank unit circle.
misconceptions: Thinking π = 180. π radians corresponds to 180°; π itself is about 3.14.
Mixing calculator modes. Check DEG vs RAD before every calculation (sin 30 should be 0.5 in degree mode).

days.guide: Cut string equal to the plate's radius and wrap it along the rim: that arc subtends 1 radian. Count about 6.28 radius-lengths around the circle. Today's task from the plan: Wrap string around a paper plate to construct one radian; convert between degrees and radians. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Convert 150° to radians and 3π/4 to degrees.
About how many degrees is 1 radian?

days.guide: Model s = rθ (θ in radians) and angular speed ω = θ/t, v = rω. Today's task from the plan: Use s = rθ to solve arc length and angular speed problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the arc length for r = 10 cm and θ = 2π/5.
A wheel of radius 0.3 m turns 10 revolutions per second. Linear speed?

days.guide: Draw 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles with hypotenuse 1 to find coordinates; fill the first quadrant then reflect. Today's task from the plan: Build a unit circle with special angles from 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give cos(π/3) and sin(π/4).

days.guide: Model finding the reference angle, then the sign from the quadrant (All Students Take Calculus). Today's task from the plan: Evaluate sine, cosine, and tangent for any angle using reference angles. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate sin(5π/6), cos(4π/3), tan(7π/4).
Evaluate sin 210°.
questions.a: −1/2 (reference 30°, Quadrant III).

days.guide: Quiz: fill in a blank unit circle and evaluate 10 expressions (about 30 minutes). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What are the coordinates of 2π/3 on the unit circle?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit circle key: points at 0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 are (1,0), (√3/2,1/2), (√2/2,√2/2), (1/2,√3/2), (0,1), reflected with signs into other quadrants. Sample 10: sin π/2 = 1; cos π = −1; tan π/4 = 1; sin 7π/6 = −1/2; cos 5π/3 = 1/2; tan 2π/3 = −√3; sin 3π/2 = −1; cos 3π/4 = −√2/2; sin 11π/6 = −1/2; tan π/6 = √3/3.

weeks.prep: The completed unit circle from last week.
misconceptions: Ignoring the quadrant when taking a square root: from cos²θ = 16/25, cos θ could be ±4/5; the quadrant decides the sign.
Thinking sec θ = 1/sin θ. 'S' goes with 'C': sec = 1/cos, csc = 1/sin.

days.guide: Point (cos θ, sin θ) on the unit circle forms a right triangle with legs |cos θ|, |sin θ| and hypotenuse 1; Pythagoras gives the identity. Today's task from the plan: Prove sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 from the unit circle and the Pythagorean theorem. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Use the identity to check sin(π/6) and cos(π/6).

days.guide: Model finding cos θ from sin θ with the identity, then the sign by quadrant. Today's task from the plan: Given sin θ = 3/5 in Quadrant II, find cos θ and tan θ. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: sin θ = 3/5 with θ in Quadrant II. Find cos θ and tan θ.

days.guide: Define sec, csc, cot as reciprocals; evaluate at special angles. Today's task from the plan: Define sec, csc, cot and evaluate them on the unit circle. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate sec(π/3), csc(π/6), cot(π/4), and sec(π/2).
questions.a: 2, 2, 1, and undefined (cos(π/2) = 0).

days.guide: Student finds all six values from one given value for 12 problems. Today's task from the plan: Solve 12 problems finding all six trig values from one value. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: cos θ = −5/13 in Quadrant III. Find the other five.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on the identity and reciprocal functions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: If tan θ = 1 and θ is in Quadrant III, find sin θ.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) proof of sin²+cos²=1 from x²+y²=1 (rubric: diagram, coordinates, Pythagorean step). 2) cos θ = 0.6 in QIV → sin θ = −0.8, tan θ = −4/3. 3) csc(3π/2) = −1. 4) sec(π/4) = √2. 5) cot(π/6) = √3. 6) sin θ = −1/3 in QIII: cos θ = −2√2/3.

weeks.prep: Desmos in radian mode. Spaghetti or string optional to 'unwrap' the unit circle.
misconceptions: Computing period as b instead of 2π/b. Larger b means MORE cycles, so a SHORTER period.
Confusing amplitude with the maximum value. Amplitude = (max − min)/2; midline = (max + min)/2.

days.guide: Plot y-values of the unit circle at each special angle against the angle; connect into the sine curve. Repeat for cosine. Today's task from the plan: Plot unit-circle y-values against angle to create the sine graph. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Where are the zeros and maximum of y = sin x on [0, 2π]?
questions.a: Zeros at 0, π, 2π; maximum 1 at π/2; minimum −1 at 3π/2.

days.guide: Graph y = a sin x + d with sliders. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = a sin x + d and interpret amplitude and midline. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give the amplitude, midline, max, and min of y = 3 sin x + 2.
questions.a: Amplitude 3, midline y = 2, maximum 5, minimum −1.

days.guide: Graph y = sin(bx) for b = 1, 2, 1/2 and derive period = 2π/b. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = sin(bx) and derive period = 2π/b. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the periods of y = sin(4x) and y = cos(x/2).

days.guide: Model reading max, min, period, and a starting point from a graph to write an equation. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = a sin(b(x−h)) + d and write equations from graphs. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A cosine graph has maximum 7 at x = 0, minimum 1, and period 8. Write it.
questions.a: Amplitude 3, midline 4, b = 2π/8 = π/4: y = 3cos(πx/4) + 4.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz: graph two sinusoids and write two equations from graphs. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the phase shift of y = 2 sin(3(x − π/6))?
questions.a: π/6 to the right.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: Graph 1: y = 2 sin x − 1 (amp 2, midline −1, period 2π). Graph 2: y = cos(2x) (period π). Equation from graph with max 3, min −3, period π starting at max at x=0: y = 3cos(2x). Equation with midline 10, amplitude 5, period 24, rising through midline at x=0: y = 5 sin(πx/12) + 10. Rubric 4 pts each: amplitude, midline, period, phase/start correct.

weeks.prep: Desmos in radian mode.
misconceptions: Thinking tan x has a maximum of 1 like sine. Tangent's range is all real numbers.
Placing secant asymptotes where cosine is 1. Secant is undefined where cosine is 0.

days.guide: Build tan x = sin x/cos x: zeros where sin = 0, asymptotes where cos = 0. Today's task from the plan: Graph y = tan x from sin/cos ratios and identify asymptotes and period π. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give the period, zeros, and asymptotes of y = tan x.
questions.a: Period π; zeros at x = kπ; vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + kπ.

days.guide: Graph sin x, then csc x = 1/sin x on top: U-shapes touching the sine peaks. Today's task from the plan: Graph csc and sec from their reciprocal sine and cosine graphs. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Where are the asymptotes of y = csc x and what is its range?
questions.a: At x = kπ (where sin x = 0). Range y ≤ −1 or y ≥ 1.

days.guide: Graph cot x = cos x/sin x and compare with tan x. Today's task from the plan: Graph cot x and compare with tan x. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does cot x differ from tan x?
questions.a: Asymptotes at x = kπ (instead of π/2 + kπ), zeros at π/2 + kπ, and it decreases on each interval while tan increases. Same period π.

days.guide: Apply a, b, h, k to tangent and secant in Desmos. Today's task from the plan: Apply transformations to tangent and secant graphs. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find the period and asymptotes of y = 2 tan(x/2).
questions.a: Period π/(1/2) = 2π; asymptotes at x = π + 2kπ.

days.guide: Quiz: match six graphs to equations (about 25 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz matching six trig function graphs and equations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Which graph has U-shaped pieces opening up at x = 0 and asymptotes at ±π/2?
questions.a: y = sec x.

weeks.assessment_key: Matching key: y = tan x ↔ increasing branches, asymptotes ±π/2, through origin; y = cot x ↔ decreasing branches, asymptotes 0 and π; y = sec x ↔ U at (0,1), asymptotes ±π/2; y = csc x ↔ U at (π/2,1), asymptotes 0, π; y = tan 2x ↔ period π/2; y = −sec x ↔ downward U at (0,−1). 1 pt each.

weeks.prep: Daylight-hours table for your city (timeanddate.com 'sunrise sunset') and NOAA Tides & Currents data for a CA station (e.g., San Francisco 9414290). Desmos.
misconceptions: Using the wrong period for monthly data (should be 12 months) or for tides (about 12.4 hours, two highs per day).
Assuming the model is exact. Discuss residuals and why weather or geography make real data deviate.

days.guide: Model a wheel with diameter 50 m, center 30 m high, one turn every 10 minutes, rider starting at the bottom. Today's task from the plan: Write a sinusoidal model for a rider's height on a Ferris wheel from given dimensions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Write h(t) for the Ferris wheel.
questions.a: h(t) = −25cos(πt/5) + 30: amplitude 25, midline 30, period 10, starting at the minimum (5 m). At t = 5, h = 55 m (top).

days.guide: Enter monthly daylight hours and fit y = a cos(b(x − h)) + d by reading max, min, and period, then refine with Desmos regression. Today's task from the plan: Collect monthly daylight hours for your California city and fit a sinusoidal model. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: If maximum daylight is 14.4 h (June) and minimum 9.9 h (December), find amplitude, midline, and period.
questions.a: Amplitude (14.4 − 9.9)/2 = 2.25 h; midline 12.15 h; period 12 months.

days.guide: Plot a day or two of NOAA hourly heights and fit a sinusoid. Today's task from the plan: Use NOAA tide data for a California station to model water height. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: High tide is 5.5 ft, low tide 0.5 ft. Give amplitude, midline, and an approximate period.
questions.a: Amplitude 2.5 ft, midline 3 ft, period about 12.4 hours (two highs per day).

days.guide: Student predicts a value from each model and compares to actual data, then writes two limitations. Today's task from the plan: Use models to predict values and compare to actual data; discuss model limits. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Name one limitation of a sinusoidal tide model.
questions.a: Real tides have unequal highs/lows (mixed tides), lunar-cycle changes, and weather effects, so a single sine with a fixed amplitude will drift from the data.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test (about 50 minutes) and collect the daylight report. Today's task from the plan: Unit 7 test on radians, unit circle, identity, and trig graphs/models. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Convert 225° to radians and evaluate its cosine.

weeks.assessment_key: Daylight report rubric (4 levels): 4 = data table and graph, model with correct amplitude/midline/period/phase, prediction compared with actual, two limitations; 3 = one parameter off or weak discussion; 2 = model attempted but major parameter wrong; 1 = data only. Unit 7 sample answers: 240° = 4π/3; arc s for r=6, θ=π/3 is 2π; sin(3π/4)=√2/2; given cos θ=4/5 in QIV, sin θ=−3/5; period of y=4 sin(πx/6) is 12; y=tan x asymptotes at π/2+kπ.

weeks.prep: Stacking cups (or blocks), ruler. A ball and tape measure for Day 4.
misconceptions: Using n instead of n − 1 in a_n = a₁ + (n − 1)d. Test with n = 1: the formula must give a₁.
Confusing arithmetic (add d) with geometric (multiply by r). Check differences and ratios first.

days.guide: Measure the height of 1, 2, 3, 4 nested cups. Write a recursive rule and an explicit rule. Today's task from the plan: Build a stacking-cup pattern and write recursive and explicit rules. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A cup stack is 12 cm for 1 cup and grows 1.5 cm per added cup. Give recursive and explicit rules.
questions.a: Recursive: h₁ = 12, hₙ = hₙ₋₁ + 1.5. Explicit: hₙ = 12 + 1.5(n − 1).

days.guide: Model finding d, writing a_n, and finding any term. Today's task from the plan: Find terms and write formulas a_n = a₁ + (n−1)d. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: a₁ = 7, d = 4. Find a₂₀.
Write a formula for 3, 10, 17, ….

days.guide: Model finding r, a_n = a₁r^(n−1), and the link to y = ab^x. Today's task from the plan: Find terms and write formulas a_n = a₁·r^(n−1); connect to exponential functions. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find a formula and the 8th term of 2, 6, 18, ….

days.guide: Drop a ball from 2 m and measure rebound heights; compute ratios. Also model a savings plan that adds $50/month. Today's task from the plan: Model a savings plan and a bouncing-ball height sequence with real measurement. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A ball dropped from 2 m rebounds to 60% of its height each time. How high after the 3rd bounce?

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on sequence formulas. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Is 5, 10, 20, 40 arithmetic or geometric? Give the next term.
questions.a: Geometric with r = 2; next term 80.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) 4, 9, 14, … a₁₅ = 74. 2) explicit for 20, 17, 14: aₙ = 23 − 3n. 3) 3, −6, 12, … aₙ = 3(−2)^(n−1), a₆ = −96. 4) recursive a₁=5, aₙ=2aₙ₋₁ → 5, 10, 20, 40. 5) Which term of 2, 5, 8 … is 62? n = 21. 6) $1,000 earning 5%/yr: aₙ = 1000(1.05)^(n−1) for the start of year n.

weeks.prep: Spreadsheet. Tell the Gauss 1-to-100 story.
misconceptions: Confusing the number of terms with the last term in Σ. Count terms as (top − bottom + 1).
Applying the infinite-series formula when |r| ≥ 1. Such series diverge (no finite sum).

days.guide: Model reading and writing Σ; student evaluates six sums by hand. Today's task from the plan: Write and evaluate sums in sigma notation. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Evaluate Σ_{k=1}^{5} (2k + 1).

days.guide: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add to derive S = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. Today's task from the plan: Derive Gauss's formula for arithmetic series and apply it. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

Derive S − rS to get S_n = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r). Apply to a loan: payment = P·i/(1 − (1 + i)^(−n)). Today's task from the plan: Derive S_n = a(1−r^n)/(1−r) and apply to mortgage/loan payment problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Sum 3 + 6 + 12 + … (8 terms).
Monthly payment on $20,000 at 6%/year for 60 months?

days.guide: Spreadsheet partial sums for r = 1/2, 0.9, 1.1; observe which level off. S = a/(1 − r) when |r| < 1. Today's task from the plan: Explore convergence when |r| < 1 with a spreadsheet. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Does Σ 2(1.1)^n converge?
questions.a: No: r = 1.1 > 1, the sums grow without bound.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test (about 50 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Unit 8 test on sequences and series. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Write 2 + 4 + 6 + … + 40 in sigma notation and evaluate.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 sample answers: 1) a₁₂ of 5, 9, 13: 49. 2) a₇ of 81, 27, 9: 1/9. 3) Σ_{k=1}^{4} k² = 30. 4) sum of first 30 odd numbers = 900. 5) 1 + 3 + 9 + … + 3⁶ = 1,093. 6) 12 − 6 + 3 − … infinite = 12/(1.5) = 8. 7) Explain why 1 + 2 + 4 + … has no sum. Rubric: formula (1), substitution (1), answer (1).

weeks.prep: Two or three recent news articles that report on a study (health or education topics work well). A random number generator (random.org or a calculator).
misconceptions: Concluding cause and effect from an observational study. Only a randomized experiment can support causation; observational studies show association.
Thinking a larger sample fixes bias. A huge convenience sample is still biased; how you sample matters more than how many.

days.guide: Define survey, experiment (treatment imposed), observational study (no treatment imposed). Student classifies 12 descriptions. Today's task from the plan: Classify 12 study descriptions as surveys, experiments, or observational studies. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Researchers compare heart health of people who already drink coffee with those who don't. Which type?
questions.a: Observational study: no treatment was assigned.

questions.q: Students are randomly assigned to study with or without music. Which type?
questions.a: Experiment: researchers impose the treatment with random assignment.

days.guide: Model each sampling method with a school-of-1,000 example. Identify bias types (undercoverage, nonresponse, voluntary response, wording). Today's task from the plan: Compare simple random, stratified, cluster, and convenience samples; identify bias. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How is stratified sampling different from cluster sampling?
questions.a: Stratified: divide into groups and randomly sample from EVERY group. Cluster: divide into groups, randomly pick some whole groups, and survey everyone in them.

questions.q: An online poll on a sports site asks readers to vote. Main bias?
questions.a: Voluntary response bias: people with strong opinions choose to respond.

days.guide: Student writes a design: question, treatments, random assignment method, control, replication, and what to measure. Today's task from the plan: Design a randomized experiment testing whether music affects reaction time. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why randomize in the music/reaction-time experiment?
questions.a: To balance unknown variables (sleep, skill) between groups so differences can be attributed to music.

days.guide: Student reads two articles and writes an evaluation: study type, sample, possible bias, and whether the headline's claim is justified. Today's task from the plan: Critique two news articles reporting on data; write an evaluation. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A headline says 'Eating breakfast causes better grades' based on a survey. Is this justified?
questions.a: No. A survey is observational; confounding variables (family routines, income, sleep) could explain the association.

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on study design and bias. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is a confounding variable?
questions.a: A variable related to both the explanatory and response variables that makes it impossible to separate their effects.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) classify 5 scenarios (survey/experiment/observational). 2) name sampling method in 4 scenarios (SRS, stratified, cluster, convenience). 3) identify bias in a mall survey: undercoverage/convenience. 4) design rubric: random assignment (1), control/comparison group (1), replication (1), clear response variable (1). 5) Explain why causation cannot be concluded from an observational study.

weeks.prep: A data set of about 100 values (measure hand spans of family/friends or use published heights). Desmos normal distribution tool or a calculator with normalcdf.
misconceptions: Applying the 68-95-99.7 rule to skewed data. Check the histogram shape first.
Comparing raw scores across different tests. Convert to z-scores to compare relative standing.

days.guide: Make a histogram of the data set; describe shape, center, spread, and outliers. Today's task from the plan: Make histograms of a real data set (e.g., 100 measured hand spans) and describe shape. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What does 'approximately normal' look like?
questions.a: Single-peaked, symmetric, bell-shaped, with mean ≈ median and few extreme values.

days.guide: Draw a normal curve with mean and ±1, 2, 3 SD marked; shade regions. Today's task from the plan: Apply the 68-95-99.7 rule to estimate percentages. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: IQ scores: mean 100, SD 15. What percent lie between 85 and 115? Above 130?
questions.a: About 68% (±1 SD). Above 130 is beyond +2 SD: about 2.5%.

days.guide: Model z = (x − μ)/σ. Compare two test results. Today's task from the plan: Calculate and compare z-scores (e.g., comparing ACT and SAT performance). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: SAT 1300 (mean 1050, SD 200) vs ACT 28 (mean 21, SD 5). Which is better relative to peers?
questions.a: SAT z = 1.25; ACT z = 1.4. The ACT score is relatively better.

days.guide: Use technology to find areas; discuss when the normal model is inappropriate (skewed incomes, wait times). Today's task from the plan: Use technology to find areas under the normal curve; recognize when a normal model is not appropriate. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: With mean 100 and SD 10, find P(X > 120).
Find P(Z < 1).

days.guide: Give the quiz (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz on normal distributions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A z-score of −1.5 means what?
questions.a: The value is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key (mean 70, SD 8): 1) % between 62 and 78 ≈ 68%. 2) % above 86 ≈ 2.5%. 3) z for 82 = 1.5. 4) P(X < 82) ≈ 0.9332. 5) P(66 < X < 74) ≈ 0.383. 6) Explain why house prices are not normally distributed (right-skewed). 1 pt each.

weeks.prep: Coins, dice, and a spreadsheet with =RAND() or =RANDBETWEEN(). Find a current poll with a margin of error.
misconceptions: Interpreting a margin of error as covering all possible errors. It accounts only for random sampling variability, not biased questions or samples.
Thinking a single unusual result proves unfairness. Compare the result with the spread of many simulated results.

days.guide: Flip a coin 50 times and count heads. In a spreadsheet, simulate 100 sets of 50 fair flips and make a dot plot of head counts. Today's task from the plan: Flip a coin 50 times; simulate 100 sets in a spreadsheet to judge whether results are consistent with fairness. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: If you got 32 heads in 50 flips, is the coin likely unfair?
questions.a: With a fair coin, 32 or more heads happens only about 3% of the time, so 32 is unusual and gives some evidence the coin is unfair (but is not proof).

days.guide: Simulate 200 samples of size 50 from a population with p = 0.40; plot the sample proportions. Today's task from the plan: Simulate many samples of size 50 from a known population proportion and plot proportions. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Describe the distribution of sample proportions.
questions.a: Centered near 0.40, roughly bell-shaped, with most proportions within about ±0.14 (2 SD, since SD = √(0.4·0.6/50) ≈ 0.069).

days.guide: Estimate the margin of error as about 2 SD from the simulation and compare with 1/√n. Today's task from the plan: Estimate margin of error from simulation and compare to 1/√n. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What is the approximate margin of error for n = 400? For n = 1,000?

days.guide: Use random numbers to pick fairly (e.g., chores); analyze a game strategy with simulation. Today's task from the plan: Use random number generators to make fair decisions and analyze strategies. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How would you use a die to choose fairly among three people?
questions.a: Assign 1–2, 3–4, 5–6 to each person; each has probability 1/3.

days.guide: Give the quiz on interpreting margins of error (about 30 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Quiz interpreting a poll's margin of error. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: A poll says 52% support a measure, ±3%. Can you conclude a majority supports it?
questions.a: No. The plausible range is 49%–55%, which includes values below 50%.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample key: 1) 45% ±4% → plausible 41%–49%. 2) Quadrupling n halves the margin of error. 3) n = 2,500 → MOE ≈ 2%. 4) Explain why a self-selected online poll's margin of error is meaningless (bias). 5) Simulation shows 18–32 heads covers about 95% of fair 50-flip results; decide whether 35 heads is unusual (yes).

weeks.prep: Index cards for shuffling data. Materials for the chosen experiment (paper for airplanes, measuring tape) — let the student choose by Day 2.
misconceptions: Concluding 'no effect' when a difference isn't significant. It means the data don't give convincing evidence, not proof of no difference.
Running all trials of one treatment first (e.g., when tired). Randomize the order of trials.

days.guide: Write each result from a two-group experiment on a card; shuffle into two piles many times and record the difference in means. Compare to the actual difference.

questions.q: If only 2 of 100 shuffles give a difference as large as observed, what do you conclude?
questions.a: About 2% chance by random assignment alone, so the difference is statistically significant (unlikely to be due to chance).

days.guide: Student writes question, two treatments, response variable, randomization plan, and controlled variables. Today's task from the plan: Design a randomized experiment with two treatments (e.g., paper airplane wing design) and collect data. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Name three variables to hold constant in a paper-airplane experiment.
questions.a: Paper type and size, launcher and launch force/angle, and location (indoors, no wind).

days.guide: Run at least 20 trials per treatment in random order; record carefully. Today's task from the plan: Run the experiment with at least 20 trials per treatment. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why at least 20 trials per treatment?
questions.a: Replication reduces the effect of chance variation so a real difference is easier to detect.

days.guide: Compute means, medians, and SDs; run a randomization test (spreadsheet or by hand with many shuffles). Today's task from the plan: Analyze results with a randomization test and summary statistics. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does the p-value from the randomization test mean in your project?
questions.a: The proportion of random re-shuffles giving a difference at least as large as observed: the chance of seeing this difference if the treatment had no effect.

days.guide: Collect the report and give the Unit 9 test (about 45 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Submit a statistics project report and take the Unit 9 test. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why can a well-designed randomized experiment show causation?
questions.a: Random assignment balances other variables, so a significant difference can be attributed to the treatment.

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric (4 levels): design (randomization, control, replication), data quality (≥20 per treatment), analysis (summary stats + randomization test), conclusion (answers question, states uncertainty and limitations). Proficient = clear design, correct statistics, and a conclusion that does not overclaim. Unit 9 test sample answers: experiment vs observational identification; z = (85−75)/5 = 2; 95% within 2 SD; MOE ≈ 1/√n; interpretation of a p-value of 0.30 → not significant.

weeks.prep: Help the student find a public data set: California Department of Finance population, NOAA monthly temperatures, etc. Desmos.
misconceptions: Choosing the model with the best R² even if it makes absurd predictions. A model must also make sense in context (e.g., population can't go negative).
Extrapolating far outside the data range. Discuss how uncertainty grows beyond the data.

days.guide: Student picks a data set of 15+ points and graphs it in Desmos, writing what pattern they see. Today's task from the plan: Choose a real data set and graph it. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: What pattern would you expect in 12 months of average temperatures?
questions.a: Periodic (sinusoidal), period 12 months.

days.guide: Fit linear, quadratic, exponential, and sinusoidal regressions; plot residuals for each. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does a good residual plot look like?
questions.a: Residuals scattered randomly around 0 with no curve or pattern.

days.guide: Student writes a one-page justification: chosen model, evidence (residuals, context), and limitations. Today's task from the plan: Write a justification for the best model, including limitations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why might an exponential model fail for long-term population predictions?
questions.a: Resources limit growth; real populations level off (logistic), so exponential overpredicts.

days.guide: Student prepares a 5-minute presentation with a graph, model equation, predictions, and limits. Rehearse once. Today's task from the plan: Prepare a 5-minute presentation of the model and predictions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should every prediction slide include?
questions.a: The input value, predicted output with units, and a statement of confidence/limitations.

days.guide: Student presents; you ask two questions about model choice and limits. Today's task from the plan: Present the capstone and answer questions. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Your model predicts a value 30 years ahead. How confident should we be?
questions.a: Not very: extrapolation far beyond the data assumes the pattern continues, which is uncertain.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone rubric (4 levels per row): Data (relevant, cited source, 15+ points); Models (at least 3 fitted, equations stated); Justification (residuals and context used to choose, limitations stated); Predictions (reasonable, within or near data range, with units); Presentation (clear, 5 minutes, answers questions). Proficient (3) = all rows present and correct with minor gaps.

weeks.prep: Final review packet (Khan Academy course challenge works well). Two quiet 60-minute exam blocks.
misconceptions: Spending review time only on favorite topics. Use the semester exam and quiz errors to target weak units.
Skipping the reflection. Error analysis is where most learning from an exam happens.

days.guide: Mixed review on Units 1–5; student marks unsure items to revisit. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on quadratics, polynomials, rationals, and radicals. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve √(x + 5) = x − 1.

days.guide: Mixed review on Units 6–9. Today's task from the plan: Mixed review on exponentials, logs, trig, sequences, and statistics. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Solve 5e^(2t) = 40.
Find the sum of the infinite series 9 + 3 + 1 + ….

days.guide: Final part 1: non-calculator (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Non-calculator section. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Evaluate log₃81 + sin(π/6).

days.guide: Final part 2: calculator and modeling (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Calculator section with modeling tasks. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: $3,000 at 5% compounded monthly; when does it reach $5,000?

days.guide: Return the graded exam; student writes a reflection on each missed item and on readiness for Precalculus. Today's task from the plan: Review exam errors and write a reflection on growth and readiness for Precalculus. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should an error reflection include?
questions.a: The item, what went wrong (concept vs careless), the correct solution, and one action to prevent it.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam representative answers: (x−3)²+2 vertex (3,2); 2x²+7x+3 = (2x+1)(x+3); x³−6x²+11x−6 zeros 1, 2, 3; (x+1)/(x²−1) = 1/(x−1); 16^(3/4)=8; log₂(x)=5 → 32; cos(5π/3)=1/2; period of 3 sin(2x) is π; a₁₀ of 2, 6, 18 is 39,366; 95% of normal data within 2 SD. Grade bands: 90%+ excellent, 75–89% proficient, 60–74% basic (review before Precalculus), below 60% needs targeted summer work. Reflection rubric: complete error analysis for every missed item = full credit.

PE.overview: Lifetime Fitness runs 45 minutes a day and alternates short classroom concepts (training science, nutrition, safety) with real workouts the student logs. Demonstrate each skill, have the student practice while you watch with the week's cues, then let them perform and record data; safety and correct form come before intensity. Keep all fitness data in one journal so the baseline, midyear, and final tests can be compared and used for the personal plan.

weeks.prep: Gather a measuring tape, stopwatch, sit-and-reach box (or a yardstick taped to a box), cones, and a notebook to serve as the fitness journal. Measure a flat 1-mile route (4 laps of a standard track) and look up current Fitnessgram Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) charts for your student's age and sex on the CDE site. Have the student wear athletic shoes and bring water.
misconceptions: Thinking a low score is a 'fail.' Explain that a baseline is just a starting point; the goal is personal improvement and reaching the Healthy Fitness Zone.
Rushing push-ups or curl-ups to get a higher count. Fitnessgram uses a cadence (1 rep every 3 seconds); reps that break form or cadence do not count.
Bouncing in the sit-and-reach. Only a slow, held reach (1 second) counts; bouncing risks strain and inflates scores.

days.guide: Introduce the five health-related fitness components (cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition). Have the student take resting heart rate for 60 seconds at the wrist or neck, warm up 5 minutes, then walk/run the measured mile while you time it. Record time and how they felt (RPE 1–10) in the journal.

questions.q: Name the five health-related components of fitness.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition.

questions.q: Where can you find your pulse, and why count for a full 60 seconds at rest?
questions.a: At the radial artery (thumb side of the wrist) or carotid artery (side of the neck, press gently). A full minute at rest gives a more accurate count than a short sample.

days.guide: Demonstrate a curl-up (knees bent ~140°, feet flat, hands slide across a 3-inch strip) and a 90° push-up (elbows bend to 90°, body straight). Play or tap a cadence of one rep every 3 seconds; the test stops at the second form correction or when cadence is broken. Record both counts.

questions.q: What is the Fitnessgram cadence for curl-ups and push-ups?
questions.a: One repetition every 3 seconds (20 per minute).

questions.q: What does the 90° push-up test measure?
questions.a: Upper-body muscular strength and endurance.

days.guide: Model the back-saver sit-and-reach: one leg straight against the box, other knee bent with foot flat, reach forward slowly four times and hold the fourth for 1 second; test each side. Then the trunk lift: lie face down and lift the upper body slowly, hold, and measure chin height (max 12 in counted). Practice once before recording.

questions.q: Why is the sit-and-reach done one leg at a time ('back-saver')?
questions.a: Bending one knee reduces strain on the lower back while still measuring hamstring flexibility of the straight leg.

questions.q: In the trunk lift, why is the score capped at 12 inches?
questions.a: Lifting higher than 12 inches can hyperextend and stress the lower back; it adds no health benefit.

days.guide: Measure waist circumference at the navel and height in the same units; compute waist ÷ height. Explain that a ratio under about 0.5 is generally considered healthy and that this is a screening tool, not a judgment. Set up a 7-day activity log (minutes, type, intensity) using a phone or pedometer.

questions.q: A student's waist is 30 in and height is 66 in. What is the waist-to-height ratio, and is it under 0.5?
questions.a: 30 ÷ 66 ≈ 0.45, which is under 0.5 (the general healthy guideline).

questions.q: How many minutes of activity per day do guidelines recommend for teens?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, including vigorous, muscle-strengthening, and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days per week.

days.guide: Help the student look up the HFZ chart for their age/sex and mark each result as 'in HFZ' or 'needs improvement.' They write three findings in the journal (one strength, one need, one surprise). Check that each finding cites an actual number.

questions.q: What does 'Healthy Fitness Zone' mean?
questions.a: A Fitnessgram criterion score that indicates a level of fitness associated with good health for that age and sex — it is a health standard, not a ranking against others.

questions.q: Which fitness component does the 1-mile run mainly measure?
questions.a: Aerobic capacity (cardiorespiratory endurance).

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline fitness profile rubric (4 levels). 4 – All tests completed with correct technique; every result recorded with units, compared with the correct HFZ, and three findings each cite data. 3 (proficient) – All tests recorded and compared with HFZ; findings reference results. 2 – Some tests missing or HFZ comparison incomplete. 1 – Data mostly missing or unlabeled.

weeks.prep: Print or draw a goal sheet (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) and a FITT planning grid. Have a jump rope, fitness journal, and a safe walking/jogging route. Review the student's week 1 baseline data so goals can be built from it.
misconceptions: Writing vague goals like 'get fit.' Push for a number and date: 'Improve my mile from 10:30 to 9:45 by December 1 by running 3x/week.'
Confusing overload with doing as much as possible. Overload means slightly more than the body is used to, increased gradually (progression).
Believing gains are permanent. Reversibility: fitness declines when training stops, so consistency matters.

days.guide: Explain each letter of SMART with an example. The student writes two goals based on baseline weaknesses, then completes a 20-minute circuit (e.g., 1 min jump rope, 15 squats, 30-sec plank, repeat). Check that each goal has a number and a deadline.

questions.q: Rewrite 'I want to be stronger' as a SMART goal.
questions.a: Example: 'I will increase my 90° push-ups from 12 to 20 by March 1 by doing push-up workouts 3 days a week.' (Must be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and dated.)

days.guide: Teach FITT: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), Type (what activity). The student fills in a FITT grid for one goal, then walks/jogs 25 minutes. Check that intensity is measurable (heart rate zone or RPE).

questions.q: Write a FITT plan for improving aerobic endurance.
questions.a: Example: F = 3–5 days/week; I = 60–80% heart rate reserve or RPE 5–7; T = 20–40 min; T = jogging, cycling, or swimming.

questions.q: Which FITT letter changes if you go from walking to jogging at the same time and frequency?
questions.a: Intensity (and arguably type) — jogging is a higher intensity.

days.guide: Define overload, progression, specificity, and reversibility with examples. Do an interval walk/jog (e.g., 2 min jog/1 min walk ×7). Afterwards ask the student to name which principle the interval session applies.

questions.q: A swimmer wants to run faster but only trains in the pool. Which principle is violated?
questions.a: Specificity — training should match the desired outcome; to improve running, you must run.

questions.q: What does reversibility mean?
questions.a: Fitness gains are lost when training stops ('use it or lose it').

days.guide: Brainstorm barriers (time, weather, motivation, cost, safety) and match each with a strategy (schedule it, indoor workout, workout partner, free resources). Then complete a 30-minute bike ride or hike and log it.

questions.q: Give one barrier to activity and a practical strategy to overcome it.
questions.a: Example: 'No time' → schedule three 20-minute sessions in the calendar before school; 'bad weather' → indoor bodyweight circuit or online workout video.

days.guide: Review the goal sheet and FITT plan with the student against the rubric; ask them to explain how they'll measure progress. They complete and log a 30-minute activity of their choice.

questions.q: How will you know if your SMART goal is met?
questions.a: By retesting the measurable outcome (e.g., push-up count or mile time) by the stated deadline and comparing to baseline.

weeks.assessment_key: Goal sheet and FITT plan rubric. 4 – Two SMART goals with all five elements based on baseline data; FITT plan specifies measurable frequency, intensity (HR zone/RPE), time, and type, and applies overload/progression. 3 (proficient) – Two SMART goals with numbers and dates; complete FITT plan. 2 – Goals missing measurable or time element or FITT incomplete. 1 – Vague goals, no FITT plan.

weeks.prep: Set out cones for a 20-m warm-up lane; have water bottles ready. Read the CDC heat illness signs (heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke) so you can teach them confidently. Plan to run the fartlek day in a shaded area or early morning.
misconceptions: Doing long static stretches before vigorous activity as a warm-up. Dynamic movement raises muscle temperature better; save long static holds for the cool-down.
Waiting until thirsty to drink. Drink before, during, and after activity, especially in heat.
Thinking heat stroke victims always sweat a lot. Heat stroke may involve hot skin and confusion (sweating may stop); it is a 911 emergency.

days.guide: Lead the student through a 10-minute dynamic warm-up down and back the cone lane: easy jog, leg swings, walking lunges, high knees, butt kicks, A-skips. Cue tall posture and controlled movement; ask how breathing and heart rate changed.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a dynamic warm-up?
questions.a: To raise heart rate and muscle temperature, increase range of motion, and prepare the nervous system for activity, lowering injury risk.

questions.q: Give a cue for an A-skip.
questions.a: Drive one knee up to hip height, stay tall on the ball of the opposite foot, and swing the opposite arm.

days.guide: After a 20-minute easy jog, model a 5–8 minute cool-down walk then static stretches held 15–30 seconds each for calves, hamstrings, quadriceps, hip flexors, chest, and shoulders. Check that the student breathes and does not bounce.

questions.q: How long should a static stretch be held?
questions.a: About 15–30 seconds (up to 60 for older adults), to mild tension, not pain.

questions.q: Why walk before stretching in a cool-down?
questions.a: To let heart rate and breathing return gradually toward resting and prevent blood pooling or dizziness.

days.guide: Teach heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea, headache — move to shade, cool, sip fluids) vs. heat stroke (body temperature 104°F+, confusion, possibly hot dry skin — call 911 and cool immediately). Then do a fartlek run in shade: easy jogging with unplanned surges to the next tree or post.

questions.q: A runner is confused and has hot skin after a run on a hot day. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat as possible heat stroke: call 911, move them to shade, and cool them rapidly (cold water, ice packs at neck/armpits/groin).

questions.q: What does 'fartlek' mean?
questions.a: Swedish for 'speed play' — continuous running with unstructured bursts of faster pace mixed with easy running.

days.guide: The student writes a warm-up (5–10 min, dynamic, specific to their workout) and a cool-down (walk plus 5–6 static stretches) and leads a family member through both. Watch for clear cues and safe demonstration.

questions.q: What should a warm-up include before a sprint workout specifically?
questions.a: General movement (easy jog), dynamic stretches for the legs and hips, then sport-specific drills and a few build-up strides (specificity).

days.guide: Have the student perform both routines while you check form, then give a short safety quiz (sample below).

questions.q: List three ways to prevent heat illness.
questions.a: Hydrate before/during/after, exercise in cooler times of day or shade, wear light breathable clothing, acclimatize gradually, and rest when symptoms start.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine demonstration: proficient = warm-up is dynamic and progressive, cool-down includes a gradual walk and static stretches held 15–30 s for major groups, cues are clear and form safe. Safety quiz key: 1) Heat exhaustion signs: heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea, headache, weakness. 2) Heat stroke signs: body temp ≥104°F, confusion/altered behavior, hot skin (may be dry), possible collapse. 3) Heat stroke first step: call 911 and cool rapidly. 4) Dynamic stretching before, static after. 5) Drink water before, during, and after activity; don't wait for thirst.

weeks.prep: Have a stopwatch or heart-rate app and a jump rope. Prepare a worked Karvonen example using the student's own age and resting heart rate from week 1. Have graph paper or a spreadsheet ready for Day 4.
misconceptions: Using 220 − age as an exact number. It is only an estimate (±10–12 bpm); RPE and the talk test help cross-check.
In the Karvonen formula, multiplying the percentage by maximum HR instead of heart rate reserve. Correct: THR = (HRmax − HRrest) × % + HRrest.
Counting the first beat as 'one' when starting a 15-second count. Start counting at zero on the first beat (or just be consistent) and multiply by 4.

days.guide: Walk through Karvonen: HRmax = 220 − age; HRR = HRmax − resting HR; THR = HRR × intensity% + resting HR. Work the example with the student's numbers, then they compute 50%, 60%, 70%, 85%. Check arithmetic.

questions.q: A 16-year-old has resting HR 70. Find her 60% and 70% target heart rates using Karvonen.
Using 220 − age only, what is 70% of max for a 17-year-old?

days.guide: Take pulse for 15 seconds × 4 at rest, after 3 min walking, after 3 min jogging, and after a 30-second sprint. The student records each with an RPE (1–10). Discuss how HR and RPE track together.

questions.q: You count 38 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate?
What is the talk test?
questions.a: At moderate intensity you can talk but not sing; at vigorous intensity you can say only a few words before pausing for breath.

days.guide: Student runs 25 minutes aiming to stay in the 60–70% zone calculated Monday; stop briefly every 5 minutes for a 15-second pulse check and adjust pace. Record the five readings.

questions.q: Your check shows HR above your 70% zone. What do you do?
questions.a: Slow the pace (or walk briefly) until HR drops back into the 60–70% zone.

days.guide: Do 10 rounds of jump rope 30 s on/30 s off. Take pulse at the end of a work bout and again 1 minute after finishing; graph HR vs. time. Explain heart rate recovery: a faster drop indicates better aerobic fitness.

questions.q: HR is 180 at the end of exercise and 140 one minute later. What is the 1-minute recovery?
questions.a: 40 bpm drop — a larger drop generally indicates better cardiovascular fitness.

days.guide: Give the quiz below and review the heart-rate graph for labeled axes, units, and a one-sentence interpretation.

questions.q: Why might RPE be useful when a heart-rate monitor isn't available?
questions.a: RPE correlates with heart rate and intensity, so a person can judge effort by feel (on a 0–10 scale, about 5–6 is moderate and 7–8 is vigorous).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) HRmax = 220 − age. 2) Karvonen THR = (HRmax − HRrest) × % + HRrest. 3) Age 15, rest 65, 70%: HRmax 205, HRR 140, 0.7 × 140 + 65 = 163 bpm. 4) 24 beats in 10 s = 144 bpm (×6). 5) On a 0–10 RPE scale, moderate ≈ 5–6 (can talk but not sing) and vigorous ≈ 7–8 (only a few words). Heart-rate graph rubric: proficient = time on x-axis, bpm on y-axis, labeled, all 10 intervals and the recovery point plotted, with a correct written interpretation of recovery.

weeks.prep: Ensure the student has supportive running shoes; set up a free route-mapping app (e.g., a GPS running app) and a training log with columns for date, distance, time, pace, RPE. Arrange access to a bike, pool, or rower for cross-training day.
misconceptions: Running every run hard. Most base training should be easy, conversational pace; hard days need easy days around them.
Overstriding (landing far in front with a heel) to go faster. Encourage quicker, shorter steps landing under the hips.
Thinking cross-training 'doesn't count.' Cycling or swimming builds the aerobic base while reducing impact stress.

days.guide: Teach run form: tall posture with slight forward lean from ankles, relaxed shoulders, arms swinging forward-back at ~90°, feet landing under the hips. Do drills (A-skips, butt kicks, strides). Count steps for 30 seconds and double to estimate cadence (aim ~160–180).

questions.q: You count 82 steps in 30 seconds. What is your cadence?
questions.a: 164 steps per minute.

questions.q: Name two cues for efficient running form.
questions.a: Run tall with a slight forward lean; land under the hips with quick light steps; relaxed shoulders; arms swing forward and back, not across the body.

days.guide: Student completes 30 minutes at conversational pace (talk test). Record distance, time, and compute average pace.

questions.q: You cover 3 miles in 33 minutes. What is your pace?
Why is 'long slow distance' useful?
questions.a: It builds the aerobic base — more capillaries and mitochondria and a stronger heart — with low injury and fatigue risk.

days.guide: Do 30 minutes of cycling, swimming, or rowing at moderate intensity (RPE 5–6). Discuss how it trains the same heart and lungs with different muscles and less impact.

questions.q: How does cross-training help a runner?
questions.a: It maintains or builds aerobic fitness while reducing repetitive impact stress, lowering overuse injury risk and adding variety.

days.guide: Explain tempo pace: 'comfortably hard' — RPE about 7, can say only a few words. Workout: 5 min easy, 10 min tempo, 5 min easy. Check HR at the end of the tempo portion.

questions.q: How should a tempo pace feel?
questions.a: Comfortably hard: sustained effort around RPE 7, breathing deep and rhythmic, only short phrases possible.

days.guide: Student completes 35 minutes easy and updates the log with weekly totals. Review the log together for completeness and an easy/hard pattern.

questions.q: What does the training log help you see?
questions.a: Weekly volume, pace trends, intensity (RPE), and whether you're progressing gradually or overdoing it.

weeks.assessment_key: Training log review rubric. 4 – All 5 sessions logged with date, type, time, distance, pace and RPE; weekly total calculated; a reflection notes trends and next-week adjustment. 3 (proficient) – All sessions logged with time, distance/type and RPE; total correct. 2 – Missing sessions or data columns. 1 – Log largely incomplete.

weeks.prep: Download an interval timer app; set cones 20 m apart for shuttles; find a moderate hill (30–60 seconds to climb). Review the student's target zones from week 4.
misconceptions: Believing HIIT should be done every day. It is stressful; 2–3 sessions per week with recovery days is plenty.
Thinking anaerobic means 'no oxygen in the body.' It means energy is produced without enough oxygen keeping up, so it can only be sustained briefly.
Using too little rest so quality drops. Work-to-rest ratios (e.g., 1:1 to 1:3) keep the work intervals truly hard.

days.guide: Explain energy systems: aerobic (with oxygen, long duration, lower intensity) vs. anaerobic (short, very intense bursts; produces fatigue quickly). Do a Tabata of squat jumps: 20 s work/10 s rest × 8 = 4 minutes.

questions.q: What is the structure of a Tabata?
questions.a: 8 rounds of 20 seconds all-out work and 10 seconds rest, totaling 4 minutes.

questions.q: Which energy system powers a 30-minute easy jog vs. a 20-second sprint?
questions.a: The jog is mostly aerobic; the 20-second sprint relies mostly on anaerobic systems (phosphocreatine and anaerobic glycolysis).

days.guide: Set cones 20 m apart. Student does 6 × 30-second shuttle runs (touch line, turn) with 90 seconds walking recovery. Count lengths each round to check if pace holds.

questions.q: What is the work-to-rest ratio of 30 s on/90 s off?

days.guide: Six hill repeats: drive knees, pump arms, lean slightly into the hill, short quick steps; walk or jog down for recovery. Watch for upright posture.

questions.q: Why are hill repeats useful?
questions.a: They build leg strength and power and raise intensity with less pounding than flat sprints.

days.guide: Student designs a 20-minute HIIT (warm-up, 4–6 exercises, work/rest ratio, cool-down) and completes it. Check that rest is adequate and exercises are safe.

questions.q: A HIIT plan has 45 s work and 15 s rest for 20 minutes of burpees. What would you change?
questions.a: Rest is too short for all-out work and a single exercise risks form breakdown; use 1:1 or 1:2 ratios, vary exercises, and include warm-up and cool-down.

days.guide: The student leads a family member through the workout, cueing form, then writes a comparison of HIIT vs. steady-state (time, intensity, benefits, risks).

questions.q: Give one advantage of HIIT and one of steady-state training.
questions.a: HIIT: improves fitness in less time and builds anaerobic capacity. Steady-state: lower injury/fatigue risk, builds aerobic base, easier to sustain and recover from.

weeks.assessment_key: HIIT design rubric. 4 – Includes warm-up, 4+ safe exercises, explicit work:rest ratio appropriate to intensity, cool-down, modifications, and correct HIIT vs. steady-state comparison. 3 (proficient) – Warm-up, exercises, safe ratio, cool-down, accurate comparison. 2 – Missing warm-up/cool-down or unsafe ratios. 1 – Incomplete plan.

weeks.prep: Measure a 5K (3.1-mile) route or register for a local fun run. Gather the student's training log and week 1 mile time. Have foam roller (optional) for recovery day.
misconceptions: Starting the race too fast. Even or negative splits (second half faster) usually produce better times.
Training hard the day before a race. Taper: reduce volume, keep a little intensity (strides).
Skipping recovery after a race. Gentle activity aids recovery more than total rest.

days.guide: Use the student's recent paces to set a goal 5K pace. Divide the 3.1 miles into splits and plan a strategy (start controlled, settle, push the last mile).

questions.q: A runner's goal 5K time is 27:54. What pace per mile is that?
What is a negative split?
questions.a: Running the second half of a race faster than the first half.

days.guide: 20-minute easy shake-out run plus 4–6 strides (20-second relaxed accelerations). Keep it easy.

questions.q: Why do a shake-out run before a race instead of a hard workout?
questions.a: To stay loose and keep legs fresh (taper) while not adding fatigue.

days.guide: Timed 5K (run, walk, or bike). Record total time and mile splits if possible; check that the student hydrates and warms up first.

questions.q: How many kilometers and miles is a 5K?
questions.a: 5 kilometers ≈ 3.1 miles.

days.guide: Easy walk 20–30 min, foam rolling of calves/quads, and static stretching. Discuss soreness vs. pain.

questions.q: How can you tell normal muscle soreness from injury?
questions.a: Soreness is dull, in both legs or muscles broadly, and improves within 1–3 days; injury pain is sharp, localized, worsens with activity, or causes limping — stop and seek care.

days.guide: Student compares 5K average pace to week 1 mile pace and writes a reflection; update SMART goals if needed.

questions.q: Why might 5K pace per mile be slower than a single mile's pace?
questions.a: Longer distances must be run at a lower intensity to be sustained, so pace per mile is usually slower.
