misconceptions: Thinking star color is random. Color shows surface temperature: blue stars are hottest, red stars coolest.
Thinking all elements formed in the Big Bang. Only hydrogen, helium, and a little lithium did; heavier elements were made in stars and stellar explosions.

days.guide: The student plots the stars on an H-R diagram (temperature decreasing to the right, luminosity up) and labels main sequence, giants, supergiants, white dwarfs.

questions.q: Where is the Sun on the H-R diagram?
questions.a: On the main sequence, in the middle (a yellow G-type star, about 5,800 K).

days.guide: Trace life cycles with a flowchart for low-mass vs high-mass stars. Today's task from the plan: Trace life cycles of low- and high-mass stars. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Describe the life cycle of a Sun-like star.
questions.a: Nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.

questions.q: What happens to a star much more massive than the Sun?
questions.a: Main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

days.guide: Build the CD spectroscope and compare spectra of light sources. Today's task from the plan: Build a CD spectroscope and view different light sources. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does a fluorescent bulb show bright lines but an incandescent bulb a continuous rainbow?
questions.a: The fluorescent bulb's excited gas atoms emit only specific wavelengths (emission lines); the hot filament emits all wavelengths (continuous spectrum).

days.guide: The student color-codes a periodic table by element origin (Big Bang, low-mass stars, massive stars/supernovae, neutron-star mergers, cosmic rays). Today's task from the plan: Create a periodic table color-coded by element origin. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does fusion in stars stop producing energy at iron?
questions.a: Fusing iron consumes energy rather than releasing it; heavier elements form in supernovae and neutron-star mergers.

days.guide: The student presents (5 minutes) how stars produce elements. Today's task from the plan: Present how stars produce elements. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does 'we are made of star stuff' mean?
questions.a: The carbon, oxygen, calcium, and iron in our bodies were made by nuclear fusion in earlier stars and scattered by stellar explosions.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (4-point per row): accurate life cycles for low- and high-mass stars; explanation of fusion up to iron and heavier elements from supernovae/mergers; use of the H-R diagram or periodic table as evidence; clear visuals and delivery. Proficient = correct sequence of element formation with one example from each source.

weeks.prep: A free star chart app (e.g., Stellarium); binoculars; a clear evening and a dark spot. Check weather and Moon phase (a new Moon is best).
misconceptions: Thinking stars are all the same distance away. The 'constellation' stars can be at very different distances.
Thinking a light-year measures time. It is a distance: how far light travels in one year (about 9.46 trillion km).

days.guide: Hold a thumb at arm's length; close one eye, then the other, and watch it shift against the background. Relate to stellar parallax. Today's task from the plan: Measure parallax with thumb and objects; relate to stellar distances. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: A star has a parallax of 0.5 arcseconds. How far away is it?
questions.a: d = 1/p = 2 parsecs ≈ 6.5 light-years.

days.guide: Observe the night sky for 30 minutes; record constellations, bright stars, planets, and the Moon. Today's task from the plan: Observe the night sky and record constellations and planets. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: How can you tell a planet from a star?
questions.a: Planets usually shine steadily (twinkle less), lie along the ecliptic, and move against the background stars over days.

days.guide: Calculate distances in light-years and light travel times. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.a: 1.5 × 10¹¹ m ÷ 3 × 10⁸ m/s = 500 s ≈ 8.3 minutes.

questions.q: Proxima Centauri is 4.24 light-years away. What does that mean?
questions.a: Its light took 4.24 years to reach us; we see it as it was then.

days.guide: Research how telescopes detect different wavelengths (radio, infrared/JWST, X-ray/Chandra). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why are X-ray telescopes placed in space?
questions.a: Earth's atmosphere absorbs X-rays, so they can only be observed above it.

days.guide: Unit 7 test. Today's task from the plan: Unit 7 test on the Sun and stars. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why do we see distant galaxies as they were in the past?
questions.a: Their light took millions or billions of years to reach us.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test key (sample): Sun's layers and fusion; E = mc²; half-life (1/8 after 3); alpha/beta decay equations; H-R diagram regions; life cycles; parallax (d = 1/p); light-year definition; spectra (emission vs continuous).

weeks.prep: A round balloon and a marker; a ruler; a short video or diagrams of galaxy spectra and the CMB map (NASA/ESA Planck).
misconceptions: Thinking the Big Bang was an explosion into empty space from one point. Space itself expanded everywhere.
Thinking galaxies are moving through space away from us at the center. Every observer sees others receding; there is no center.

days.guide: Draw dots on a partly inflated balloon, measure distances between dots, inflate more, measure again. Today's task from the plan: Draw dots on a balloon and inflate it to model expansion. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Which dots moved apart fastest, and what does it model?
questions.a: The dots farthest apart moved apart most: in an expanding universe, more distant galaxies recede faster.

days.guide: Show a hydrogen spectrum from a lab lamp and the same lines in a distant galaxy shifted toward red. The student measures the shift and explains what it means about the galaxy's motion.

questions.q: What is redshift and what does it show?
questions.a: Spectral lines shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths, showing the galaxy is moving away from us.

days.guide: Give a table of galaxy distances (Mpc) and recession velocities (km/s). The student graphs velocity vs distance, draws a best-fit line through the origin, and finds the slope (Hubble's constant), then estimates the universe's age as 1/H₀.

questions.q: If H₀ ≈ 70 km/s/Mpc, how fast is a galaxy 100 Mpc away receding?
questions.a: v = H₀d = 7,000 km/s.

questions.q: How does Hubble's constant estimate the age of the universe?
questions.a: Age ≈ 1/H₀ ≈ 14 billion years (current best value 13.8 billion years).

days.guide: Show the Planck all-sky CMB map and explain it is the oldest light we can see. The student writes how the CMB was predicted, discovered accidentally in 1965 by Penzias and Wilson, and why its near-uniform 2.7 K temperature supports the Big Bang.

questions.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
questions.a: Leftover radiation from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, now cooled to about 2.7 K and filling the whole sky.

days.guide: CER on the Big Bang. Today's task from the plan: Write a CER on the Big Bang. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Name three pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
questions.a: Redshift of distant galaxies (Hubble's law), the CMB, and the observed abundance of light elements (~75% hydrogen, ~25% helium by mass).

weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric (4 = exemplary, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning). Claim: answers the question about the evidence for the Big Bang in one sentence. Evidence: specific data from the student's own lab/simulation with numbers and units. Reasoning: connects the evidence to the scientific principle. A proficient response: redshift and Hubble's law (velocity proportional to distance), the uniform CMB at 2.7 K, and light-element abundances, explaining how each matches predictions of an expanding universe that began hot and dense.

weeks.prep: NASA element-abundance chart; string, washers, a tube (pen barrel) for the rotation model; NASA's dark matter and dark energy overviews.
misconceptions: Thinking dark matter is just dark dust or black holes. It does not emit, absorb, or reflect light and doesn't interact with normal matter except through gravity.
Confusing dark matter and dark energy. Dark matter pulls (gravity); dark energy is causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate.

days.guide: Give the cosmic abundance data (by mass: H ≈ 74%, He ≈ 24%, everything else ≈ 2%). The student makes a bar or pie chart and explains why so much H and He points to Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

questions.q: Why does the ~75% hydrogen / ~25% helium mix support the Big Bang?
questions.a: Big Bang nucleosynthesis predicts these ratios from the first few minutes, matching observations.

days.guide: Swing a washer on a string threaded through a pen barrel with a weight hanging below; then look at a real galaxy rotation curve. The student compares the expected (Keplerian, falling) curve with the observed flat curve.

questions.q: If most of a galaxy's mass were in its bright center, how should outer star speeds behave?
questions.a: They should decrease with distance (like planets around the Sun); instead they stay roughly flat, suggesting unseen mass.

days.guide: Read NASA's dark matter overview together; the student lists three independent lines of evidence and explains each in one sentence. Today's task from the plan: Read NASA's dark matter overview and list three independent lines of evidence (rotation curves, lensing, cluster motions). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Name three pieces of evidence for dark matter.
questions.a: Flat galaxy rotation curves, gravitational lensing stronger than visible mass explains, and galaxy cluster motions too fast for visible mass.

days.guide: Read about the 1998 supernova discovery; debate evidence for unseen things. Today's task from the plan: Read about the 1998 Type Ia supernova discovery and sketch a graph of expansion rate over time; hold a structured debate on what counts as 'evidence' for something unseen. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What did the 1998 Type Ia supernova observations show?
questions.a: Distant supernovae were dimmer than expected, meaning the expansion of the universe is accelerating—attributed to dark energy.

days.guide: Quiz on the composition of the universe. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on composition of the universe with two short CER items. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What are the approximate shares of ordinary matter, dark matter, and dark energy?
questions.a: About 5%, 27%, and 68%.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) universe ≈ 5% ordinary matter, 27% dark matter, 68% dark energy. 2) H ≈ 75%, He ≈ 25% by mass. 3) dark matter evidence: rotation curves, lensing, cluster motions. 4) dark energy evidence: Type Ia supernovae. CER items scored with the 4-point CER rubric.

weeks.prep: Two colors of candy or beans (100 of one color) in a bag; images of Moon craters; a roll of toilet paper or 4.6 m of string; NASA solar system formation overview.
misconceptions: Thinking Earth's oldest rocks date Earth's formation. Plate tectonics and erosion recycle crust; meteorites and Moon rocks preserve older ages.
Thinking radiometric dating measures how much of an element is in a rock. It uses the ratio of parent to daughter isotopes and the known half-life.

days.guide: Read NASA's overview of solar system formation. The student draws a 5-step diagram: collapsing nebula → spinning disk → planetesimals (accretion) → molten young Earth → differentiated layers (iron sinks to form the core).

questions.q: What is accretion?
questions.a: Dust and rock clump together by collisions and gravity into larger bodies (planetesimals and planets).

days.guide: Shake the bag; replace 'decayed' candies with the other color each round. Use ratios to date mystery samples. Today's task from the plan: Shake a bag of 100 'parent' candies, swap 'decayed' ones for a second color each round, and use the parent/daughter ratio to date mystery samples. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A sample has 25% parent and 75% daughter. If the half-life is 1.3 billion years, how old is it?
questions.a: Two half-lives: 2.6 billion years.

days.guide: Give data on ages: Jack Hills zircons (~4.4 billion years), oldest rocks (~4.0 billion), meteorites (~4.57 billion), Moon rocks (up to ~4.5 billion). The student explains why these differ and what they tell us about Earth's age.

questions.q: Why are Earth's oldest rocks (~4.0 billion years) younger than meteorites (~4.57 billion years)?
questions.a: Earth's surface is constantly recycled by plate tectonics, erosion, and early melting; meteorites have been unchanged since the solar system formed.

days.guide: Unroll 4.6 m of string or toilet paper on the floor (1 m = 1 billion years). The student marks Earth's formation, oldest minerals, first life, oxygen rise, first animals, dinosaurs, and humans, then reflects on how recent humans are.

questions.q: How far from 'now' is the dinosaurs' extinction (66 million years ago)?

days.guide: Unit 8 test. Today's task from the plan: Unit 8 test on Big Bang evidence, stellar elements, and Earth's origin. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How old is Earth?
questions.a: About 4.54 billion years.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline rubric: key events placed at correct scale (formation 4.6 m, oldest zircons 4.4 m, first life ~3.5–3.8 m, oxygen rise ~2.4 m, Cambrian 0.54 m, dinosaurs extinct 6.6 cm, humans ~0.3 mm). Unit 8 test key: Big Bang evidence; dark matter/dark energy; stellar nucleosynthesis; radiometric dating; age of Earth.

weeks.prep: California Energy Commission electricity-mix data (energy.ca.gov 'Total System Electric Generation'); a home electric bill; appliance labels.
misconceptions: Thinking any one energy source is perfect. Every source has trade-offs (cost, land use, emissions, reliability).
Confusing kW (power) with kWh (energy).

days.guide: Download the California Energy Commission 'Total System Electric Generation' data. The student graphs the share of each source for at least three years since 2010 and describes the trends.

questions.q: What trends are visible in California's electricity mix since 2010?
questions.a: Solar and wind have grown sharply, coal has nearly disappeared, and natural gas remains a large share.

days.guide: Use a home electric bill to find monthly kWh, then appliance labels to estimate which devices use the most. Multiply kWh by an emissions factor (use the utility's stated value, or about 0.2 kg CO₂/kWh) to estimate emissions.

questions.q: A home uses 500 kWh/month; with an emissions factor of 0.2 kg CO₂/kWh, how much CO₂?
questions.a: 100 kg CO₂ per month.

days.guide: The student builds a matrix comparing solar, wind, natural gas, nuclear, and geothermal on cost per kWh, land use, CO₂ emissions, and reliability (can it run at night or on calm days?), citing a source for each row.

questions.q: Why can't solar alone meet evening peak demand?
questions.a: Solar output drops after sunset when demand peaks, requiring storage or other sources.

days.guide: Pose the scenario: a town of 10,000 homes needs power during the 6–9 p.m. peak. The student defines criteria (reliability, low emissions) and constraints (budget, land, existing grid) and considers batteries or other storage.

questions.q: Name one criterion and one constraint for a town energy plan.
questions.a: Criterion: meet peak demand reliably. Constraint: budget or land available.

days.guide: The student writes a one-page recommendation for the town and presents it in 5 minutes, defending trade-offs with data from the matrix. Today's task from the plan: Write and present a one-page recommendation for a community energy plan defending trade-offs. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What makes a strong energy recommendation?
questions.a: Clear criteria, evidence-based comparison, and honest trade-offs.

weeks.assessment_key: Recommendation rubric (4-point): states criteria/constraints; compares at least three sources with data; addresses evening peak and storage; justifies trade-offs.

weeks.prep: Small 3–6 V DC hobby motor (to use as a generator), cardboard or cut plastic-bottle blades, a hub (bottle cap or cork), hot glue (adult), an LED (or multimeter), a box fan, a ruler and protractor. Safety: keep fingers clear of spinning blades and fan.
misconceptions: Thinking more blades always means more power. Extra blades add drag and mass; real turbines usually use three as a balance of efficiency, cost, and stability.
Changing several things between tests and recording nothing. Keep a data table and change one variable (blade angle OR number) at a time.

days.guide: Set criteria (light the LED; maximize voltage at the highest fan speed) and constraints (materials list, 30 cm maximum blade length). Read how turbines convert wind energy using induction.

questions.q: How does a wind turbine produce electricity?
questions.a: Wind pushes on angled blades, turning a shaft connected to a generator; coils rotating in a magnetic field induce current (electromagnetic induction).

days.guide: Use a wind-turbine simulation (or online interactive) to explore blade number and pitch; sketch three designs and choose one with a decision matrix. Today's task from the plan: Use a PhET or online wind simulation to explore blade number and angle, then sketch three designs and pick one with a decision matrix. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Why does blade angle (pitch) matter?
questions.a: The angle determines how much of the wind's push becomes rotation; too flat catches little force, too steep creates drag and stalls.

days.guide: Build the turbine: attach blades evenly to the hub, press the hub onto the motor shaft, wire the motor leads to the LED (try both polarities, since LEDs conduct one way).

questions.q: Why can a DC motor act as a generator?
questions.a: Turning its shaft spins coils inside the motor's magnetic field, which induces a voltage across its leads.

days.guide: Test at three fan speeds and two blade angles, recording voltage or LED brightness (3 trials each). Revise once based on the data and retest. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What should the data table contain?
questions.a: Fan speed setting, blade angle, number of blades, trial number, and voltage (or brightness rating), plus averages.

days.guide: The student gives a 5-minute engineering briefing: final design, data table, the revision and why, and an efficiency discussion. Today's task from the plan: Present the final device, data table, and efficiency discussion in a 5-minute engineering briefing. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why is a small homemade turbine's efficiency low?
questions.a: Energy is lost to air passing between blades, friction in the motor, electrical resistance (heat), and turbulence; real turbines can capture at most about 59% of wind energy (Betz limit).

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone design rubric (4-point per row): Problem definition (criteria and constraints stated); Design process (three sketches and decision matrix); Data (multiple conditions with repeated trials, organized table/graph); Iteration (one change justified by data, with retest results); Explanation (correct physics of induction and energy conversion, honest efficiency discussion). Proficient = LED lights or measurable voltage, data supports the chosen revision, explanation uses induction correctly.

weeks.prep: Final review packet with mixed problems from all nine units; the student's lab notebook and returned tests; two quiet 60-minute exam blocks.
misconceptions: Studying only favorite or easy topics. Use earlier test errors to choose what to review first.
Skipping data-analysis practice. Part 2 of the exam uses unfamiliar data; practice reading axes, units, and trends.

days.guide: The student reworks every missed problem from Units 1–3 tests, then completes a mixed set on momentum and energy conservation. Today's task from the plan: Rework missed problems from Units 1–3 tests and complete a mixed problem set on momentum and energy conservation. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: A 1,500 kg car at 20 m/s hits a stopped 1,000 kg car and they lock together. What is their speed afterward?
questions.a: Total momentum 30,000 kg·m/s ÷ 2,500 kg = 12 m/s.

days.guide: Concept map linking charges, fields, induction, and EM waves; then 10 wave/circuit problems. Today's task from the plan: Complete a concept map linking fields, induction, and EM waves, then solve 10 wave/circuit problems. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How are electromagnetic waves produced?
questions.a: Accelerating (oscillating) charges create changing electric fields that create changing magnetic fields, and vice versa; the linked fields travel as an EM wave at the speed of light.

questions.q: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz. Wavelength?

days.guide: The student writes a one-page study sheet on plate tectonics, stellar life cycles, and Big Bang evidence. Today's task from the plan: Make a one-page study sheet on plate tectonics, stellar life cycles, and Big Bang evidence. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give three lines of evidence for plate tectonics.
questions.a: Seafloor age increasing from ridges with symmetric magnetic striping, matching fossils and rocks across oceans, and earthquakes/volcanoes concentrated along plate boundaries.

days.guide: Final exam part 1: multiple-choice and short answer across all nine units (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Multiple-choice and short-answer covering all nine units. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: State Newton's third law and give an example.
questions.a: For every force one object exerts on another, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first; e.g., a rocket pushes gas backward and the gas pushes the rocket forward.

days.guide: Final exam part 2: interpret two unfamiliar data sets and write CER explanations (60 minutes). Today's task from the plan: Data-analysis section: interpret two unfamiliar data sets and write CER explanations. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What steps should the student follow with an unfamiliar graph?
questions.a: Read the title, axes, and units; describe the trend with numbers; identify the relevant principle; then write a CER linking the data to that principle.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key (representative items): 1) a = Δv/Δt (0→30 m/s in 6 s = 5 m/s²). 2) F = ma (1,200 kg × 2 m/s² = 2,400 N). 3) momentum conservation (12 m/s above). 4) PE→KE speed after 20 m drop ≈ 19.8 m/s. 5) Q = mcΔT. 6) Ohm's law (24 V, 8 Ω → 3 A). 7) induction requires a changing field. 8) v = fλ. 9) photoelectric effect → particle model. 10) S-wave shadow zone → liquid outer core. 11) high-mass star → supernova → neutron star/black hole. 12) redshift + CMB + light-element abundance → Big Bang. Part 2 CERs scored with the 4-point rubric. Grade bands: 90%+ excellent, 75–89% proficient, below 75% revisit weak units.

VAPA.overview: Theatre & Performing Arts runs 50 minutes a day and moves from ensemble and improvisation to acting technique, theatre history, design, playwriting, and a directed one-act. Model each exercise briefly, then let the student do it while you watch for the week's cues; recruit family or friends as scene partners and audiences, and keep everything in the performance journal. Preview the plays (notes are in each week's prep), grade performances with the rubrics given, and value specific, evidence-based reflection as much as performance.

weeks.prep: Clear an open space and get a notebook for the performance journal. Learn the rules of Zip-Zap-Zop and mirror so you can play along; recruit one or two family members for focus games and as the Day 5 audience. Pick a familiar fairy tale for the tableaux.
misconceptions: Thinking theatre is only about the lead actor. Ensemble means every member serves the whole story; praise listening and support, not just big moments.
Treating focus games as just 'fun.' Tie each game to a skill (concentration, eye contact, reacting) in the debrief.
Tableaux that are flat lines facing the audience. Use levels (high, medium, low), clear focus, and open body positions.

days.guide: Discuss how theatre differs from film: live, shared space with the audience, no retakes, the audience's imagination fills in. The student sets up the journal with 3 goals for the year.

questions.q: Name two ways theatre differs from film.
questions.a: Theatre is live and unrepeatable, with performers and audience sharing the same space and time; film is recorded, edited, and the camera controls what the viewer sees.

days.guide: Play mirror (partners mirror slowly so an observer can't tell the leader), Zip-Zap-Zop (pass energy with eye contact and a clap), and 'count to 20' (group counts one at a time; restart if two speak). Student journals what helped concentration.

questions.q: What does the mirror game train?
questions.a: Focus, close observation, and responding to a partner — the leader must move slowly so they stay connected.

days.guide: Lead a trust walk (partner guides a 'blind' walker by the shoulder, safely). Teach neutral stance (feet under hips, arms relaxed, weight even, eyes forward). Space walk at tempos 1 (slowest) to 10 (fastest) filling empty spaces.

questions.q: Describe neutral stance.
questions.a: Feet hip-width and parallel, weight balanced, knees soft, arms relaxed at sides, spine long, eyes forward, face relaxed — no character choices.

days.guide: Build a story one word at a time. Then create three frozen images (beginning, middle, end) of a fairy tale; check for levels and clear focus.

questions.q: What is a tableau, and what makes it readable?
questions.a: A frozen stage picture; clear focus (everyone directs attention to the important point), varied levels, open body positions, and expressive faces make it readable.

days.guide: Perform the 3-tableau story for family (with a title for each frame), then write a journal reflection on ensemble skills.

questions.q: What does 'ensemble' mean in theatre?
questions.a: A group of performers working together as a unit, supporting each other rather than competing for focus.

weeks.assessment_key: Tableau performance and journal rubric. 4 – Three clear, frozen images with varied levels, strong focus, and expression that tell the beginning, middle, and end; reflection names specific ensemble skills and personal goals. 3 (proficient) – Three readable tableaux with levels and focus; reflection describes ensemble skills. 2 – Images unclear or unstill; reflection vague. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Make suggestion cards (locations, relationships, occupations, quirks). Get a timer. Learn the rules of Freeze, Three-Line Scene, and Party Quirks (any improv games website).
misconceptions: Asking questions instead of making offers ('Who are you?'). Make statements that give information ('Grandpa, the barn's on fire!').
Saying 'yes, but' and blocking partner ideas. Accept the offer and add to it.
Trying to be funny. Truthful reactions to clear situations create comedy naturally.

days.guide: Do two-person dialogues: first with 'yes, but' (scene stalls), then 'yes, and' (scene grows). Identify blocks in examples.

questions.q: Partner says, 'Let's go fishing.' Give a 'yes, and' response and a blocking response.
questions.a: 'Yes, and I brought the giant net for the shark!' (accepts and adds). Block: 'There's no lake here' or 'I don't want to.'

days.guide: Teach CROW: Character, Relationship, Objective, Where. Improvise 2-minute scenes; the observer checks whether all four were clear within 30 seconds.

questions.q: What does CROW stand for?
questions.a: Character, Relationship, Objective, Where.

days.guide: Explore status: high status (still, open, eye contact, measured speech) vs. low status (fidgeting, small, avoiding eye contact, hesitant). Play short scenes swapping status.

questions.q: Give two physical signs of high status.
questions.a: Stillness, upright open posture, steady eye contact, slow deliberate movement and speech.

days.guide: Play Freeze, Three-Line Scene, and Party Quirks; journal which choices worked.

questions.q: In a Three-Line Scene, what must the three lines accomplish?
questions.a: Establish who the characters are, their relationship, and where they are (the scene's basic CROW) in only three lines.

days.guide: Perform three scenes from audience suggestions; self-evaluate with the CROW rubric.

questions.q: What is an 'offer' in improv?
questions.a: Any line or action that gives information or direction to the scene.

weeks.assessment_key: Improvisation rubric (each scene scored 1–4 on C, R, O, W plus acceptance). 4 – All CROW elements clear within 30 s, consistent acceptance and building of offers, committed characters, a clear ending. 3 (proficient) – CROW mostly clear early, accepts offers, stays in scene. 2 – Missing elements, frequent questions or blocks. 1 – Breaks character or stalls repeatedly.

weeks.prep: Gather costume pieces (hats, scarves, glasses, jackets). Choose a pet to observe or an animal video. Prepare 15 hot-seat questions (childhood, fears, daily routine, secrets).
misconceptions: Building characters only from voice. Start with the body (center, tempo, gesture) and let the voice follow.
Cartoonish animal work. Keep the animal's essence (rhythm, focus, weight) but make it a believable human.
Answering hot-seat questions with 'I don't know.' Make a specific choice; commitment beats perfection.

days.guide: Walk with the head leading, then chest, belly, knees. After each, ask: Who is this person? How do they speak? Create a quick character for each.

questions.q: What kind of character might a chest-led walk suggest?
questions.a: Often a proud, confident, or aggressive character — chest forward, assertive (answers may vary but should connect body to personality).

days.guide: Observe an animal for 5 minutes noting rhythm, weight, focus, and stillness. Move as the animal, then gradually stand and humanize it.

questions.q: What qualities from an animal transfer to a human character?
questions.a: Tempo, rhythm, weight, the way it focuses or scans, how it reacts to sound and danger.

days.guide: Hot seat: student stays in character answering questions for 5 minutes. Push for specific details.

questions.q: What is the purpose of hot seating?
questions.a: To deepen a character by forcing the actor to invent specific history, opinions, and voice in character.

days.guide: Student picks a costume piece and improvises a 1-minute monologue in character (who they are, what they want right now).

questions.q: What are given circumstances?
questions.a: The facts of a character's situation — who, what, where, when, why — that shape choices.

days.guide: Perform two contrasting characters; write a profile (name, age, walk, voice, want, fear, history).

questions.q: What makes two characters 'contrasting'?
questions.a: Clear differences in body (center, tempo), voice, status, and objective.

weeks.assessment_key: Character profile and performance rubric. 4 – Two clearly contrasting, sustained characters with distinct leading centers, tempo, voice, and objectives; profile is specific (history, want, fear, physical traits) and connects to performance choices. 3 (proficient) – Two distinct characters and a complete profile. 2 – Characters similar or inconsistent; profile thin. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print the story spine template: Once upon a time… Every day… But one day… Because of that… Because of that… Until finally… And ever since then… Find a short professional improv clip (e.g., a long-form set on a reputable channel); preview for content. Recruit 2–3 players for Day 4–5.
misconceptions: Introducing new ideas instead of reusing earlier ones. Long-form rewards callbacks and connections.
Skipping the 'until finally' climax. Stories need a turning point and resolution.
Thinking long-form is just many short scenes. Scenes connect through themes, characters, and callbacks.

days.guide: Teach the story spine and improvise five stories from random titles; check each has a 'But one day' and 'Until finally.'

questions.q: Recite the story spine.
questions.a: Once upon a time… Every day… But one day… Because of that… Because of that… Until finally… And ever since then…

days.guide: Play scenes where a character or line from an earlier scene returns later (callback). Practice linking three scenes.

questions.q: What is a callback?
questions.a: Bringing back a character, line, or idea from earlier in the performance, often for comic or thematic payoff.

days.guide: Watch the clip; student writes a response identifying three offers and one callback.

questions.q: What is a 'Harold'?
questions.a: A long-form improv structure (developed by Del Close) with an opening, three sets of scenes interwoven with group games, connected by a theme and callbacks.

days.guide: Rehearse a 10-minute structured piece: opening, three scene beats, a group game, and a returning beat. Agree on the structure, not the lines.

questions.q: What is a 'beat' in improv or acting?
questions.a: A unit of action — a section where one objective or idea is pursued until something changes.

days.guide: Perform the long-form piece and write a Unit 1 growth reflection.

questions.q: What made a scene connection work in your piece?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong answers name a specific callback or recurring character and explain how it tied scenes together.

weeks.assessment_key: Long-form performance rubric. 4 – Clear opening, scenes connected by theme and at least two callbacks, strong 'yes, and' support, satisfying ending, ~10 minutes; reflection identifies growth with examples. 3 (proficient) – Connected scenes with at least one callback and an ending; reflection. 2 – Disconnected scenes. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather a mat, a hardback book, a mirror, and a recording app. Find (or record) the student's week 1 voice sample; choose a short poem (14–20 lines). Measure 5, 15, and 30 feet in a hall or yard.
misconceptions: Projection means shouting. It means supported breath and resonance; shouting strains the throat.
Breathing high in the chest with lifted shoulders. Breath should expand the belly and lower ribs.
Mumbling final consonants. Crisp final consonants carry meaning to the back row.

days.guide: Lie down with a book on the abdomen; inhale so the book rises, exhale slowly. Time a sustained 's' sound three times and record the best.

questions.q: What is the diaphragm's role in breathing?
questions.a: It is a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs; it contracts and flattens to draw air in, and relaxes as you exhale.

days.guide: Hum and feel vibration in the chest (low), mask/face (mid), and head (high). Do sirens up and down the range.

questions.q: Where is 'mask' resonance felt?
questions.a: In the front of the face — lips, nose, cheekbones.

days.guide: Drill 10 tongue twisters slowly, then faster; record before and after.

questions.q: Which articulators are used in speech?
questions.a: Lips, teeth, tongue, hard and soft palate, and jaw.

days.guide: Deliver the poem to a partner at 5, 15, and 30 feet without shouting; partner raises a hand if words are lost.

questions.q: How do you project to 30 feet without shouting?
questions.a: Use full breath support, open resonance (especially mask), slightly slower pace, and crisp articulation, aiming the voice at the back listener.

days.guide: Student leads their designed 5-minute warm-up (breath, resonance, articulation) then reads the poem; compare with the week 1 recording.

questions.q: Why warm up the voice before performing?
questions.a: To prepare breath, relax tension, and wake up resonance and articulators, preventing strain and improving clarity.

weeks.assessment_key: Vocal recording comparison rubric. 4 – Designed warm-up covers breath, resonance, and articulation; final reading shows clear improvement in projection, articulation, and breath support; written comparison cites specific moments. 3 (proficient) – Complete warm-up, audible/clear reading, comparison notes improvements. 2 – Little improvement or missing comparison. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Prepare a music playlist with varied qualities. Learn Laban effort chart: Weight (strong/light), Time (sudden/sustained), Space (direct/indirect). Find a short clip from a physical theatre company (e.g., Frantic Assembly or Complicité); preview.
misconceptions: Mime objects that change size or disappear. Keep the object consistent (fixed point).
Physical theatre without a story. Movement must have a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Confusing flow with speed. Flow is bound (controlled) vs. free (released), separate from time.

days.guide: Explore the eight efforts: punch/thrust (strong, sudden, direct), slash (strong, sudden, indirect), press (strong, sustained, direct), wring (strong, sustained, indirect), dab (light, sudden, direct), flick (light, sudden, indirect), glide (light, sustained, direct), float (light, sustained, indirect).

questions.q: Which Laban effort is light, sustained, and indirect?
questions.a: Float.

questions.q: What are the three factors combined in the eight efforts?
questions.a: Weight (strong/light), time (sudden/sustained), and space (direct/indirect).

days.guide: Teach mime illusions: wall (fixed point, flat hands), rope pull (hands stay in line, weight shifts), lifting weight (bend knees, show strain). Create a 1-minute mime scene.

questions.q: What is a 'fixed point' in mime?
questions.a: Keeping a hand or body part still in space so an imaginary object seems solid.

days.guide: Watch the clip; student lists techniques (lifts, repetition, slow motion, ensemble unison, objects as symbols).

questions.q: What is physical theatre?
questions.a: Performance where the story is told mainly through movement and the body rather than spoken text.

days.guide: Explore neutral movement then a wordless arc: a character enters, discovers something, and changes.

questions.q: Why start from neutral?
questions.a: Neutral removes personal habits, so every movement choice becomes intentional and readable.

days.guide: Perform a 2-minute wordless piece with a clear beginning, middle, and end.

questions.q: How can an audience see a character change without words?
questions.a: Through shifts in tempo, posture, Laban effort, focus, and use of space.

weeks.assessment_key: Physical theatre piece rubric. 4 – Clear wordless story with beginning, middle, end; at least three Laban efforts clearly contrasted; consistent mime objects; controlled, committed movement. 3 (proficient) – Readable story, varied efforts, mostly consistent mime. 2 – Story unclear or movement unvaried. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find the International Dialects of English Archive (IDEA) website. Choose a choral text (Whitman 'I Hear America Singing' or a Greek chorus ode, e.g., the 'Ode to Man' from Antigone in a public-domain translation). Recording app ready; recruit voices.
misconceptions: Treating dialect as a joke or stereotype. Dialects are real people's speech; use them respectfully and only when the character requires it.
Choral speaking with everyone speaking the whole time. Contrast (solo, small group, full chorus) creates interest.
Inflection only at the end of lines. Pitch variety should follow meaning and operative words.

days.guide: Read 'I didn't say she took the money' ten ways, stressing a different word or using different pitch/inflection; partner guesses the subtext.

questions.q: How does stressing 'she' change 'I didn't say SHE took the money'?
questions.a: It implies someone else took the money.

days.guide: Listen to 3–4 IDEA samples; discuss features (vowels, rhythm, melody) and respectful use: research, specificity, avoid caricature.

questions.q: What is a dialect?
questions.a: A variety of a language with distinctive pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar, associated with a region or group.

days.guide: Divide the text into solo, small-group, and unison lines; add simple movement or gestures.

questions.q: What is choral speaking?
questions.a: A group speaking a text together with planned variation in voices, dynamics, and pacing.

days.guide: Rehearse for unison (breathe together), contrast (loud/soft, fast/slow), and staging.

questions.q: How do groups stay in unison?
questions.a: Breathe together, follow a leader's cue, agree on pace and pauses, and listen to each other.

days.guide: Perform the choral piece; student completes a voice-and-movement self-assessment.

questions.q: Name two vocal elements you varied.
questions.a: Pitch, pace, volume (dynamics), inflection, and tone.

weeks.assessment_key: Choral performance rubric. 4 – Precise unison, purposeful contrasts in volume, pace and grouping, clear articulation, staging supports meaning; thoughtful self-assessment. 3 (proficient) – Mostly unified, clear contrasts, audible, complete self-assessment. 2 – Ragged unison or little variation. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find an overview of Stanislavski's system (e.g., a reputable theatre education site) and a public-domain copy of Chekhov's The Proposal (Lomov comes to propose to Natalya; they quarrel over Oxen Meadows and their dogs). Pick a 1-page scene for beat work.
misconceptions: Playing an emotion ('be angry') instead of an action. Actors pursue objectives with tactics; emotion results.
Writing objectives as states ('to be happy'). Use active, playable verbs aimed at the partner ('to win her approval').
Thinking the 'magic if' means pretending you are the character. It means asking 'What would I do if I were in these circumstances?'

days.guide: Read the overview: Constantin Stanislavski co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre (1898) and developed a system for truthful acting: magic if, given circumstances, objectives, super-objective.

questions.q: What is the 'magic if'?
questions.a: The question 'What would I do if I were in this character's situation?' — it engages imagination to produce truthful behavior.

days.guide: Improvise: one actor must get a partner to open a door using five tactics (beg, charm, threaten, bribe, trick). Debrief which worked.

questions.q: Define objective, obstacle, and tactic.
questions.a: Objective: what the character wants. Obstacle: what stands in the way. Tactic: the action used to overcome the obstacle and get the objective.

days.guide: For a short scene of The Proposal, list who, what, where, when, why.

questions.q: What are Lomov's given circumstances when he arrives at Chubukov's house?
questions.a: He is a nervous, hypochondriac landowner in 19th-century rural Russia who has come in formal dress to propose to his neighbor's daughter, Natalya Stepanovna.

days.guide: Divide a 1-page scene into beats (new beat when the topic or tactic changes); title each with an active verb (to flatter, to accuse).

questions.q: When does a new beat begin?
questions.a: When the character's objective, tactic, or the subject changes — something shifts.

days.guide: Give the quiz and score the scene analysis.

questions.q: What is a super-objective?
questions.a: The character's overarching goal for the whole play, which all scene objectives serve.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Stanislavski co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre (1898). 2) Magic if: 'What would I do if…'. 3) Given circumstances: who/what/where/when/why. 4) Objective = want; obstacle = what blocks it; tactic = action to get it. 5) Super-objective = overarching goal for the play. 6) Beat = unit of action with one objective/tactic. Scene analysis (proficient): accurate given circumstances, playable objective per character, beats marked with active verbs.

weeks.prep: Borrow monologue books from the library (contemporary and classical) and check Drama Notebook lists. Pre-screen choices for age-appropriate content. The student must be able to get the full play the monologue comes from.
misconceptions: Choosing a monologue for length or 'drama' without reading the full play. Context determines the objective.
Memorizing with a flat line reading. Score first, then memorize with intention.
Treating a monologue as talking to the audience. Most monologues speak to a specific person (imaginary partner).

days.guide: Read 10 monologues; shortlist 3; choose one (1–2 minutes) suited to age and type. Explain the choice.

questions.q: What makes a good audition monologue choice?
questions.a: Age-appropriate, close to the actor's type, 1–2 minutes, a clear objective and change, from a published play the actor has read.

days.guide: Read the full play; write the given circumstances and the moment in the story.

questions.q: Why read the whole play?
questions.a: To understand the character's relationships, history, and objective so the choices are accurate.

days.guide: Score: mark beats, tactics (active verbs), operative words (key words to stress), and pauses.

questions.q: What is an operative word?
questions.a: The most important word in a line, which carries meaning and is emphasized.

days.guide: Memorize by chunking (one thought at a time) and walking rehearsal (moving while repeating).

questions.q: Name two memorization strategies.
questions.a: Chunking by thoughts/beats, writing out lines, recording and listening, walking/moving while speaking, first-letter cue sheets.

days.guide: Student performs off-book for family; feedback uses 'one strength, one note.'

questions.q: What is subtext?
questions.a: The unspoken thoughts and meaning beneath the lines.

weeks.assessment_key: Monologue progress check: proficient = fully off-book (≤2 prompts), clear objective, scored script with beats/tactics/operative words, given circumstances written. 4 adds varied tactics and a clear change; 2 = several prompts or unscored; 1 = not memorized.

weeks.prep: Mirror, recording app, and the scored monologue. Arrange a coach (drama teacher, community theatre actor) or a family member for Day 4.
misconceptions: Moving without reason ('wandering'). Every cross should come from a tactic change.
Looking at the floor or audience randomly. Place the imaginary partner at a fixed focal point just above audience heads.
Starting cold. The 'moment before' sets the energy for the first line.

days.guide: Improvise the 60 seconds before the monologue begins; go straight into the first line.

questions.q: What is the 'moment before'?
questions.a: What happened to the character immediately before the scene starts, which motivates the first line.

days.guide: Block with purposeful movement tied to beats; set a focal point for the imaginary listener.

questions.q: Where should the focal point usually be in an audition monologue?
questions.a: Slightly above the auditors' heads, out front, not looking directly at the auditors.

days.guide: Record and score with a rubric (objective, tactics, voice, movement, focus).

questions.q: Why watch your own video?
questions.a: To see habits (fidgeting, dropped volume) you can't feel while performing.

days.guide: Coach gives 2–3 specific notes; student re-runs applying each.

questions.q: What is emotional recall?
questions.a: Using a memory from one's own life with similar emotions to fuel a character's feelings (associated with Stanislavski's early work and Method acting).

days.guide: Perform refined version; write a rehearsal journal entry.

questions.q: What is blocking?
questions.a: The planned movement and positions of actors on stage.

weeks.assessment_key: Rehearsal journal rubric. 4 – Entries for each day with specific notes received, what changed, evidence from video, and next goals; uses terms (moment before, focal point, tactic). 3 (proficient) – Daily entries naming notes and adjustments. 2 – General entries. 1 – Missing.

weeks.prep: Set up a performance space and camera. Find a professional monologue video (e.g., a filmed stage production) to critique; preview. Invite an audience for Day 3.
misconceptions: Slating in character. Slate as yourself: warm, confident, 'Hi, I'm ___, and I'll be performing ___ from ___ by ___.'
Critique as only opinion. Use criteria (objective, voice, movement, truthfulness) and evidence.
Apologizing after mistakes. Keep going; recovery is part of performance.

days.guide: Teach slating and audition etiquette: walk in confidently, slate, take a moment, perform, hold a beat, say thank you.

questions.q: What information goes in a slate?
questions.a: Your name, the monologue's title/character, the play, and the playwright.

days.guide: Run the monologue twice; give and apply notes.

questions.q: What should you do if you forget a line during performance?
questions.a: Stay in character, keep the objective, paraphrase or move to the next thought — don't apologize.

days.guide: Perform for the audience; record.

questions.q: Why take a moment before starting?
questions.a: To focus, step into the given circumstances and 'moment before,' and make the transition from self to character.

days.guide: Watch a professional monologue and write a critique using criteria.

questions.q: Name four criteria for evaluating a monologue.
questions.a: Clarity of objective and tactics, vocal expression and projection, purposeful movement/focus, emotional truthfulness/believability.

days.guide: Self-assess with the rubric; set two goals.

questions.q: What is the difference between critique and criticism?
questions.a: Critique evaluates against criteria with evidence and balanced strengths/weaknesses; criticism is often just negative opinion.

weeks.assessment_key: Monologue performance rubric (each 1–4): Slate/etiquette; Objective & tactics (clear want, at least 3 tactic shifts); Voice (projected, articulate, varied); Body (purposeful blocking, fixed focal point); Truthfulness/commitment. Proficient (3) = clear objective, audible and varied voice, motivated movement, off-book, confident slate.

weeks.prep: Find Sophocles' Antigone on Project Gutenberg (public-domain translation) and choose key scenes: Antigone and Ismene (opening), Creon and Antigone, Creon and Haemon, Tiresias. Gather paper plates, paint, string. Read about the Theatre of Dionysus layout.
misconceptions: Thinking Greek plays had violence on stage. Deaths happen offstage and are reported by messengers.
Assuming women acted. All roles were played by men wearing masks.
Viewing Creon as purely a villain. He is a tragic figure whose pride (hubris) leads to his downfall.

days.guide: Read about the City Dionysia festival in Athens and the theatre: theatron (seating), orchestra (circular dancing place for the chorus), skene (scene building), parodos (entrances). Thespis is traditionally the first actor.

questions.q: What were the orchestra and skene in a Greek theatre?
questions.a: The orchestra was the circular performance area for the chorus; the skene was the building behind it used as backdrop and changing area.

questions.q: For which god were Athenian dramatic festivals held?
questions.a: Dionysus.

days.guide: Read key scenes. Discuss: Creon forbids burial of Polyneices; Antigone buries him, obeying divine law and family duty over the king's law.

questions.q: What is the central conflict in Antigone?
questions.a: Antigone's duty to bury her brother Polyneices (divine law, family loyalty, conscience) versus Creon's decree forbidding it (state law).

days.guide: Make a tragedy mask with an exaggerated expression; explore how a mask requires larger, clearer movement and turning the whole head.

questions.q: Why did Greek actors wear masks?
questions.a: To show character/emotion to a large outdoor audience, allow few actors to play many roles (including women), and amplify the voice somewhat.

days.guide: Stage a short chorus ode with unison movement (strophe moving one way, antistrophe the other).

questions.q: What was the role of the chorus?
questions.a: To comment on the action, represent the community's view, provide background, and link episodes through song and dance.

days.guide: Give the quiz and watch the chorus performance.

questions.q: What is catharsis?
questions.a: The emotional release or purging of pity and fear the audience experiences through tragedy (Aristotle).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Festival = City Dionysia, honoring Dionysus. 2) Theatron = seating; orchestra = chorus area; skene = stage building. 3) Thespis = first actor. 4) Hubris = excessive pride. 5) Catharsis = release of pity and fear. 6) Antigone buries Polyneices against Creon's decree. 7) Consequences: Antigone dies (hangs herself in the tomb), Haemon kills himself, and Eurydice (Creon's wife) kills herself. 8) Three actors played all roles, all male, masked. Chorus performance (proficient): unified movement, clear choral speaking, masks used with enlarged gestures.

weeks.prep: Gather commedia stock character images and short Noh and kabuki clips (e.g., from Japan Arts Council or museum channels); preview. Read about mystery and morality plays (York cycle, Everyman).
misconceptions: Thinking commedia was scripted. It used scenarios (plot outlines) and improvised dialogue with rehearsed lazzi.
Seeing Noh and kabuki as the same. Noh is older (14th c.), slow, spare, masked; kabuki (17th c.) is colorful, dramatic, with elaborate makeup.
Assuming medieval theatre was all religious services. Mystery plays were performed by town guilds outdoors in the vernacular.

days.guide: Read about mystery plays (Bible stories performed by guilds on pageant wagons, e.g., York cycle) and morality plays (allegories such as Everyman).

questions.q: What is a pageant wagon?
questions.a: A movable stage on wheels used in medieval mystery cycles, moving from station to station in town.

days.guide: Teach stock characters: Arlecchino (acrobatic, hungry servant), Pantalone (old, greedy Venetian merchant), Il Dottore (pompous scholar), Il Capitano (bragging coward), the Innamorati (lovers, unmasked). Practice each character's walk and lazzi.

questions.q: What are lazzi?
questions.a: Rehearsed comic bits of physical business (e.g., catching a fly and eating it) inserted into commedia performances.

days.guide: Improvise a commedia scenario (e.g., Pantalone hides his money; Arlecchino tries to steal food) with masks or half-mask gestures.

questions.q: Who is Pantalone?
questions.a: An old, miserly Venetian merchant, often a father blocking young lovers.

days.guide: Watch Noh and kabuki clips; compare with Western theatre (masks, music, stylized movement, hanamichi runway in kabuki, male actors including onnagata).

questions.q: Name one convention of kabuki.
questions.a: Male actors (onnagata play women), the hanamichi runway through the audience, mie (dramatic frozen poses), kumadori makeup.

questions.q: Name one convention of Noh.
questions.a: Masked lead (shite), slow stylized movement, a bridgeway (hashigakari), chorus and musicians, minimal set with a painted pine tree.

days.guide: Student writes a comparison of two traditions (e.g., commedia vs. kabuki): origins, actors, staging, audience.

questions.q: How are commedia and kabuki similar?
questions.a: Both rely on stock characters/types, stylized physical performance, and popular audiences.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison writing rubric. 4 – Accurately compares two traditions on origin/time, performers, conventions, staging, and audience with specific examples and a thesis. 3 (proficient) – Accurate comparison with at least three points and examples. 2 – Some inaccuracies or list-like. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Get the Folger Shakespeare text of A Midsummer Night's Dream (free at folger.edu). Choose a short speech (e.g., Puck's 'If we shadows have offended' or Helena's 'How happy some o'er other some can be'). Find images or a virtual tour of the Globe.
misconceptions: Pausing at the end of every line. Follow punctuation and thought; enjambed lines run on.
Thinking Shakespeare's language is 'Old English.' It is Early Modern English.
Stressing every syllable evenly. Iambic pentameter is da-DUM ×5; stress falls on the important words.

days.guide: Explore the Globe (built 1599): open-air, thrust stage, groundlings standing in the yard, daylight performances, minimal sets, boys playing women.

questions.q: Who were the groundlings?
questions.a: Audience members who paid a penny to stand in the yard around the stage.

days.guide: Teach iambic pentameter: five iambs (unstressed-stressed). Scan 'The course of true love never did run smooth' (1.1). Speak lines aloud, tapping stress.

questions.q: Scan 'The course of true love never did run smooth.'
questions.a: the COURSE / of TRUE / love NEV / er DID / run SMOOTH — five iambs, 10 syllables.

days.guide: Student paraphrases the chosen speech line by line, then circles operative words.

questions.q: Paraphrase Puck's 'If we shadows have offended, / Think but this, and all is mended, / That you have but slumber'd here / While these visions did appear.'
questions.a: If we actors displeased you, just imagine you were asleep and dreamed all this, and everything will be fine.

days.guide: Perform a sonnet (e.g., Sonnet 18) focusing on rhythm and the turn. Optionally play with Shakespearean insults for verbal energy.

questions.q: What is the structure of a Shakespearean sonnet?
questions.a: 14 lines of iambic pentameter: three quatrains and a final couplet, rhymed ABAB CDCD EFEF GG.

days.guide: Student performs the speech from memory.

questions.q: Why do some characters speak in prose and others in verse?
questions.a: Verse is often used by nobles and for heightened emotion; prose by lower-class or comic characters (e.g., the mechanicals mostly speak prose).

weeks.assessment_key: Shakespeare speech rubric. 4 – Memorized, meaning clear (paraphrase evident), rhythm felt without sing-song, operative words stressed, breath at punctuation, physical and vocal commitment. 3 (proficient) – Memorized, clear meaning, audible, mostly natural rhythm. 2 – Meaning unclear or several prompts. 1 – Not ready.

weeks.prep: Use the Folger text of A Midsummer Night's Dream. Act 3.1: the mechanicals rehearse 'Pyramus and Thisbe'; Puck gives Bottom an ass's head; Titania wakes and falls in love with him. Act 3.2: Lysander and Demetrius, enchanted, now both love Helena; Hermia and Helena quarrel. Find the 1999 film (dir. Michael Hoffman, Kevin Kline as Bottom) and a Globe recording. Tape out a stage. Prepare the history test.
misconceptions: Rushing comic lines. Comedy needs a clear setup, a pause, and the punchline.
Ignoring the verse/prose difference: the lovers speak verse, the mechanicals mostly prose.
Asides spoken to the other characters. An aside is to the audience (or self) and unheard by others on stage.

days.guide: Choose 3.1 or 3.2; read aloud and paraphrase every line.

questions.q: In 3.1, what does Puck do to Bottom?
questions.a: He transforms Bottom's head into an ass's (donkey's) head, scaring off the other mechanicals.

questions.q: In 3.2, why are Lysander and Demetrius both pursuing Helena?
questions.a: The love-juice from the flower (applied by Puck and Oberon) makes each fall in love with Helena when he wakes.

days.guide: Block on the taped stage; mark entrances, crosses, and asides in the script.

questions.q: What is an aside?
questions.a: A short remark spoken to the audience that other characters on stage are not meant to hear.

days.guide: Rehearse comic timing: pause before punchlines, take reactions, physical bits (Bottom's braying; Hermia's 'little' fury).

questions.q: Hermia is mocked for being short. What line does Helena say about her?
questions.a: 'And though she be but little, she is fierce.'

days.guide: Watch the scene in two versions; chart differences in setting, casting, comic business, and pacing.

questions.q: Where is the 1999 film set?
questions.a: In a fictional Tuscan town (Monte Athena) in Italy around 1900 — updated from ancient Athens.

days.guide: Perform the scene; give the Unit 4 history test.

questions.q: Define soliloquy vs. aside.
questions.a: Soliloquy: a speech alone on stage revealing thoughts. Aside: a brief remark to the audience while others are present.

weeks.assessment_key: Scene performance rubric: proficient = memorized, clear meaning, motivated blocking, comic timing with pauses, distinguishes verse/prose. History test key (Greek–Elizabethan): 1) Greek drama honored Dionysus. 2) Skene/orchestra/theatron. 3) Antigone by Sophocles. 4) Hubris, catharsis. 5) Medieval mystery plays on pageant wagons by guilds; morality plays like Everyman. 6) Commedia: improvised from scenarios, stock characters (Arlecchino, Pantalone), lazzi. 7) Noh 14th-c. Japan, masked, slow; kabuki 17th-c., onnagata, hanamichi. 8) Globe 1599, thrust stage, groundlings, boys played women. 9) Iambic pentameter = five iambs. 10) Sonnet = 14 lines ending in a couplet.

weeks.prep: Borrow a contemporary two-person scene collection (pre-screen for content). Recruit a scene partner for the week. Read about Sanford Meisner's repetition exercise.
misconceptions: Waiting for your cue instead of listening. Real listening changes how you respond.
Low stakes ('it doesn't really matter'). Raise stakes: what does the character lose if they fail?
Blocking for convenience. Each cross should come from a tactic change.

days.guide: Read three scenes; choose one with a partner; read the full play.

questions.q: Why do actors need to know the whole play for a two-person scene?
questions.a: The relationship history and what happens before/after determine objectives and stakes.

days.guide: Table work: given circumstances, objectives, relationship history.

questions.q: What are 'stakes'?
questions.a: What the character stands to win or lose — high stakes create urgency.

days.guide: Repetition exercise: partners face each other; A makes an observation ('You're smiling'); B repeats it from their point of view ('I'm smiling'); continue, letting changes in tone come from impulse. 15 minutes.

questions.q: What does the Meisner repetition exercise train?
questions.a: Listening and responding truthfully to a partner in the moment, rather than planning line readings.

days.guide: Block so every cross is motivated by a tactic change; note blocking in scripts.

questions.q: A character moves away from her partner. What tactic might this show?
questions.a: Withdrawing, punishing, or regrouping — e.g., 'to make him chase me' or 'to protect myself.'

days.guide: Run off-book; journal on one truthful moment.

questions.q: What made a moment feel 'truthful'?
questions.a: Answers vary; strong ones describe genuinely reacting to the partner's behavior rather than a planned reading.

weeks.assessment_key: Off-book run and journal rubric. 4 – Fully memorized, active listening, clear objectives and tactic shifts, motivated blocking; journal analyzes a specific truthful moment and why. 3 (proficient) – Off-book with ≤2 prompts, clear objectives, journal entry. 2 – Several prompts, little listening. 1 – Not memorized.

weeks.prep: Gather costume pieces and simple props; access to a printer for programs and posters. Line up a coach for Day 1. Set the showcase date and invite guests.
misconceptions: Adding props that distract. Choose only props the action needs or that reveal character.
Ignoring transitions. Plan who moves what and when between pieces.
Skipping the curtain call rehearsal. Bows should be rehearsed and unified.

days.guide: Identify the three highest-stakes moments; work each with the coach to raise stakes and sharpen transitions.

questions.q: How can an actor 'raise the stakes' in a moment?
questions.a: Make the consequence of failure bigger and more personal, increasing urgency in the objective.

days.guide: Choose costume pieces and props that reveal character; write a prop list (item, scene, who handles it, preset location).

questions.q: What should a prop list include?
questions.a: Each prop, the scene where it's used, who uses it, and where it is preset.

days.guide: Design a program (title, order of pieces, playwrights, bios, thanks) and a poster (who, what, when, where).

questions.q: What information must a theatre poster include?
questions.a: Title of the event, date, time, location, and how to attend.

days.guide: Full dress rehearsal of all three pieces in costume, timed.

questions.q: What is a dress rehearsal?
questions.a: A full run with costumes, props, and all elements as in performance.

days.guide: Give notes; rehearse transitions and curtain call.

questions.q: What are 'notes'?
questions.a: The director's or coach's feedback after a rehearsal, to be applied in the next run.

weeks.assessment_key: Dress rehearsal notes rubric. 4 – Notes recorded for each piece with specific actions taken; all notes applied in the next run; transitions and curtain call clean; prop list and program complete. 3 (proficient) – Notes recorded and mostly applied; materials complete. 2 – Notes not applied. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Set up the performance space and video camera. Prepare the semester exam (key below). Print the acting rubric for video review.
misconceptions: Treating the video review as a highlight reel. Identify growth areas honestly with timestamps.
Reflections that summarize instead of analyze. Cite specific moments and explain why they worked or didn't.
Mixing up Greek and Elizabethan conventions on the exam.

days.guide: Run the show at performance pace including curtain call; time it.

questions.q: Why rehearse at performance pace?
questions.a: To build stamina and set correct timing and transitions.

days.guide: Perform the winter showcase and record it.

questions.q: What does 'house' mean in theatre?
questions.a: The audience area (and by extension the audience).

days.guide: Watch the recording; log three strengths and three growth areas with timestamps using the acting rubric.

questions.q: Give an example of a specific, useful growth note.
questions.a: 'At 3:42 I dropped my volume on the last line; support the final phrase with breath.'

days.guide: Write a 500-word reflection citing specific moments.

questions.q: What makes a reflection analytical?
questions.a: It explains causes and effects of choices with evidence, not just describes what happened.

days.guide: Give the semester exam.

questions.q: Define objective and super-objective.
questions.a: Objective: what a character wants in a scene. Super-objective: the overarching goal throughout the play.

weeks.assessment_key: Showcase rubric: proficient = memorized, audible, clear objectives, motivated blocking, professional transitions and curtain call. Semester exam key: 1) Ensemble = group working as one. 2) Yes, and = accept and build. 3) CROW = character, relationship, objective, where. 4) Stanislavski: magic if, given circumstances, objective/obstacle/tactic, super-objective; Moscow Art Theatre. 5) Laban efforts: weight, time, space. 6) Greek: City Dionysia, chorus, masks, skene/orchestra, Sophocles' Antigone, hubris, catharsis. 7) Medieval: mystery/morality plays, pageant wagons. 8) Commedia: stock characters, lazzi, scenarios. 9) Noh/kabuki conventions. 10) Globe Theatre: thrust stage, groundlings, iambic pentameter, sonnet form (14 lines). Grade: 90%+ advanced, 75–89% proficient.

weeks.prep: Find Susan Glaspell's Trifles (1916, public domain) and an excerpt of Ibsen's A Doll's House (e.g., the final scene). Parental note: Trifles involves a murder investigation (a husband strangled with a rope); it is not graphic.
misconceptions: Thinking nothing happens in realism. Action is internal and revealed through subtext and small details.
Reading the women's lines literally. Their talk about quilting and preserves carries hidden meaning about Minnie's life and motive.
Assuming the men find the evidence. The men search and dismiss 'kitchen things'; the women discover the motive.

days.guide: Read about realism: Ibsen and Chekhov in the late 1800s brought everyday life, real social problems, and the 'fourth wall' (invisible wall between stage and audience). Read the final scene of A Doll's House.

questions.q: What is the 'fourth wall'?
questions.a: The imaginary wall at the front of a realistic set through which the audience watches; actors behave as if it's a real, closed room.

questions.q: Why was the ending of A Doll's House shocking in 1879?
questions.a: Nora leaves her husband and children to find her own identity — slamming the door on conventional marriage and gender roles.

days.guide: Read Trifles aloud by roles; list clues the women find.

questions.q: List the clues Mrs. Hale and Mrs. Peters find.
questions.a: The half-cleaned kitchen and unfinished work, broken jars of frozen preserves, erratic quilt stitching, the birdcage with a broken door hinge, and the dead canary with its neck wrung in a box in the sewing basket.

days.guide: Analyze subtext: for 5 lines, write what each line literally says and really means.

questions.q: What is the subtext when Mrs. Hale says she wishes she had visited Minnie?
questions.a: She feels guilty — she sees that Minnie's isolation and loneliness with a harsh husband contributed to the crime, and she shares responsibility for neglecting her.

days.guide: Rehearse the final scene emphasizing silence and small gestures (looking at the box, hiding it).

questions.q: How does Trifles end?
questions.a: The women hide the box with the dead bird, concealing the motive; Mrs. Hale answers the county attorney that Minnie was going to 'knot it.'

days.guide: Perform; student writes a paragraph on how Glaspell uses objects.

questions.q: What does the canary symbolize?
questions.a: Minnie herself — her lost voice and joy (she sang as Minnie Foster) and her life caged and silenced by her husband, who killed the bird as he killed her spirit.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric. 4 – Thesis on objects as storytelling; analyzes at least three objects (preserves, quilt, birdcage/canary) with quotations; explains how they reveal motive and the women's solidarity. 3 (proficient) – Two or three objects explained with evidence. 2 – Summary rather than analysis. 1 – Inaccurate. Scene performance: proficient = honors silences, small purposeful gestures, clear shift as the women decide to hide the evidence.

weeks.prep: Borrow Thornton Wilder's Our Town (1938) from the library. Know: three acts (Daily Life, Love and Marriage, Death/Eternity), set in Grover's Corners, New Hampshire, beginning in 1901; the Stage Manager narrates; Emily Webb and George Gibbs. Parental note: Act III takes place in the town cemetery after Emily's death in childbirth.
misconceptions: Thinking a bare stage means low effort. Wilder's minimalism is deliberate: it makes the story universal and asks the audience to imagine.
Mixing up presentational and representational. Presentational acknowledges the audience (Stage Manager); representational maintains the fourth wall.
Pantomime with vague hands. Specific weight, size, and steps make invisible objects real.

days.guide: Read Act I; discuss the Stage Manager, who talks directly to the audience, controls time, and plays small roles; the stage uses only tables, chairs, and ladders.

questions.q: What is the Stage Manager's role in Our Town?
questions.a: A narrator who addresses the audience directly, introduces characters, shifts time, and occasionally plays minor parts.

days.guide: Pantomime everyday tasks with precise detail (making breakfast, stringing beans as Mrs. Gibbs and Mrs. Webb do).

questions.q: Why does Wilder use pantomime instead of real props?
questions.a: To focus attention on the universal everyday actions and people, not the objects, and to make the play timeless.

days.guide: Read Act III; discuss Emily's choice to relive her twelfth birthday and her question.

questions.q: What does Emily ask the Stage Manager, and how does he answer?
questions.a: 'Do any human beings ever realize life while they live it?—every, every minute?' He answers, 'No.' Then: 'The saints and poets, maybe—they do some.'

days.guide: Stage Emily's goodbye speech ('Good-by, Grover's Corners… Mama's sunflowers…') with no set and minimal props.

questions.q: What is the theme of Emily's goodbye?
questions.a: People fail to appreciate the ordinary wonders of everyday life while they are living it.

days.guide: Perform; write a comparison of Wilder's presentational style and Glaspell's realism.

questions.q: How do Our Town and Trifles differ in style?
questions.a: Our Town is presentational: bare stage, narrator addresses the audience, time jumps. Trifles is realistic: detailed kitchen, fourth wall, continuous real time, meaning via subtext.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance and comparison rubric. 4 – Emily's speech performed with clear specificity of each remembered item and emotional arc; essay compares staging, audience relationship, acting style, and theme with evidence from both plays. 3 (proficient) – Committed performance; essay accurately contrasts presentational vs. realistic styles with examples. 2 – General comparison. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Borrow A Raisin in the Sun (Hansberry, 1959) and Fences (Wilson, 1985 premiere/1987 Broadway) for excerpts, and find Luis Valdez's acto Las Dos Caras del Patroncito (1965) — in it a farmworker and his masked boss trade places. Parental note: Fences contains strong language; select excerpts.
misconceptions: Treating actos as polished plays. Actos were short, improvised-feeling sketches performed on flatbed trucks and in fields to educate and energize striking farmworkers.
Reading these plays as only about race. They are also about family, dreams, dignity, and generational conflict.
Researching a playwright without the community context.

days.guide: Learn about El Teatro Campesino (founded 1965 by Luis Valdez during the Delano grape strike, with the United Farm Workers), using masks, placards, humor, and bilingual dialogue.

questions.q: What was the purpose of the actos of El Teatro Campesino?
questions.a: To dramatize farmworkers' conditions, explain the strike and union, and inspire workers — theatre as social action.

days.guide: Rehearse Las Dos Caras del Patroncito with a pig-like mask for the boss and placards naming characters.

questions.q: Why use placards and masks in an acto?
questions.a: They identify characters instantly, make types broad and clear for outdoor audiences, and add satire.

days.guide: Read excerpts: Raisin (the Younger family's $10,000 insurance check; Mama buys a house in all-white Clybourne Park; Walter loses money; refuses Lindner's buyout). Fences (Troy Maxson, former Negro Leagues player and Pittsburgh sanitation worker, blocks his son Cory's football scholarship). Compare the father/son and family conflicts.

questions.q: What does Walter Lee ultimately decide when Karl Lindner offers to buy the family out?
questions.a: He refuses the offer and the family moves into the house in Clybourne Park, reclaiming his dignity.

questions.q: Why does Troy oppose Cory's football recruitment?
questions.a: Troy was kept out of the major leagues by racism and believes Cory will be hurt the same way; he also resents and fears his son's opportunities — he insists Cory keep his job.

days.guide: Student researches one playwright of color: biography, key works, community, and themes.

questions.q: What is August Wilson's Century Cycle?
questions.a: Ten plays, each set in a different decade of the 20th century, depicting African American life (nine set in Pittsburgh's Hill District).

days.guide: 4-minute research talk with a performed excerpt.

questions.q: Where does the title A Raisin in the Sun come from?
questions.a: Langston Hughes's poem 'Harlem': 'What happens to a dream deferred? / Does it dry up / like a raisin in the sun?'

weeks.assessment_key: Research talk rubric. 4 – Accurate biography, two works, community/historical context, themes explained, well-chosen performed excerpt connected to the research, sources cited, within 4 minutes. 3 (proficient) – Accurate facts, context, excerpt performed. 2 – Thin research or no connection. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find two professional theatre reviews (e.g., a major newspaper review of a recent production). Arrange to attend a local production or choose a full filmed play (e.g., a National Theatre at Home or BroadwayHD title); preview content.
misconceptions: Retelling the plot. A critique evaluates choices with evidence.
Only praising or only criticizing. Balance strengths and weaknesses.
Vague vocabulary ('the lighting was good'). Use specific terms: 'warm, low-angle side light isolated the actor…'

days.guide: Read two reviews; identify structure (hook, context, evaluation of acting/design/direction, verdict) and criteria.

questions.q: What are the main parts of a theatre review?
questions.a: Introduction with production info and thesis, brief context/plot, evaluation of acting, direction, design with evidence, and an overall judgment.

days.guide: Attend/watch; take notes on acting, design, direction with specific moments.

questions.q: What does 'production values' refer to?
questions.a: The quality of the technical and design elements — sets, lighting, costumes, sound.
