days.guide: Draft a 700-word critique evaluating three elements with evidence.

questions.q: Give a strong thesis example.
questions.a: 'Director X's spare staging focuses attention on the family's tension, but uneven pacing in Act II weakens the climax.'

days.guide: Revise for precise vocabulary and balance.

questions.q: Replace 'the lights were cool' with precise language.
questions.a: Example: 'Cold blue backlight and a single downlight isolated Emily, creating a lonely, otherworldly mood.'

days.guide: Submit critique; give a short American theatre quiz.

questions.q: Who wrote Trifles and when?
questions.a: Susan Glaspell, 1916.

weeks.assessment_key: Critique rubric. 4 – Clear thesis; evaluates three production elements with specific evidence and theatre vocabulary; balanced; ~700 words; polished. 3 (proficient) – Thesis, three elements with examples, mostly precise vocabulary. 2 – Mostly summary. 1 – Incomplete. Quiz key: 1) Trifles — Glaspell 1916, realism. 2) Our Town — Wilder, Stage Manager, presentational. 3) A Raisin in the Sun — Hansberry, 1959, title from Hughes. 4) Fences — Wilson, Century Cycle. 5) El Teatro Campesino — Luis Valdez, 1965, Delano, actos.

weeks.prep: Gather graph paper, a ruler, a shoebox, cardboard, glue, and craft knife (supervise). Have Trifles to reread for set requirements.
misconceptions: Forgetting sightlines on thrust and arena stages. Furniture must not block views from the sides.
Drawing a ground plan in perspective. It is a bird's-eye, to-scale view.
Designing pretty sets that ignore the script. Every element should be required by or support the text.

days.guide: Compare proscenium (picture frame, audience on one side), thrust (audience on three sides), arena/in-the-round (all sides), black box (flexible). Draw each.

questions.q: Which stage type has the audience on three sides?
questions.a: Thrust stage.

days.guide: List every set requirement implied by Trifles (kitchen: stove, table, rocking chair, cupboard, doors to outside, upstairs, and a shed/other room, window, sewing basket, birdcage location).

questions.q: Name three set requirements of Trifles.
questions.a: A kitchen with a stove, a table, a rocking chair, a cupboard with jars, a door to the outside and a stair door, and a place for the sewing basket/birdcage.

days.guide: Draw a 1/4-inch = 1-foot ground plan of the kitchen with all doors and furniture.

questions.q: At 1/4" = 1', how long is a 12-foot wall on paper?
questions.a: 3 inches.

days.guide: Build the shoebox model to scale.

questions.q: Why do designers make model boxes?
questions.a: To visualize the set in 3D and communicate it to the director and team before building.

days.guide: Present the model and explain how it supports the mood (cold, bleak, isolated farmhouse).

questions.q: How can set design create a sense of isolation for Trifles?
questions.a: Sparse, worn furniture, cold colors, small window, gloomy lighting, disorder in the unfinished kitchen.

weeks.assessment_key: Model box presentation rubric. 4 – Accurate scale ground plan; model includes all script-required elements; clear concept linking design to mood/theme; presentation uses terms (proscenium, ground plan, sightlines). 3 (proficient) – Scaled plan and model with required elements and mood explanation. 2 – Missing elements or scale. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather flashlights, colored cellophane (warm and cool), desk lamps, and an audio editor/free sound libraries (e.g., freesound.org with proper licensing). Choose a short scene (e.g., from Trifles or Our Town).
misconceptions: Lighting only the face from the front. Front light alone flattens; side and back light add depth.
Sound cues that are too loud. Underscore supports, it shouldn't compete with dialogue.
Calling cues without numbers. Every cue is numbered and placed exactly in the script.

days.guide: In a dim room, light a face from front, side, below, above, and back; add warm (amber) and cool (blue) gels. Note emotional effects.

questions.q: What mood does light from below create?
questions.a: Eerie, unnatural, or frightening — it reverses normal shadows.

questions.q: Which has a warmer color temperature: 2700 K or 5600 K?
questions.a: 2700 K (warmer/amber); 5600 K is cooler, like daylight.

days.guide: Write a cue sheet with 8 lighting cues (cue number, page/line, description, timing).

questions.q: What information goes on a lighting cue sheet?
questions.a: Cue number, the exact line or action where it happens, what changes, and the fade time.

days.guide: Find or record sound effects and underscore for the scene; check licensing.

questions.q: What is underscore?
questions.a: Music played softly beneath dialogue or action to support mood.

days.guide: Write the sound cue sheet with timings and levels.

questions.q: What is a 'cue' in theatre?
questions.a: A signal for a technical change (light, sound) or an actor's entrance/line, triggered at a set moment.

days.guide: Run the scene with light and sound cues for family; adjust.

questions.q: What are the four controllable qualities of stage light?
questions.a: Intensity, color, distribution (angle/shape/focus), and movement (changes over time).

weeks.assessment_key: Cue run rubric. 4 – 8 numbered light cues and complete sound cue sheet, all executed on time, levels and colors purposeful for mood, explanation of choices. 3 (proficient) – Cue sheets complete, most cues on time, mood supported. 2 – Missed cues or incomplete sheets. 1 – Not run.

weeks.prep: Gather colored pencils, paper, thrift/closet pieces, and basic makeup (neutral foundation, brown/gray contour, highlight, brushes). Choose a play with a clear period (e.g., Trifles, 1916 rural Iowa; Our Town, 1901–1913 New Hampshire). Check for skin sensitivities.
misconceptions: Designing costumes to look fashionable instead of revealing character and period.
Using too much contour so aging looks like dirt. Blend and follow natural lines.
Forgetting quick changes and movement needs in the costume plot.

days.guide: Research the period: silhouettes, fabrics, social class indicators.

questions.q: What clothing might Mrs. Hale wear in Trifles (1916 rural farm)?
questions.a: A long, plain cotton or wool dress (ankle length), apron, sturdy shoes, a coat, hat, and scarf for the cold.

days.guide: Draw renderings for three characters with fabric notes and swatches.

questions.q: What is a costume rendering?
questions.a: A drawing of a character in costume showing color, silhouette, and details, used to communicate the design.

days.guide: Create a costume plot: chart of each character's costume per scene.

questions.q: Why make a costume plot?
questions.a: To track which costume each actor wears in each scene and plan changes.

days.guide: Practice aging makeup: find natural creases, add shadow with contour, highlight above each line, blend.

questions.q: How do highlight and shadow create aging?
questions.a: Shadow makes areas recede (hollows, wrinkle lines) and highlight makes areas come forward, imitating sagging and creases under stage light.

days.guide: Present the portfolio: research, renderings, plot, makeup photos.

questions.q: What does 'silhouette' mean in costume design?
questions.a: The overall outline or shape of the costume on the body.

weeks.assessment_key: Costume portfolio rubric. 4 – Period research with sources, three detailed renderings reflecting character and period, complete costume plot, makeup demonstration photos, written rationale. 3 (proficient) – Research, three renderings, plot, makeup practice. 2 – Missing elements. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather design materials and previous work (model, cue sheets, renderings). Decide tentatively on the one-act for Unit 9 (e.g., Trifles or The Proposal). Prepare the technical theatre quiz.
misconceptions: A concept that's just a theme word. A concept states how the production will interpret the play and how design will express it.
Designers working separately. Unity requires collaboration around the concept.
Taking design feedback personally. Revisions serve the production.

days.guide: Write a concept statement (1 paragraph): interpretation, central image or metaphor, and how design will express it.

questions.q: Write a sample concept statement for Trifles.
questions.a: Example: 'A cage: the Wright farmhouse is staged as a cramped, cold enclosure in grays, with the only warmth the red of the quilt and the women's discovery — showing how isolation silences women.'

days.guide: Build a mood board of images, colors, textures.

questions.q: What is a mood board for?
questions.a: To communicate the visual feel (color, texture, atmosphere) of the production concept.

days.guide: Mock design meeting: present set, lights, sound, costumes; family responds.

questions.q: Who usually leads a design meeting?
questions.a: The director, guided by the production concept, with designers and stage manager.

days.guide: Revise designs based on feedback.

questions.q: Why is unity important in production design?
questions.a: All elements should support one coherent interpretation so the audience gets a consistent experience.

days.guide: Submit portfolio; give the quiz.

questions.q: Name the four main stage configurations.
questions.a: Proscenium, thrust, arena (in-the-round), and black box (flexible).

weeks.assessment_key: Design portfolio and quiz. Portfolio proficient = concept statement, mood board, set plan/model, light and sound cue sheets, costume renderings, revised after feedback, all unified. Quiz key: 1) Proscenium/thrust/arena/black box. 2) Ground plan = scale bird's-eye view. 3) Light qualities: intensity, color, distribution, movement. 4) Lower Kelvin = warmer. 5) Underscore = background music. 6) Costume plot = costume per character per scene. 7) Rendering = design drawing. 8) Concept = unifying interpretation.

weeks.prep: Have Trifles and a play-format template (character names in caps centered or flush left, stage directions in italics/parentheses). Gather paper for character design.
misconceptions: Characters explaining feelings directly ('I am angry because…'). Good dialogue uses subtext.
Scenes without conflict. Two characters must want incompatible things.
Writing novel-style description in stage directions. Keep them brief, present tense, playable.

days.guide: Map Freytag's pyramid onto Trifles: exposition (men arrive; Hale's account of finding Mr. Wright), rising action (the women find preserves, quilt, birdcage), climax (discovery of the strangled canary), falling action (they decide what to do as men return), resolution (they hide the box; 'knot it').

questions.q: What is the climax of Trifles?
questions.a: The discovery of the dead canary with its neck wrung — revealing the motive and forcing the women's choice.

days.guide: Write a 1-page scene with only dialogue: two characters want the same object.

questions.q: How can dialogue show action without stage directions?
questions.a: Characters reference what they do or see ('Put that down!'), and conflict is revealed through what they say and withhold.

days.guide: Teach play format; reformat the scene.

questions.q: Where do stage directions go in play format and what tense are they in?
questions.a: Set off (often in italics or parentheses), indented, written in present tense.

days.guide: Create two characters with want, fear, and secret; write bios.

questions.q: Why give a character a secret?
questions.a: It creates subtext and potential for revelation and conflict.

days.guide: Submit a 3-page scene draft with the two characters in conflict.

questions.q: What is an inciting incident?
questions.a: The event that sets the main conflict in motion.

weeks.assessment_key: Scene draft rubric. 4 – Correct play format; two distinct characters with clear competing wants; conflict escalates to a turning point; subtext in dialogue; concise stage directions; 3 pages. 3 (proficient) – Correct format, clear conflict, distinct characters. 2 – Format errors or weak conflict. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Play-format template, a recording app, and 2–4 volunteers for a table read. Read one or two published ten-minute plays as models if available.
misconceptions: Too many characters or locations for ten minutes. Keep 2–3 characters and one setting.
Late conflict. Start close to the conflict; the turning point should come around minute 7.
Ignoring table-read reactions. Where listeners drift, the script needs cutting or sharpening.

days.guide: Brainstorm 10 premises from personal, family, or community stories; choose one with clear conflict and one setting.

questions.q: What makes a premise work for a ten-minute play?
questions.a: A single setting, two or three characters, an immediate conflict with stakes, and a possible change by the end.

days.guide: Outline in 6–8 beats with the turning point around minute 7 (about page 7; one page ≈ one minute).

questions.q: About how long does one script page run in performance?
questions.a: About one minute.

days.guide: Write the full 8–10 page draft.

questions.q: What is a dramaturg?
questions.a: A theatre professional who researches context and helps develop scripts with the playwright and director.

days.guide: Hold a recorded table read; mark where listeners lost interest.

questions.q: What is a table read?
questions.a: A seated read-through of a script aloud by actors to hear the play and find problems.

days.guide: Revise using the recording: cut repetition, sharpen climax; submit draft 2.

questions.q: Name two revision strategies for dialogue.
questions.a: Cut lines that repeat information, replace explanation with subtext, end scenes on a turn, read aloud for natural rhythm.

weeks.assessment_key: Ten-minute play second draft rubric. 4 – 8–10 pages in correct format, clear conflict from page 1, turning point near page 7, satisfying resolution, distinct voices, revision log shows meaningful changes from the table read. 3 (proficient) – Correct length/format, clear arc, revisions evident. 2 – Weak structure or little revision. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find short documentary clips about Tectonic Theater Project's The Laramie Project (verbatim interviews in Laramie, Wyoming after the 1998 murder of Matthew Shepard) and about Frantic Assembly; preview content. Prepare interview questions on a theme such as 'home.' Get permission to record interviewees.
misconceptions: Thinking devised theatre has no structure. It is built collaboratively from sources, then shaped and edited.
Editing verbatim text to change meaning. Verbatim theatre must respect speakers' actual words and consent.
Moving randomly in Viewpoints. Respond to tempo, space, and others with awareness.

days.guide: Watch clips; list devising methods (interviews, moment work, physical scores, chair duets, building from tasks).

questions.q: What is verbatim theatre?
questions.a: Theatre made from the exact words of real people, usually gathered through interviews.

days.guide: Interview two community members on the theme; collect found text (letters, articles).

questions.q: What ethical steps should you take with interviews?
questions.a: Get consent to record and use words, represent people accurately, and let them review or remain anonymous if they wish.

days.guide: Explore Viewpoints: tempo, spatial relationship, repetition (plus shape, gesture, architecture) to generate movement.

questions.q: Name three Viewpoints.
questions.a: Tempo, duration, kinesthetic response, repetition, shape, gesture, architecture, spatial relationship, topography (any three).

days.guide: Combine verbatim lines and movement into three short compositions.

questions.q: What is a composition in devising?
questions.a: A short piece created by an ensemble combining elements (text, movement, image) around a prompt.

days.guide: Shape into a 6–8 minute piece; show for feedback.

questions.q: What did Tectonic Theater Project use as the source for The Laramie Project?
questions.a: Hundreds of interviews with residents of Laramie, Wyoming, plus journals and news reports, after the murder of Matthew Shepard.

weeks.assessment_key: Devised showing rubric. 4 – 6–8 minutes; integrates verbatim text accurately with purposeful movement from Viewpoints; clear structure and theme; ethical use of sources; ensemble commitment. 3 (proficient) – Clear theme, verbatim text and movement combined, shaped piece. 2 – Loosely connected material. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Binders for scripts, music stands or chairs, volunteer actors. Read Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process (4 steps). Invite an audience.
misconceptions: Thinking a staged reading needs memorization. Actors hold scripts; focus is on hearing the play.
Talkbacks becoming opinion free-for-alls. Use the Critical Response Process order.
Defending the play in a talkback. The playwright listens and asks questions.

days.guide: Cast and rehearse the ten-minute play as a staged reading (one person reads stage directions).

questions.q: What is a staged reading?
questions.a: A performance where actors read from scripts with minimal staging, to present and develop a new play.

days.guide: Refine stage-direction reading and transitions; finalize devised piece.

questions.q: Why read only key stage directions?
questions.a: To keep momentum while giving the audience necessary information.

days.guide: Present the staged reading and devised piece.

questions.q: What should the audience understand before a staged reading?
questions.a: That it's a work in progress, read with scripts, to help the playwright develop the play.

days.guide: Lead the talkback with the Critical Response Process: 1) statements of meaning, 2) artist asks questions, 3) responders ask neutral questions, 4) opinion time (with the artist's permission).

questions.q: List the four steps of Liz Lerman's Critical Response Process.
questions.a: 1) Statements of meaning, 2) Artist as questioner, 3) Neutral questions from responders, 4) Opinion time (permissioned opinions).

days.guide: 400-word reflection on learning as playwright and deviser.

questions.q: What is a 'neutral question'?
questions.a: A question without an embedded opinion, e.g., 'What were you going for with the ending?' rather than 'Why was the ending so confusing?'

weeks.assessment_key: Festival rubric. 4 – Staged reading well-rehearsed with clear transitions; devised piece polished; talkback follows all four CRP steps and feedback recorded; 400-word reflection analyzes specific learning and next revisions. 3 (proficient) – Both pieces presented, CRP used, reflection complete. 2 – Talkback disorganized or reflection thin. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather public-domain one-acts: Trifles (5 characters), Chekhov's The Proposal (3 characters), and an Oscar Wilde excerpt. Find an interview with a working director (e.g., from a theatre company website). Get a binder for the prompt book. If using a co-op, arrange audition time.
misconceptions: Thinking the director only tells actors where to stand. The director unifies interpretation, actors, and design.
Choosing a play the available cast can't fill. Match cast size and audience.
Forgetting royalties. Public-domain plays require no royalties; copyrighted plays need licenses even for small performances with an audience.

days.guide: Read about the director's history (rise in the late 1800s with the Duke of Saxe-Meiningen and later Stanislavski) and watch an interview.

questions.q: What does a director do?
questions.a: Interprets the script, sets the concept, casts, stages and coaches actors, and unifies all production elements.

days.guide: Read three one-acts; choose one based on cast size, audience, and resources.

questions.q: Why can a homeschool group perform Trifles without a license?
questions.a: It is in the public domain (published 1916), so no royalties are required.

days.guide: Prompt book: script analysis of structure, characters, themes, given circumstances.

questions.q: What is a prompt book?
questions.a: The director's/stage manager's master script binder with analysis, blocking, cues, and notes.

days.guide: Director's concept statement linked to the Unit 7 design concept.

questions.q: How should a director's concept relate to design?
questions.a: It provides the unifying interpretation that all design elements express.

days.guide: Hold auditions (cold reads from sides) and post a cast list.

questions.q: What are 'sides'?
questions.a: Short excerpts from the script used for auditions.

weeks.assessment_key: Prompt book check. Proficient = script in binder with margins, analysis (structure, characters with objectives, themes), concept statement, cast list. 4 adds research on period/playwright and design references. 2 = analysis partial. 1 = missing.

weeks.prep: Masking tape for the floor plan, prompt book, pencils (blocking changes!). Review stage areas: from the actor's view facing the audience, stage right is the actor's right; upstage is away from the audience.
misconceptions: Confusing stage right with house right. Stage directions are from the actor's perspective facing the audience.
Blocking in ink. Blocking changes; always use pencil.
Actors turning their backs to the audience unintentionally. Use open positions and cheat out.

days.guide: Review the nine stage areas (USR, USC, USL, CR, C, CL, DSR, DSC, DSL) and notation (X = cross, DSR, etc.). Tape the floor plan.

questions.q: An actor faces the audience and moves to her right and toward the audience. Where does she go?
questions.a: Downstage right (DSR).

questions.q: Write the notation for 'Mrs. Hale crosses to the stove downstage left.'
questions.a: Mrs. H X DSL to stove (X = cross).

days.guide: Pre-block the first half in the prompt book, using composition (levels, triangles) and picturization (relationships shown in pictures).

questions.q: What is picturization?
questions.a: Arranging actors so the stage picture visually tells the story and relationships at that moment.

days.guide: Block the first half with actors; adjust for sightlines.

questions.q: What does 'cheat out' mean?
questions.a: Angle the body toward the audience while still appearing to relate to another actor.

days.guide: Block the second half; record all blocking.

questions.q: Which stage area is traditionally considered strongest?
questions.a: Down center (DSC/DC) — closest to and central for the audience.

days.guide: Stumble-through of the whole play; give notes.

questions.q: What is a stumble-through?
questions.a: The first run of the whole play after blocking, with stops and errors expected, to see the shape of the show.

weeks.assessment_key: Blocking documentation rubric. 4 – Every movement recorded in pencil with correct notation and ground-plan diagrams; composition and sightlines considered; notes from the stumble-through recorded. 3 (proficient) – Complete blocking with correct notation. 2 – Gaps in blocking. 1 – Missing.

weeks.prep: Calendar to performance week, prompt book, a line-notes form (line, error type: dropped, paraphrased, called for line).
misconceptions: Vague notes ('make it better'). Notes should be specific and actionable ('pick up the cue on page 4').
No off-book deadline. Set and enforce one.
Working the whole play every day. Prioritize scenes that need the most work.

days.guide: Build a rehearsal schedule to performance week with an off-book deadline, tech, and dress dates.

questions.q: What should a rehearsal schedule include?
questions.a: Dates/times, scenes and actors called, off-book deadline, tech rehearsal, dress rehearsals, performances.

days.guide: Lead an actor workshop on objectives for each character.

questions.q: Give an objective for Natalya in The Proposal.
questions.a: Example: 'To prove the Oxen Meadows belong to my family' / 'to win the argument with Lomov' (later, to get him back to propose).

days.guide: Work two key scenes for pacing (picking up cues) and stakes.

questions.q: What does 'pick up your cues' mean?
questions.a: Start your line promptly after the previous one ends, without dead air (unless a pause is intentional).

days.guide: Off-book run; track line errors on the notes form.

questions.q: Why give actors line notes?
questions.a: So they correct paraphrases and dropped lines, honoring the playwright's text and giving partners accurate cues.

days.guide: Practice giving specific notes; write a rehearsal report (date, attendance, what was worked, notes, problems, next steps).

questions.q: What goes in a rehearsal report?
questions.a: Date, who attended, scenes worked, notes for departments (props, costumes), issues, and next rehearsal plan.

weeks.assessment_key: Rehearsal report rubric. 4 – Complete schedule; report includes attendance, work done, specific actor notes, department notes, line-error tracking, and next steps. 3 (proficient) – Schedule and report with specific notes. 2 – Vague report. 1 – Missing.

weeks.prep: Gather set pieces, props, costumes, lights, and sound from the Unit 7 designs. Prepare a cue list for the stage manager. Plan the call time.
misconceptions: Running the whole play at tech. Cue-to-cue skips dialogue between cues to focus on technical transitions.
Fixing problems silently. Write production notes so nothing is forgotten.
Costume parades as fashion shows. Check fit, movement, quick changes, and visibility under lights.

days.guide: Build or gather set, props, costumes per the design portfolio; preset props.

questions.q: What is a preset?
questions.a: The position of props, set, and costumes before the show starts.

days.guide: Cue-to-cue: jump from cue to cue, running only the lines around each technical change.

questions.q: What is a cue-to-cue rehearsal?
questions.a: A technical rehearsal that skips from one cue to the next to set timing of lights and sound.

days.guide: Costume parade under lights; note and fix fit/color issues.

questions.q: What do you check in a costume parade?
questions.a: Fit, ability to move, period accuracy, color under the lights, quick-change feasibility.

days.guide: Tech run: full play with all technical elements.

questions.q: What is a stage manager's job during performances?
questions.a: Calling cues, managing backstage, keeping the prompt book, and running the show once the director's work is done.

days.guide: Write production notes and fix issues.

questions.q: What is a call time?
questions.a: The time cast and crew must arrive before a rehearsal or performance.

weeks.assessment_key: Tech run rubric. 4 – All cues executed on time, set/props/costumes complete and functional, production notes documented and addressed, stage manager calls cues confidently. 3 (proficient) – Most cues on time, elements complete, notes written. 2 – Several cue/prop problems. 1 – Not ready.

weeks.prep: All production elements, printed programs, a house manager (family member) for seating, video camera. Plan strike crew assignments.
misconceptions: Skipping notes after the preview audience. Audience reactions reveal timing (laughs, holds).
Breaking character when the audience laughs. Hold for laughs, then continue.
Leaving strike unplanned. Assign who returns what.

days.guide: Full dress rehearsal with timing; give notes.

questions.q: What is 'holding for a laugh'?
questions.a: Pausing in character until the laugh peaks and begins to fade before the next line.

days.guide: Final dress with a preview audience; adjust.

questions.q: Why invite a preview audience?
questions.a: To practice with real reactions and adjust timing and volume.

days.guide: Perform the one-act.

questions.q: What does the house manager do?
questions.a: Manages the audience: seating, tickets/programs, start time, and safety in the house.

days.guide: Second performance; record it.

questions.q: Why is a second performance often stronger?
questions.a: Actors are more relaxed, notes from the first performance are applied, and timing settles.

days.guide: Strike: dismantle set, return materials, clean space.

questions.q: What is strike?
questions.a: Taking down the set and clearing the performance space after the final performance.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric. 4 – Polished production: memorized, clear objectives, consistent blocking, smooth tech, strong pacing and audience connection, professional front-of-house and strike. 3 (proficient) – Memorized, audible, motivated staging, tech mostly smooth. 2 – Noticeable gaps. 1 – Incomplete.

weeks.prep: Production video, performance journal, headshot photo, résumé template, monologue video, design files, ten-minute play. Prepare the final exam.
misconceptions: Self-critiques that only praise or only criticize. Balance with evidence.
Artistic statements that are generic. Use specific experiences from this year.
Portfolio clutter. Select the best work and label it.

days.guide: Watch the production video; log strengths and growth with timestamps.

questions.q: Name one criterion for evaluating direction.
questions.a: Clarity of story/concept, staging and pictures, pacing, unity of performances and design.

days.guide: Write a 600-word self-critique using criteria.

questions.q: What does a strong self-critique include?
questions.a: A thesis, evaluation of acting, direction, and design with specific moments, and lessons for future work.

days.guide: Write an artistic statement about what theatre means to you.

questions.q: What is an artistic statement?
questions.a: A short first-person statement of an artist's values, approach, and goals.

days.guide: Assemble a digital portfolio: headshot, résumé, monologue video, design work, play.

questions.q: What goes on a theatre résumé?
questions.a: Name and contact, roles with play/company/director, training, special skills.

days.guide: Give the final exam.

questions.q: Name three production roles and their jobs.
questions.a: Director (interpretation and staging), stage manager (calls cues, runs rehearsals/shows), designer (creates set/lights/costumes/sound), house manager (audience).

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio rubric: proficient = headshot, résumé formatted correctly, monologue video, design samples, ten-minute play, artistic statement, 600-word self-critique — all labeled. Final exam key: 1) Ensemble, yes-and, CROW. 2) Stanislavski: magic if, objective/obstacle/tactic, super-objective, given circumstances. 3) Laban efforts; Viewpoints. 4) Greek: Dionysus, chorus, skene, Antigone. 5) Commedia, Noh, kabuki conventions. 6) Shakespeare: Globe, iambic pentameter. 7) Realism and fourth wall (Ibsen, Chekhov, Glaspell's Trifles). 8) Wilder's Our Town presentational; Stage Manager. 9) Hansberry, Wilson (Century Cycle), Valdez (El Teatro Campesino). 10) Stage types; ground plan; light qualities; costume plot. 11) Freytag's pyramid. 12) Director, stage manager, designers, house manager; cue-to-cue; strike. 90%+ advanced, 75–89% proficient.

WL.overview: Spanish IV meets about 50 minutes a day and is taught mostly in Spanish, following AP-style themes. Each week introduces an advanced structure or theme early, uses authentic readings, audio, art, and literature midweek, and ends with a performance assessment (essay, presentation, debate, or test). Model new structures aloud, insist on full Spanish answers, and require evidence from sources in essays and comparisons. You do not need to be fluent: rely on the answers and rubrics given here, SpanishDict or WordReference for checking forms, and native-speaker recordings. Preview literature and films flagged in the prep notes, keep an error log by category, and reteach any structure scored below 80%.

weeks.prep: Print preterite and imperfect charts (regular endings; irregulars ser/ir, tener, estar, hacer, decir, poder, poner, querer, venir, traer; i→y and stem-changing -ir verbs: pidió, durmió). Find a short authentic blog post by a young Latino writer about identity (e.g., from a teen or university blog, Remezcla, or BBC Mundo testimonials). Set up a phone or computer to record.
misconceptions: Choosing the tense from the English verb: 'was' can be fue/estuvo (completed) or era/estaba (background). Decide by aspect: completed event = preterite; ongoing background, description, habit = imperfect.
Forgetting stem changes in third-person preterite of -ir verbs: pedir → pidió/pidieron, dormir → durmió/durmieron, sentir → sintió.
Saying 'Me llamo es…' or 'Mi apodo se llama…': Me llamo… / Mi apodo es…

days.guide: Your child writes and records a 2-minute self-introduction (heritage, personality, interests, goals) after you model a short one. Listen for verb accuracy and note errors by category.

questions.q: Translate: 'My ancestors came from Michoacán and I am proud of my heritage.'
questions.a: Mis antepasados vinieron de Michoacán y estoy orgulloso/a de mi herencia.

questions.q: How would you state a goal for this year in Spanish?
questions.a: Example: Este año quiero hablar con más fluidez y leer una novela en español.

days.guide: Drill 30 preterite verbs orally, then play a story chain: each person adds a sentence in the preterite to a shared story.

questions.q: Give the preterite of: hacer (ella), poner (yo), traer (ellos), pedir (él), dormir (ellos).
questions.a: hizo, puse, trajeron, pidió, durmieron

questions.q: Translate: 'We went to the beach and had a good time.'
questions.a: Fuimos a la playa y lo pasamos bien (nos divertimos).

days.guide: Contrast English and Spanish past tenses with a timeline. Your child rewrites a childhood memory, labeling each verb B (background) or E (event).

questions.q: Explain the tenses in: 'Llovía mucho cuando salimos de casa.'
questions.a: Llovía = imperfect (ongoing background); salimos = preterite (completed event that happened within it).

days.guide: Read the blog post together; your child answers comprehension questions and identifies the author's main idea and tone.

questions.q: What strategy helps when you meet an unknown word in an authentic text?
questions.a: Use context, cognates, and word parts first; look it up only if it blocks the main idea.

days.guide: Your child writes the 200-word narrative and takes the preterite/imperfect quiz.

questions.q: Fill in: Cuando yo ___ (ser) pequeño, mi familia ___ (mudarse) a California.
questions.a: era; se mudó

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric ('Un recuerdo que me define', 200 words): 4 = clear memory with setting in the imperfect and events in the preterite, explains why it defines the writer, 10+ accurate past verbs, transitions; 3 = minor errors; 2 = tense confusion or under 150 words; 1 = incomplete. Quiz sample key: 1) Cuando tenía seis años, vivíamos en Fresno 2) Un día mi abuelo me regaló una guitarra 3) Ella dormía cuando sonó el teléfono 4) Ellos pidieron pizza 5) Yo fui al parque y vi a mi amiga 6) De niño, siempre jugaba al fútbol 7) Supe la verdad ayer (found out) 8) Hacía sol y los pájaros cantaban.

weeks.prep: Choose a TED en Español (or TEDx in Spanish) talk on bilingualism, 10–15 minutes; preview it for appropriateness and turn on Spanish subtitles for a second viewing. Optionally read a short excerpt about Gloria Anzaldúa's ideas on language and identity (Borderlands/La Frontera, 1987). Print a present-subjunctive chart with emotion triggers (me alegra que, es triste que, me molesta que, me sorprende que, ojalá que).
misconceptions: Using the indicative after emotion (*Me alegra que hablas español): Me alegra que hables español.
Using que + subjunctive when there is no change of subject: 'Me alegra hablar dos idiomas' (one subject) vs. 'Me alegra que mis hermanos hablen dos idiomas'.
Thinking Spanglish means someone cannot speak either language: code-switching is a normal, rule-governed bilingual practice; registers still matter in formal writing.

days.guide: Watch the talk once for gist; your child writes three main ideas in Spanish, then rewatches with subtitles to confirm.

questions.q: Translate: 'The speaker says that being bilingual opens doors.'
questions.a: El/la conferenciante dice que ser bilingüe abre puertas.

days.guide: Review present-subjunctive formation (yo form, drop -o, opposite vowel; DISHES irregulars) and emotion triggers. Your child writes 10 sentences.

questions.q: Translate: 'It's sad that some children lose their mother tongue.'
questions.a: Es triste que algunos niños pierdan su lengua materna.

questions.q: Give the subjunctive of ser (ellos), ir (nosotros), and saber (tú).
questions.a: sean, vayamos, sepas

days.guide: Hold a 10-minute conversation on the advantages of speaking two languages; push for follow-up questions and reasons.

questions.q: Ask: 'Do you think it is important to be bilingual? Why?'
questions.a: ¿Crees que es importante ser bilingüe? ¿Por qué?

days.guide: Your child compares attitudes toward Spanglish in the U.S. and in Latin America in a Venn diagram, using examples (parquear, lonche, textear).

questions.q: What do 'parquear' and 'lonche' mean, and where do they come from?
questions.a: To park and lunch — Spanglish adaptations of English words common in U.S. Spanish (standard: estacionar, almuerzo).

days.guide: Your child writes an opinion paragraph with five subjunctive expressions.

questions.q: Correct: 'Me sorprende que mucha gente piensa que el spanglish es malo.'
questions.a: Me sorprende que mucha gente piense que el spanglish es malo.

weeks.assessment_key: Opinion paragraph rubric (5 subjunctive expressions): 4 = clear opinion on bilingualism with 2–3 reasons and an example, five correct emotion/impersonal + subjunctive structures, transitions; 3 = 3–4 correct structures or minor errors; 2 = few subjunctives or unclear opinion; 1 = incomplete. Model sentence: 'Me alegra que cada vez más jóvenes hablen español, pero es triste que algunos pierdan su lengua materna.'

weeks.prep: Find Spanish-language biographies of Sonia Sotomayor, Frida Kahlo, and César Chávez (e.g., BBC Mundo, Biografías y Vidas, or Spanish Wikipedia checked against a second source). Chart doubt vs. certainty: dudar que, no creer que, no es cierto que, es posible que + subjunctive; creer que, estar seguro de que, es cierto que, no hay duda de que + indicative.
misconceptions: Using subjunctive after affirmative creer/pensar (*Creo que sea): Creo que es...; No creo que sea...
Treating 'quizás/tal vez' as fixed: either mood is possible; subjunctive expresses more doubt.
Forgetting that 'no dudar que' expresses certainty and takes the indicative: No dudo que ella tiene razón.

days.guide: Read the Sotomayor biography; your child summarizes her achievements in 6 Spanish sentences.

questions.q: Why is Sonia Sotomayor historically significant?
questions.a: In 2009 she became the first Hispanic justice of the U.S. Supreme Court (and the third woman), nominated by President Obama.

questions.q: Describe her background.
questions.a: Born in 1954 in the Bronx to Puerto Rican parents; she was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes as a child, lost her father at nine, and studied at Princeton and Yale Law School.

days.guide: Teach doubt vs. certainty; your child completes 20 sentences and labels the trigger.

questions.q: Choose: 'No creo que ___ (ser) fácil ser juez.' / 'Estoy seguro de que ___ (ser) difícil.'
questions.a: sea; es

questions.q: Translate: 'I doubt that he knows the answer.'
questions.a: Dudo que él sepa la respuesta.

days.guide: Your child chooses a Hispanic public figure (e.g., Frida Kahlo, César Chávez, Dolores Huerta, Ellen Ochoa, Roberto Clemente) and takes notes in Spanish from two sources.

questions.q: Translate: 'He fought for farmworkers' rights.'
questions.a: Luchó por los derechos de los trabajadores agrícolas (campesinos).

days.guide: Your child gives a 3-minute presentation with slides; ask one question afterward.

questions.q: Ask a follow-up question about the figure.
questions.a: Example: ¿Qué obstáculos tuvo que superar? / ¿Por qué lo/la admiras?

days.guide: Give the quiz on subjunctive with doubt and impersonal expressions.

questions.q: Correct: 'Es posible que mi hermano viene mañana.'
questions.a: Es posible que mi hermano venga mañana.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (3 minutes with slides): 4 = biography in accurate past tenses, 3 key achievements, why the person matters, slides with key words only, answers a question; 3 = minor errors; 2 = reads from slides or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Quiz sample key: 1) Dudo que él gane 2) Creo que él gana 3) No es cierto que ella sea abogada 4) Es cierto que ella es jueza 5) Es posible que lleguen tarde 6) No dudo que tienes razón 7) No creo que haya examen 8) Es necesario que estudiemos 9) Es obvio que hace calor 10) Es importante que todos voten.

weeks.prep: Gather three short sources on heritage-language maintenance: a Spanish article (e.g., BBC Mundo or El País on second-generation Latinos losing Spanish), a chart (e.g., Pew Research data on Spanish use by generation), and a short audio clip (podcast or radio). Print a list of 20 connectors (además, sin embargo, por lo tanto, en cambio, por un lado/por otro lado, según, en conclusión, aunque, ya que, debido a) and a revision checklist. Write the Unit 1 test (reading and listening on identity themes).
misconceptions: Using 'pero' to start every contrast: vary with sin embargo, no obstante, en cambio, aunque.
Citing sources vaguely: name them (Según la fuente 1, el artículo de BBC Mundo..., La gráfica muestra que...).
Forgetting accents on question words and past tenses (qué, cómo, habló), and on -ión words (la opinión, la conclusión).

days.guide: Your child reads the article, analyzes the chart, and listens to the audio, taking notes in Spanish on each source's main point.

questions.q: What trend do studies (e.g., Pew Research) usually show about Spanish use across generations in the U.S.?
questions.a: Spanish use declines from the immigrant generation to the second and especially the third generation, while English use rises.

days.guide: Teach 20 connectors by function (adding, contrasting, cause, result, concluding). Your child combines 10 pairs of sentences.

questions.q: Combine with a connector: 'Hablo español en casa. No lo escribo bien.'
questions.a: Hablo español en casa; sin embargo, no lo escribo bien.

questions.q: What does 'por lo tanto' mean?
questions.a: Therefore.

days.guide: Your child drafts the 300-word essay: introduction with thesis, two or three body paragraphs citing sources, counterargument, conclusion.

questions.q: Write a thesis for the prompt.
questions.a: Example: Es importante mantener la lengua de los antepasados porque conecta a los jóvenes con su familia, su cultura y más oportunidades profesionales.

days.guide: Your child revises using the checklist (agreement, accents, subjunctive triggers, connectors). Mark errors with codes rather than correcting them.

questions.q: Correct: 'Es necesario que los padres habla español con sus hijos.'
questions.a: Es necesario que los padres hablen español con sus hijos.

days.guide: Collect the final essay and give the Unit 1 listening and reading test.

questions.q: Translate: 'According to source 2, most third-generation Latinos speak mainly English.'
questions.a: Según la fuente 2, la mayoría de los latinos de tercera generación hablan principalmente inglés.

weeks.assessment_key: Persuasive essay rubric (300 words): 4 = clear thesis, three supported reasons citing all three sources, a counterargument and rebuttal, 6+ connectors, accurate subjunctive after opinion/impersonal expressions; 3 = cites two sources or minor errors; 2 = weak organization or frequent errors; 1 = incomplete. Unit 1 test: reading and listening items keyed to the chosen texts (main idea, purpose, details, vocabulary in context) plus grammar sample: 1) era/fue choices with reasons 2) Me alegra que mantengas el español 3) Dudo que sea fácil.

weeks.prep: Find a household-size chart (INE for Spain, INEGI for Mexico, U.S. Census) and a Spanish article on extended families. Make cards for 25 family terms (el/la bisabuelo/a, el/la suegro/a, el yerno, la nuera, el/la cuñado/a, el/la padrastro/madrastra, el/la hermanastro/a, el/la medio/a hermano/a, el padrino, la madrina, el compadre, la comadre, criar, convivir). Chart the present perfect (he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han + participle; irregular participles).
misconceptions: Confusing 'los padres' (parents) and 'los parientes' (relatives).
Misunderstanding compadrazgo: compadres are the parents and godparents of a child in relation to each other — a lifelong bond of mutual support, not just friends.
Making the participle agree after haber (*La familia ha cambiada): it never changes — ha cambiado.

days.guide: Teach 25 family terms; your child builds a family tree with a descriptive sentence for each person.

questions.q: What are 'el suegro' and 'la nuera'?
questions.a: Father-in-law; daughter-in-law.

questions.q: What is 'el compadrazgo'?
questions.a: The relationship between a child's parents and godparents (compadres), a lasting bond of mutual help.

days.guide: Teach the present perfect; your child writes 8 sentences about how the family has changed (Mi familia se ha mudado dos veces...).

questions.q: Translate: 'My family has lived in California for twenty years.'
questions.a: Mi familia ha vivido en California durante veinte años (Hace veinte años que mi familia vive en California).

questions.q: Give the participles of volver, morir, and abrir.
questions.a: vuelto, muerto, abierto

days.guide: Your child analyzes the household-size chart and writes 5 data statements.

questions.q: Translate: 'In Mexico households are larger than in Spain.'
questions.a: En México los hogares son más grandes que en España.

days.guide: Your child interviews a family member about traditions (in Spanish or translating) and notes answers.

questions.q: Ask: 'What traditions has our family kept?'
questions.a: ¿Qué tradiciones ha mantenido nuestra familia?

days.guide: Your child writes the comparison of family life in two cultures.

questions.q: Write a comparison sentence with a diferencia de.
questions.a: Example: A diferencia de muchas familias estadounidenses, en muchas familias mexicanas los abuelos viven con sus hijos y nietos.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison writing rubric (family life in two cultures, ~250 words): 4 = 3 specific points of comparison (household size, roles, traditions such as compadrazgo or Sunday meals) supported by data, comparison structures (al igual que, a diferencia de, mientras que, más/menos... que), present perfect used correctly, no stereotypes; 3 = minor errors; 2 = general or few comparisons; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find short videos on Día de Muertos (Mexico, November 1–2) and Las Fallas (Valencia, March 15–19). Gather poster paper or ofrenda materials (photos, candles, paper for papel picado, optional marigolds). Chart adjective clauses: known antecedent → indicative (Tengo una amiga que baila); unknown or nonexistent → subjunctive (Busco a alguien que baile; No hay nadie que sepa).
misconceptions: Using the indicative for a hypothetical antecedent (*Busco una fiesta que tiene música en vivo): Busco una fiesta que tenga música en vivo.
Using personal 'a' with unknown people: it is usually dropped with an indefinite person (Busco un guía que hable inglés), but kept with alguien/nadie (No conozco a nadie que...).
Calling Día de Muertos a sad or scary holiday: it is a joyful remembrance welcoming the spirits of loved ones.

days.guide: Watch the videos; your child takes notes on when, where, what people do, and why.

questions.q: What are 'las fallas' and what happens to them?
questions.a: Huge papier-mâché and wood sculptures (often satirical) built in Valencia's streets; they are burned on the night of March 19 (la Cremà), the feast of San José.

questions.q: Why do families build ofrendas for Día de Muertos?
questions.a: To welcome and honor the spirits of deceased loved ones, who are believed to return to visit; families place photos, favorite foods, candles, and marigolds.

days.guide: Teach adjective clauses with the subjunctive; your child writes 10 sentences (Busco una fiesta que tenga..., No hay nadie que...).

questions.q: Choose: 'Necesito un disfraz que ___ (ser) barato.'
questions.a: sea

questions.q: Choose: 'Tengo un amigo que ___ (saber) bailar salsa.'
questions.a: sabe (known person → indicative)

days.guide: Your child creates a practices–products–perspectives chart for one celebration.

questions.q: Give one product and its perspective for Día de Muertos.
questions.a: Example: el pan de muerto (product) — it is an offering of food to share with the returning spirits (perspective: death is part of life and loved ones stay connected).

days.guide: Your child builds an ofrenda or poster with written explanations of each element.

questions.q: Translate: 'The candles light the way for the spirits.'
questions.a: Las velas iluminan el camino de los espíritus (las almas).

days.guide: Your child presents the project for 3 minutes; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Translate: 'There is no one in my family who doesn't celebrate.'
questions.a: No hay nadie en mi familia que no celebre.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric (3 minutes): 4 = explains practices (what people do), products (objects/foods), and perspectives (beliefs/values) of the celebration, uses adjective clauses and present/past tenses accurately, clear delivery with the ofrenda or poster; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = only describes products or many errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find the Spanish-language page of a local nonprofit (food bank, library literacy program, community health center, immigrant legal aid). Chart commands: tú affirmative (él form; irregular di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven), tú negative (no + subjunctive), usted/ustedes (subjunctive), with pronoun placement.
misconceptions: Mixing tú and usted in the same text: choose one register (a volunteer guide may use usted/ustedes; a formal email always uses usted).
Placing pronouns before affirmative commands (*Me llame): Llámeme; negative: No me llame.
Forgetting the written accent when pronouns are attached: Ayúdenos, Dígame, Explíquemelo.

days.guide: Your child reads the nonprofit page and summarizes its mission, services, and how to help.

questions.q: What does 'la misión' of an organization describe?
questions.a: Its purpose — whom it serves and what it aims to do.

days.guide: Review all command forms; your child writes a 10-step volunteer instruction guide (Llegue a las nueve, Lávese las manos, No comparta datos personales...).

questions.q: Give the usted commands for llegar, traer, and ponerse los guantes.
questions.a: Llegue, Traiga, Póngase los guantes

questions.q: Give the negative tú command of decir and of ir.
questions.a: No digas; No vayas

days.guide: Role-play recruiting a volunteer: your child persuades you to join, explains tasks, and answers questions.

questions.q: Translate: 'Join our team! We need people who speak Spanish.'
questions.a: ¡Únase a nuestro equipo! Necesitamos personas que hablen español.

days.guide: Your child writes a formal email asking about volunteering.

questions.q: Write a polite request with the conditional.
questions.a: Example: ¿Podría decirme qué requisitos hay para ser voluntario?

days.guide: Give the quiz on commands and community vocabulary.

questions.q: Correct: 'Señora, no me llama después de las nueve, por favor.'
questions.a: Señora, no me llame después de las nueve, por favor.

weeks.assessment_key: Formal email rubric: 4 = proper greeting (Estimado/a señor/a...:), purpose stated, 2–3 polite questions with the conditional (¿Podría...?, Me gustaría saber...), usted throughout, closing (Atentamente / Quedo a la espera de su respuesta); 3 = minor errors; 2 = register mixed; 1 = incomplete. Quiz sample key: 1) hacer — haz / no hagas / haga (Ud.) 2) ir — ve / no vayas / vaya 3) decir — di / no digas / diga 4) ser — sé / no seas / sea 5) donar (Uds.) — donen 6) 'Help us' (Ud.) — Ayúdenos 7) el voluntariado = volunteering; la ONG = nonprofit; donar = to donate; colaborar = to collaborate.

weeks.prep: Write timed prompts for simulated conversations (5 turns, 20 seconds to respond each) and a cultural comparison prompt (e.g., ¿Cómo participan los jóvenes en su comunidad en tu país y en un país hispanohablante?). Write the Unit 2 test (family, celebrations, community vocabulary; present perfect, adjective-clause subjunctive, commands; a reading, a listening, and a short writing).
misconceptions: Pausing silently when stuck: use fillers (Bueno..., Pues..., A ver..., Es una buena pregunta...) and circumlocution.
Giving a cultural comparison about only one culture: a comparison must address both your community and a Spanish-speaking one, with specific examples.

days.guide: Your child plans a 2-minute cultural comparison on community traditions with an outline (intro, 2 similarities/differences, conclusion).

questions.q: Give an opening sentence for a cultural comparison.
questions.a: Example: Hoy voy a comparar cómo se celebra la comunidad en mi ciudad y en Oaxaca, México.

days.guide: Practice simulated conversations: you read each prompt, and your child answers within 20 seconds.

questions.q: Respond in 20 seconds: '¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana pasado para ayudar a alguien?'
questions.a: Example: Pues, el sábado ayudé a mi vecina a llevar las compras y luego cuidé a mi hermanito.

days.guide: Your child records the cultural comparison, then listens back and lists two improvements.

questions.q: Name two phrases that signal comparison.
questions.a: Al igual que..., A diferencia de..., Mientras que..., Tanto en... como en...

days.guide: Review Unit 2 vocabulary and grammar with a mixed practice set.

questions.q: Translate: 'My parents have always told me that family comes first.'
questions.a: Mis padres siempre me han dicho que la familia es lo primero.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: Fill in: No hay ninguna fiesta que ___ (ser) tan grande como Las Fallas.
questions.a: sea

weeks.assessment_key: Cultural comparison rubric (2 minutes, AP-style): 4 = clear comparison of both cultures with specific examples, organized (intro, similarities, differences, conclusion), comparison phrases (al igual que, a diferencia de, mientras que), mostly accurate varied grammar; 3 = one culture less developed or some errors; 2 = mostly description of one culture; 1 = off topic. Unit 2 test sample grammar key: 1) Hemos celebrado... 2) Busco un voluntario que hable español 3) Conozco a una mujer que habla tres idiomas 4) No le digas / Dígale 5) vocabulary: criar = to raise; convivir = to live together; la ofrenda = altar offering.

weeks.prep: Find a Spanish-language infographic on social media use in Latin America (e.g., from Statista en español, We Are Social/Hootsuite Digital reports, or BBC Mundo). Prepare a screen-time survey and a future-tense chart (endings -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án; irregular stems tendr-, saldr-, pondr-, vendr-, podr-, sabr-, querr-, habr-, har-, dir-).
misconceptions: Using English word order and false friends: 'la aplicación' (app), not 'el app' in formal writing; 'realizar' = to carry out, not to realize (darse cuenta).
Regularizing future stems (*tenerá, *salirá, *hacerá): tendrá, saldrá, hará.
Forgetting that the future can express probability: ¿Dónde estará mi celular? = I wonder where my phone is.

days.guide: Teach 25 technology terms (la pantalla, el algoritmo, la privacidad, descargar, compartir, el dispositivo); your child surveys family on screen time.

questions.q: Translate: 'The algorithm decides what videos I see.'
questions.a: El algoritmo decide qué videos veo.

questions.q: What does 'la privacidad' mean?
questions.a: Privacy.

days.guide: Teach the future; your child writes predictions about technology in 2050.

questions.q: Translate: 'In 2050 we will have cars that drive themselves.'
questions.a: En 2050 tendremos coches (carros) que se conducen (se manejan) solos.

questions.q: Give the future of hacer (nosotros), decir (ellos), and poder (yo).
questions.a: haremos, dirán, podré

days.guide: Your child analyzes the infographic and writes 5 data statements (La mayoría de..., El X por ciento de...).

questions.q: Translate: 'Sixty percent of young people use social networks every day.'
questions.a: El sesenta por ciento de los jóvenes usa (usan) las redes sociales todos los días.

days.guide: Debate whether social media helps or harms teens; each side gives 3 arguments and a rebuttal.

questions.q: Give a rebuttal phrase in Spanish.
questions.a: Example: Entiendo tu punto, pero no creo que sea verdad porque...

days.guide: Your child writes predictions with 10 future verbs.

questions.q: Correct: 'En el futuro, los robots hacerán la tarea.'
questions.a: En el futuro, los robots harán la tarea.

weeks.assessment_key: Writing rubric (predictions with 10 future verbs): 4 = 10+ correct future verbs including 4 irregulars, specific predictions about technology in 2050 with reasons, varied vocabulary; 3 = 1–2 errors; 2 = several errors or fewer verbs; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find Spanish articles on Severo Ochoa, Ellen Ochoa, and Guillermo González Camarena (e.g., Biografías y Vidas, NASA en español, Mexican government or museum pages). Chart the conditional (infinitive + -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían; same irregular stems as the future). Prepare infographic paper or a template.
misconceptions: Mixing up the two Ochoas: Severo Ochoa was a Spanish biochemist (Nobel Prize, 1959); Ellen Ochoa is a Mexican-American engineer and astronaut — they are not related.
Regularizing conditional stems (*tenería, *podería): tendría, podría.
Using the conditional for past habits: 'When I was a child I would read' = De niño leía (imperfect).

days.guide: Read about the three scientists; your child fills a chart: nationality, field, discovery or invention, impact.

questions.q: What is Severo Ochoa known for?
questions.a: Spanish-American biochemist who shared the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (with Arthur Kornberg) for work on the synthesis of RNA.

questions.q: What did Guillermo González Camarena invent?
questions.a: An early color television system (patented in the 1940s), making him a pioneer of color TV in Mexico.

questions.q: Who is Ellen Ochoa?
questions.a: The first Hispanic woman to go to space (1993, space shuttle Discovery) and later director of NASA's Johnson Space Center.

days.guide: Teach the conditional; your child writes 8 sentences about what they would invent and why.

questions.q: Translate: 'I would invent a machine that would clean the ocean.'
questions.a: Inventaría una máquina que limpiaría el océano.

questions.q: Give the conditional yo of hacer, saber, and querer.
questions.a: haría, sabría, querría

days.guide: Your child researches one scientist further and creates an infographic in Spanish.

questions.q: Translate: 'She investigated how to improve optical systems.'
questions.a: Ella investigó cómo mejorar los sistemas ópticos.

days.guide: Your child presents the infographic for 2 minutes and answers a question.

questions.q: Ask a follow-up question in Spanish.
questions.a: Example: ¿Qué problemas tuvo que superar? / ¿Cómo cambió su invento la vida diaria?

days.guide: Give the conditional quiz.

questions.q: Correct: 'Yo me gustaría trabajar en la NASA.'
questions.a: Me gustaría trabajar en la NASA.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz sample key: 1) inventar/yo — inventaría 2) tener/tú — tendrías 3) poder/ella — podría 4) hacer/nosotros — haríamos 5) decir/ellos — dirían 6) salir/yo — saldría 7) venir/ustedes — vendrían 8) haber — habría 9) 'I would like to be a scientist' — Me gustaría ser científico/a 10) 'What would you invent?' — ¿Qué inventarías? Infographic presentation: 4 = accurate facts (birth, field, key discovery/invention, impact), Spanish captions, 2-minute clear explanation; 3 = minor errors; 2 = thin; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find a BBC Mundo (or similar) article on artificial intelligence in schools. Chart the imperfect subjunctive: ellos preterite minus -ron + -ra, -ras, -ra, -'ramos, -rais, -ran (hablaron → hablara; tuvieron → tuviera; fueron → fuera; pidieron → pidiera). Chart sequence of tenses: present/future/command main verb → present subjunctive; preterite/imperfect/conditional main verb → imperfect subjunctive.
misconceptions: Building the imperfect subjunctive from the infinitive (*tenera, *hacera): it comes from the preterite ellos stem — tuviera, hiciera.
Keeping the present subjunctive after a past trigger (*Quería que vengas): Quería que vinieras.
Forgetting the accent on nosotros forms: habláramos, tuviéramos.

days.guide: Read the article; your child lists three benefits and three risks of AI in schools in Spanish.

questions.q: Give one benefit and one risk of AI in schools.
questions.a: Example: Beneficio: puede ofrecer tutoría personalizada. Riesgo: los estudiantes pueden copiar sin aprender, o la IA puede dar información falsa.

days.guide: Teach formation from the ellos preterite; your child conjugates 20 verbs.

questions.q: Give the imperfect subjunctive yo form of ir, hacer, and estar.
questions.a: fuera, hiciera, estuviera

questions.q: Give the nosotros form of poder.
questions.a: pudiéramos

days.guide: Your child transforms 15 sentences from present to past and explains the rule in English.

questions.q: Transform: 'Mis padres quieren que yo use la IA con cuidado.'
questions.a: Mis padres querían que yo usara la IA con cuidado.

questions.q: State the rule in English.
questions.a: When the main verb is in a past tense (or conditional), the subordinate subjunctive verb shifts to the imperfect subjunctive.

days.guide: Hold a 10-minute discussion: ¿Debería la IA tomar decisiones médicas? Your child must use Era necesario que... and Me preocupaba que...

questions.q: Translate: 'I was worried that doctors would trust the machine too much.'
questions.a: Me preocupaba que los médicos confiaran demasiado en la máquina.

days.guide: Give the imperfect subjunctive quiz.

questions.q: Correct: 'El profesor nos pidió que no usemos la IA en el examen.'
questions.a: El profesor nos pidió que no usáramos la IA en el examen.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz sample key: 1) hablar/yo — hablara 2) comer/tú — comieras 3) tener/él — tuviera 4) ser/nosotros — fuéramos 5) decir/ellos — dijeran 6) poder/ustedes — pudieran 7) pedir/yo — pidiera 8) Quiero que estudies → Quería que estudiaras 9) Es necesario que la IA sea segura → Era necesario que la IA fuera segura 10) Me preocupa que reemplace a los maestros → Me preocupaba que reemplazara a los maestros.

weeks.prep: Gather three sources on teens and smartphones: a Spanish article (e.g., on Spain's or Mexico's school phone restrictions), a graph on teen phone use, and a podcast or radio segment (2–3 minutes). Print an argumentative-essay outline and checklist. Write the Unit 3 test (technology, science, AI vocabulary; future, conditional, imperfect subjunctive; reading and listening).
misconceptions: Writing only one side: an argumentative essay acknowledges a counterargument and refutes it (Aunque algunos dicen que..., sin embargo...).
Copying sentences from sources: paraphrase and cite (Según la fuente 1...).
Using the indicative after 'es importante que' or 'no creo que' in arguments.

days.guide: Your child reads the article, interprets the graph, and listens to the podcast, taking notes in Spanish on each source's claim and evidence.

questions.q: What three things should notes on each source include?
questions.a: The source's main claim, its key evidence (data/examples), and its point of view or purpose.

days.guide: Your child outlines the essay: thesis, three reasons with sources, counterargument and refutation, conclusion.

questions.q: Write a thesis for '¿Deben prohibirse los teléfonos celulares en las escuelas?'
questions.a: Example: Los teléfonos celulares deben prohibirse durante las clases porque distraen a los estudiantes, afectan su rendimiento y aumentan el acoso escolar.

days.guide: Your child writes the 350-word essay citing all three sources.

questions.q: Write a sentence citing the graph.
questions.a: Example: Según la gráfica (fuente 2), el 70 por ciento de los adolescentes usa el celular más de tres horas al día.

days.guide: Your child revises for tense accuracy, accents, and transitions, then reads it aloud and explains it in English.

questions.q: Write a counterargument sentence with refutation.
questions.a: Example: Aunque algunos dicen que el celular es útil en emergencias, las escuelas ya tienen teléfonos para comunicarse con las familias.

days.guide: Collect the essay and give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: Fill in: Era importante que los estudiantes ___ (prestar) atención en clase.
questions.a: prestaran

weeks.assessment_key: Argumentative essay rubric (350 words): 4 = clear thesis, three supporting points citing all three sources, counterargument and refutation, logical organization with connectors, accurate grammar including subjunctive; 3 = cites two sources or minor errors; 2 = weak argument or frequent errors; 1 = incomplete. Unit 3 test: interpretive items keyed to chosen texts; grammar sample: 1) habrá, tendremos 2) Me gustaría que... / Si pudiera... 3) Quería que apagaras el celular 4) vocabulary: la tesis, la evidencia, refutar.

weeks.prep: Open the Museo del Prado online collection (Las Meninas, 1656; El 3 de mayo de 1808, painted 1814) and the Museo Reina Sofía site (Guernica, 1937). Chart the passive voice: ser + participle (agreeing) + por (El cuadro fue pintado por Velázquez) and passive se (Se pintó en 1656; Se pintaron muchos retratos). Preview: Goya's and Picasso's paintings show executions and wartime death.
misconceptions: Forgetting participle agreement in the passive with ser: the participle agrees with the subject — La obra fue pintada por Goya; Los murales fueron pintados por Rivera.
Making passive se singular with a plural subject (*Se vende libros): Se venden libros.
Thinking Guernica shows a battle between soldiers: it depicts the 1937 bombing of civilians in a Basque town.

days.guide: Explore Las Meninas; your child describes it in 8 sentences with hay, está/están, and se ve/se ven.

questions.q: Who appears in Las Meninas?
questions.a: The Infanta Margarita Teresa with her maids of honor (meninas), a dwarf and a dog, Velázquez himself at a canvas, and King Philip IV and Queen Mariana reflected in the mirror at the back.

questions.q: Translate: 'In the mirror one sees the king and queen.'
questions.a: En el espejo se ven los reyes.

days.guide: Teach the passive with ser and the passive se; your child rewrites 15 active sentences.

questions.q: Rewrite in the passive: 'Los romanos construyeron el acueducto de Segovia.'
questions.a: El acueducto de Segovia fue construido por los romanos.

questions.q: Rewrite with passive se: 'Venden entradas en línea.'
questions.a: Se venden entradas en línea.

days.guide: Analyze El 3 de mayo de 1808; your child writes a paragraph on how Goya conveys violence.

questions.q: What historical event does El 3 de mayo de 1808 show?
questions.a: French soldiers executing Spanish civilians in Madrid after the uprising of May 2, 1808, against Napoleon's occupation.

questions.q: How does Goya create sympathy for the victims?
questions.a: The central man in a white shirt is lit by a lantern with arms raised like Christ on the cross, while the soldiers are faceless, lined up like a machine; dead bodies lie in blood in the foreground.

days.guide: Read about the bombing of Guernica; discuss Picasso's symbols in Spanish (el toro, el caballo herido, la madre con el hijo muerto, la bombilla/el ojo, la espada rota).

questions.q: When and why was Guernica bombed?
questions.a: April 26, 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, by German (and Italian) aircraft supporting Franco; many civilians died.

questions.q: Give a possible interpretation of the screaming mother holding her dead child.
questions.a: She represents the suffering of innocent civilians, recalling a Pietà image of grief.

days.guide: Your child writes a 200-word comparison of two paintings; give the passive voice quiz.

questions.q: Translate: 'Guernica was painted in 1937 and is exhibited in Madrid.'
questions.a: Guernica fue pintado en 1937 y se exhibe (está expuesto) en Madrid.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph rubric (200 words, two paintings): 4 = describes both with hay/se ve/está, compares subject, color, and message, includes historical context, 3+ correct passive constructions; 3 = minor errors; 2 = describes only one well; 1 = incomplete. Passive quiz sample key: 1) Velázquez pintó el cuadro Las Meninas → El cuadro Las Meninas fue pintado por Velázquez 2) Goya pintó El 3 de mayo en 1814 → El 3 de mayo fue pintado por Goya en 1814 3) Picasso pintó Guernica en 1937 → Guernica fue pintado por Picasso en 1937 4) Se construyó el museo en 1819 (Prado) 5) Se venden carteles en la tienda 6) Se pintaron murales.

weeks.prep: Gather images of Diego Rivera murals (Detroit Industry, 1932–33, Detroit Institute of Arts; Pan American Unity, 1940, City College of San Francisco), works by Orozco and Siqueiros, Frida Kahlo's Las dos Fridas (1939), and California murals (Mission District's Balmy Alley and the Women's Building; Judy Baca's Great Wall of Los Angeles, which is in the San Fernando Valley, and East LA murals such as those at Estrada Courts). Chart relative pronouns: que, quien(es) (people, after prepositions or commas), lo que (idea/what), el cual/la cual/los cuales/las cuales (after longer prepositions or for clarity).
misconceptions: Using 'quien' as a general 'who' without a preposition or comma (*El pintor quien...): El pintor que pintó el mural...; El pintor con quien hablé...
Using 'que' for 'what' at the start of a statement (*Que me gusta es...): Lo que me gusta es...
Assuming muralism was only decoration: post-Revolution murals were political and educational, celebrating Indigenous history and workers.

days.guide: Study los tres grandes (Rivera, Orozco, Siqueiros) and the purpose of muralism after the Mexican Revolution.

questions.q: Why did the Mexican government sponsor murals in the 1920s?
questions.a: After the Revolution (1910–1920), the government (led in education by José Vasconcelos) used public murals to teach history, build national identity, and honor Indigenous people and workers, reaching people who could not read.

questions.q: Name los tres grandes.
questions.a: Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros.

days.guide: Teach relative pronouns; your child writes 20 sentences describing murals.

questions.q: Fill in: 'El muralista con ___ hablamos vive en Oakland.'
questions.a: quien

questions.q: Fill in: '___ más me impresiona es el color.'
questions.a: Lo que

days.guide: Analyze Las dos Fridas; discuss how Kahlo represents identity.

questions.q: Describe Las dos Fridas.
questions.a: Two Fridas sit holding hands: one in a white European-style dress, one in a Tehuana (Mexican) dress; their exposed hearts are connected by a vein; the European Frida holds surgical scissors with blood dripping, and the Mexican Frida holds a small portrait of Diego.

questions.q: What might the painting express?
questions.a: Her dual European and Mexican heritage and the pain of her divorce from Diego Rivera (1939).

days.guide: Explore California murals online; your child describes one with relative pronouns.

questions.q: What is the Great Wall of Los Angeles?
questions.a: A half-mile-long mural directed by Judy Baca, painted with youth from 1976 onward in the Tujunga Wash, showing California history from the perspective of people of color and women.

days.guide: Your child designs a mural (sketch) and writes a 150-word explanation.

questions.q: Translate: 'The mural, which shows my neighborhood, is what I am proudest of.'
questions.a: El mural, el cual (que) muestra mi barrio, es lo que más me enorgullece.

weeks.assessment_key: Mural design rubric (sketch + 150 words): 4 = clear theme tied to community or identity, explains symbols and colors, 4+ correct relative pronouns, purpose stated, accurate grammar; 3 = minor errors; 2 = vague explanation; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Build a playlist: flamenco (Spain), tango (Argentina/Uruguay), cumbia (Colombia), son cubano (Cuba), and salsa (New York with Cuban and Puerto Rican roots). Preview song lyrics: 'Pedro Navaja' (Rubén Blades, 1978) narrates a street crime in which two people are killed — preview for maturity; 'La camisa negra' (Juanes, 2005) is about heartbreak. Chart adverbial conjunctions that always take subjunctive: para que, antes de que, a menos que, con tal de que, sin que, en caso de que.
misconceptions: Using the indicative after para que or antes de que (*para que aprendes): para que aprendas.
Using que + subjunctive with the same subject: 'Practico para bailar mejor' (same subject) vs. 'Practico para que mi hermana baile mejor'.
Thinking salsa was invented in Cuba: it developed in New York in the 1960s–70s from Cuban son and Puerto Rican music.

days.guide: Listen to five genres; your child maps each to its country and cultural roots.

questions.q: Where does flamenco come from and what influences shaped it?
questions.a: Andalusia, southern Spain; Roma (gitano) culture with Moorish, Jewish, and Castilian influences.

questions.q: What are the roots of son cubano?
questions.a: Spanish guitar traditions (the tres) and song forms combined with African rhythms and percussion (bongó, clave, maracas).

days.guide: Teach the adverbial conjunctions; your child writes 10 sentences about music and dance.

questions.q: Translate: 'I'll play the song so that you can dance.'
questions.a: Pondré la canción para que puedas bailar.

questions.q: Translate: 'Let's practice before the party starts.'
questions.a: Practiquemos antes de que empiece la fiesta.

days.guide: Analyze song lyrics for theme and figurative language.

questions.q: In 'La camisa negra', what does the black shirt symbolize?
questions.a: Mourning — the singer's heartbreak over a lost love (his soul is 'black' with sorrow).

questions.q: What story does 'Pedro Navaja' tell?
questions.a: A street hustler with a knife attacks a woman in the barrio; she shoots him as he stabs her, both die, and a drunk passerby takes their things — the refrain says life is full of surprises.

days.guide: Learn the basic cumbia or salsa step from a video; your child narrates the process with commands or se.

questions.q: Translate: 'Step back with the right foot and then return.'
questions.a: Da un paso atrás con el pie derecho y luego vuelve.

days.guide: Your child records a 2-minute presentation comparing a Hispanic genre with a U.S. genre.

questions.q: Write a comparison sentence.
questions.a: Example: Al igual que el jazz, la salsa nació en comunidades urbanas y mezcla raíces africanas y europeas.

weeks.assessment_key: Recorded presentation rubric (2 minutes, Hispanic vs. U.S. genre): 4 = compares origins, instruments, rhythm, and cultural role of both genres with examples, uses comparison phrases and at least two adverbial-clause subjunctives, clear pronunciation; 3 = minor errors; 2 = little comparison; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Open UNESCO World Heritage pages (whc.unesco.org/es) for the Alhambra (Granada, Spain), Machu Picchu (Peru), and Chichén Itzá (Mexico). Find a Spanish reading on the California missions (21 missions, 1769–1823). Chart the pluperfect: había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían + participle. Preview: mission history includes forced labor and disease among Indigenous Californians.
misconceptions: Using the preterite for the earlier of two past actions: Cuando llegaron los españoles, los incas ya habían construido Machu Picchu.
Presenting the missions only as romantic history: they also brought forced labor, harsh punishment, loss of land and culture, and disease that devastated Indigenous populations.
Calling the Alhambra a church: it is a palace and fortress complex built mainly by the Nasrid dynasty (13th–14th centuries).

days.guide: Explore the three UNESCO pages; your child records five facts about each.

questions.q: Who built Machu Picchu and when?
questions.a: The Inca, in the mid-1400s (associated with the ruler Pachacuti), high in the Andes of Peru.

questions.q: What is El Castillo at Chichén Itzá known for?
questions.a: The pyramid of Kukulcán; at the equinoxes the shadows on its stairway look like a serpent descending.

days.guide: Teach the pluperfect; your child narrates what had happened before the Spanish arrived.

questions.q: Translate: 'The Maya had developed a calendar and writing system.'
questions.a: Los mayas habían desarrollado un calendario y un sistema de escritura.

questions.q: Translate: 'When Pizarro arrived, the Inca had already fought a civil war.'
questions.a: Cuando llegó Pizarro, los incas ya habían luchado (tenido) una guerra civil.

days.guide: Read about the California missions; discuss their complex legacy in Spanish.

questions.q: Who founded the first missions, and when did the system begin?
questions.a: Franciscan friars led by Junípero Serra, beginning with San Diego de Alcalá in 1769.

questions.q: Give one negative effect of the missions on Indigenous peoples.
questions.a: Forced labor and confinement, loss of land and culture, and epidemics that caused a steep population decline.

days.guide: Your child writes and records a 2-minute virtual tour of one site.

questions.q: Write a tour-guide sentence with the passive.
questions.a: Example: Este palacio fue construido por los nazaríes en el siglo XIV.

days.guide: Give the pluperfect and Unit 4 vocabulary quiz.

questions.q: Fill in: Cuando los turistas llegaron, la tienda ya ___ (cerrar).
questions.a: había cerrado

weeks.assessment_key: Virtual tour rubric (2 minutes): 4 = 6+ accurate facts, location and history, pluperfect and passive used correctly, engaging guide phrases (Aquí pueden ver..., Fíjense en...); 3 = minor errors; 2 = few facts or many errors; 1 = incomplete. Quiz sample key: 1) Cuando llegó Colón, los mayas ya habían abandonado muchas ciudades 2) había construido / habíamos visto / habían dicho 3) la mezquita = mosque; las ruinas = ruins; el patrimonio = heritage; la catedral = cathedral 4) Machu Picchu was built by the Inca in the 15th century 5) The first California mission was San Diego de Alcalá (1769).

weeks.prep: Find three Spanish-language ads (magazine or online) and an article on social media filters and teen self-esteem. Chart the future perfect (habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habréis, habrán + participle) and conditional perfect (habría, habrías, habría, habríamos, habríais, habrían + participle). Preview content on body image and be ready for a sensitive conversation.
misconceptions: Confusing 'habré' (future perfect: will have) and 'habría' (conditional perfect: would have).
Using the conditional perfect in the si clause (*Si habría sabido): Si hubiera sabido, habría... (pluperfect subjunctive in the si clause).
Treating beauty standards as universal: they vary by culture and era and are shaped by media and advertising.

days.guide: Your child analyzes three ads: the beauty ideal shown, the target audience, and persuasive techniques.

questions.q: Name two persuasive techniques in ads.
questions.a: Emotional appeal, celebrity endorsement, before/after images, statistics, slogans, urgency.

days.guide: Read the article; your child summarizes the author's argument and evidence in 6 sentences.

questions.q: Translate: 'The author argues that filters create unrealistic expectations.'
questions.a: El autor sostiene que los filtros crean expectativas poco realistas.

days.guide: Teach the future perfect and conditional perfect; your child writes 12 sentences about how standards will have or would have changed.
